Chapter 4: How to read a training study

Draft · 4,406 words · 27 October 2026

In 2006 Chris Beedie and colleagues at Canterbury Christ Church University told six well-trained cyclists that they were taking part in a study of caffeine [1]. Each rider would do three 10-kilometre time trials, the researchers explained, after a capsule containing either no caffeine, a moderate dose or a high dose. Before each ride the rider was told which one he had been given.

Every capsule was a placebo. When the riders believed they had taken the high dose, they produced 3.1% more power than in their baseline rides. When they believed they had taken the moderate dose, 1.3% more. When they believed they had been given nothing, 1.4% less. All six reported feeling the effects of caffeine [1].

That is easily retold as “belief alone is worth 3%”. But the range of uncertainty around every result includes zero: for the 3.1%, it runs from a loss of 0.4% to a gain of 6.7%. The paper’s wording, that the effect was “likely beneficial”, comes from a statistical method that sports science later had to abandon [1].

The order of the results fits the evidence in Chapter 3 that expectation changes performance. A placebo effect on cycling performance probably exists; six riders cannot say how large it is. C

Three kinds of evidence

The first is mechanism. A study shows that a session switches on a pathway, or raises a marker, and the claim follows by reasoning: this should make you fitter because of what it does in the cell. The single-session studies of PGC-1α in Chapter 2 are mechanism evidence. So are most of the arguments for any new training idea in its first few years, because mechanism studies are quick and cheap and a training study takes months.

The second is observation. Researchers measure people as they are, without changing anything, and look for patterns: professional cyclists who do more easy riding fade less late in a race; athletes tolerate more pain than non-athletes. Observation can study people and timescales that experiments can’t, including elite riders over whole seasons. What it can’t do is separate cause from effect. Riders who are naturally durable may be the ones who can tolerate big volumes, and people who tolerate pain may be the ones who take up endurance sport.

The third is the experiment, in which the researchers decide who does what. The strongest form is the randomised controlled trial. Volunteers are allocated by chance to the training being tested or to a comparison. The two groups then differ in nothing systematic except the training, so any difference at the end can be credited to it.

Randomisation matters more than it might seem. In the Australian pain study in Chapter 3 the volunteers chose whether to join the training group or the control group, and the two groups turned out to differ in fitness before anything had happened. The Oxford trial that followed allocated people by a computer-generated list, balanced for fitness, and its result can be trusted further for that reason alone.

The evidence grades used in this book follow from this division. Grade A needs several randomised trials, or a good pooled analysis of them, pointing the same way. Grade B is consistent evidence from trials that are small or short or from a single laboratory, or from one well-designed trial. Grade C is observation, mechanism, case studies or expert opinion. Training fashions typically arrive at grade C and are talked about as though they were grade A.

Who was studied

The commonest volunteers are untrained or lightly active young men, often students, and exercise physiology knows the young male student about as well as it knows the laboratory rat. In untrained people almost any training works, and works fast: the nine men in the biopsy study in Chapter 2 raised their peak oxygen uptake by 12% in two weeks [s1]. A trained cyclist does not gain 12% from anything. So a comparison of two methods in untrained people mostly shows that both work, and a method that wins among beginners may do nothing for someone with five years of riding behind them.

Studies of trained athletes are rarer, smaller and shorter, because trained athletes are few and unwilling to hand over their season to a research protocol. Studies of professionals are almost always observational. Women are under-represented at every level, and several of the studies in this book had none.

Will Hopkins, a New Zealand sports scientist, has written a great deal about measuring performance. In a 1999 paper he put the rule in one line: results apply only to athletes like those in the study, in ability and in how they train [2].

What was compared

A training group that improves has shown very little by itself, because people who are tested twice tend to do better the second time. Hopkins and colleagues pooled 101 studies of how repeatable performance tests are. With no training in between, people improved by 1.2% from their first attempt at a test to their second, and by 0.2% between later attempts [3]. That is why good studies include a familiarisation trial that doesn’t count, and why a study with no comparison group can’t separate training from practice.

When there is a comparison group, look at what it did. Doing nothing is a weak comparison: it shows the training beats no training. The informative comparisons are between two kinds of training, and there the detail to find is what was held equal.

Two methods can be matched for total work, time spent, or neither. In Chapter 2, intervals beat steady riding for mitochondrial enzymes when the work done by each leg was matched to within a kilojoule. That comparison leaves out the advantage of easy riding: far more of it can be done. Matching time instead gives the interval group more training stress. Read the methods to find out which comparison the researchers made.

Then there is everything around the test itself. A review from the Australian Institute of Sport lists influences on a performance test that studies often fail to control or report. They include how the test was explained, how much the rider was shouted at, whether they knew how far they had to go, who was watching, whether music was playing, and whether they arrived mentally tired [s2]. Chapter 3 showed that several of these change performance by a few per cent, which is as large as the training effects most studies are looking for.

What was measured

Outcomes come at three levels. The lowest is a marker inside the body, such as an enzyme, a messenger molecule or haemoglobin mass. Above that is a physiological capacity like VO2max, the lactate threshold or efficiency, and at the top is performance: how fast or how far.

A change at one level does not guarantee a change at the next. The heat-training chapter describes trials in which haemoglobin mass rose and performance didn’t measurably follow. When a study reports only a marker, it has shown that a mechanism was engaged and nothing more.

Performance itself is measured in two ways that produce very different-looking numbers. In a time trial the rider covers a set distance, or does a set amount of work, as fast as possible. In a time to exhaustion test the rider holds a fixed power for as long as possible. The first resembles a race and the second does not: nobody wins a race by lasting longest at 300 watts.

Time to exhaustion is also much noisier. Kevin Currell and Asker Jeukendrup reviewed the reliability of performance tests. Time-to-exhaustion results vary by more than 10% from one attempt to the next in the same rider, where time-trial results vary by less than 5% [4].

And time to exhaustion exaggerates. The reason is in Chapter 1. Above critical power, the time a rider can last is the fixed reserve W′ divided by how far above critical power they are riding. Take a rider with a critical power of 250 watts and a W′ of 20 kilojoules. At 300 watts they are 50 watts over, and last 400 seconds. Raise their critical power by 4%, to 260 watts, and at the same 300 watts they are only 40 over, and last 500 seconds. A 4% gain in fitness has become a 25% gain in the test.

That arithmetic is an illustration with round numbers. It explains a result like the one in Chapter 3, where six weeks of intervals raised time to exhaustion by 148% [s3]. Nobody got 148% fitter. When a study reports that a method improved endurance by half or doubled it, check which test was used before being impressed.

How many people

Of the 22 studies in people described in Chapters 2 and 3, the median had 11 participants. Only three had more than 50. Recruiting is expensive when every participant needs weeks of supervised training and several muscle biopsies.

Imagine that one training method really is better than another, by a fixed amount. People vary, so any one trial will measure that advantage with some luck added or subtracted. With few people, the luck is large.

To see how large, I ran a simulation. Suppose the better method truly raises some measure by 3 points more than the other, and that individual results scatter around the group average with a standard deviation of 5 points. That is a modest amount of spread for a training response: in the six-week study in Chapter 2, VO2max rose by 9% on average with a standard deviation of 8 [s4]. I simulated 20,000 trials with 10 people in each group, analysed each one with the standard statistical test, and did the same for trials with 50 in each group.

With 10 in each group, the trials observed everything from a small advantage for the wrong method to more than double the true effect. Nine per cent of them pointed the wrong way. Only a quarter reached statistical significance, so three times out of four a real effect would have been reported as “no significant difference”.

To be significant with so few people, the observed difference has to be big, so the significant trials were the lucky ones: on average they reported an advantage of 5.7 points, almost twice the truth. Journals publish significant results far more readily than others, so the small trials a reader gets to see are drawn mostly from that lucky quarter.

With 50 in each group, 84% of trials reached significance, and those reported an average of 3.3.

In 2013 a group led by Katherine Button showed that studies in neuroscience were typically too small to detect the effects they were looking for. They set out what follows: real effects are missed, the effects that are found are overestimated, and results fail to repeat [5]. Everything in their argument applies to training studies of 10 people a side.

A small study that finds nothing has shown very little, because it would probably have found nothing even if the effect were real. And a small study that finds a large effect has probably overestimated it. The surprising, dramatic result from 16 volunteers is the kind most likely to shrink when someone repeats it with 60.

How big, and how sure

Most results in a training paper come from one calculation. The researchers take the difference they observed between the groups and divide it by its standard error. That is an estimate of how much the difference would vary by chance if the study were run again with different volunteers. The answer is a t-statistic: the signal measured in units of the noise. A t of 1 means the difference is no bigger than chance routinely produces; by convention a result counts once t passes about 2. With 10 people in each group, as in the simulation, the threshold is 2.1.

The noise shrinks with the square root of the number of people, so halving it takes four times the volunteers.

The t-statistic is then converted into a p-value, the number most papers report. By convention, “statistically significant” means a p-value below 0.05. The p-value answers one narrow question: if the training truly made no difference, how often would chance alone produce a difference at least as large as the one observed? Below 0.05 means less than one time in twenty.

It does not say how big the effect is, and it does not say whether the effect matters. With enough people, a difference too small for any rider to notice will be significant. With too few, a difference that would decide a race will not be.

More useful are the size of the effect in real units, such as watts, seconds or per cent, and the confidence interval around it: the range within which the true effect plausibly lies, given the data. A wide interval means the study couldn’t pin the effect down.

Currell and Jeukendrup point out that first and second place in sport are typically separated by less than 1% [4]. Hopkins calculated how many athletes a study needs to detect the smallest improvement that would change an elite athlete’s results. If each one tries both treatments, it needs somewhere between 16 and 65; if separate groups are used, between 65 and 260 [2]. Compare that with the median of 11 in the preceding chapters.

The best tests available vary by about 1 to 2% from one attempt to the next in the same person [3]. So an improvement of 1%, which would be worth having, is smaller than the noise in a single measurement, and small studies cannot see it. They can detect large effects in untrained people. They are close to blind to the small effects that matter to trained ones.

The trial of EPO on Mont Ventoux, described in the chapter on drugs, shows what reporting looks like when it is done well. It had 48 riders, randomly allocated, with neither riders nor testers knowing who had the drug, and it gave each result as a difference with its confidence interval. The reader can see which effects were pinned down and which were not [s5].

Choices made after the data are in

A researcher analysing a training study has many decisions to make: which of the dozen outcomes measured is the main one, whether to leave out the rider who fell ill, whether to compare two intervention groups separately or pool them, whether to adjust for starting fitness.

Each decision is defensible. The trouble comes when they are made after seeing the data. It is then very easy, without any dishonesty, to settle on the choices that give the more interesting result. In 2011 three psychologists showed by simulation and experiment that this flexibility pushes the rate of false positives far above the one in twenty that the p-value promises [6]. The practice is now called p-hacking.

There are signs of it in sports science. In 2020 a group in Dublin looked at 129 studies published over five months in four leading sports medicine journals and counted how many reported that their main hypothesis had been supported. The answer was 82% [7]. Researchers are not right that often. The likelier explanation is that hypotheses which fail go unpublished, or are quietly replaced by ones the data happen to support.

For about a decade many sports science papers used a home-grown statistical method called magnitude-based inference. It described results in phrases such as “likely beneficial” and “possibly harmful”, and was promoted as better suited to small studies than conventional tests. In 2018 Kristin Sainani, a statistician at Stanford, re-ran the method’s own published simulations. At the sample sizes its developers recommended, it produced false positives at two to six times the rate of standard testing [8]. Her paper ends: “Magnitude-based inference should not be used.” A reader who meets “likely beneficial” in a paper from those years should read it as “not statistically significant by ordinary standards”.

The defence against all of this is preregistration: the researchers publish their hypothesis, their main outcome and their analysis plan before collecting data, so that they cannot adjust them afterwards. It is required for clinical trials in medicine and still unusual in training research. When a study is preregistered, the paper says so, and it counts in its favour.

Without it, look for the signs. Be wary when the result appears only in a subgroup, or only after groups were pooled, or only on one of many outcomes. Be wary too when the headline measure is not the one the methods section seemed to be building towards.

When studies are repeated

Repeating published studies tests how well their findings hold up.

Psychology did this first on a large scale. In 2015 a collaboration of psychologists repeated 100 studies from three of the field’s journals, using the original materials where they could and designs with more statistical power [9]. Of the original studies, 97% had reported a significant result. Of the repeats, 36% did, and the effects they measured were half the size. The reading of those figures has been disputed, and one group of critics argued that the project’s statistics were flawed and the true rate of replication was high [s6]. The problem it pointed to is now known as the replication crisis, and other fields have since checked their own work.

Sports science did so in 2025. A project led from Technological University Dublin recruited volunteer laboratories to repeat 25 studies published between 2016 and 2021 in the field’s highest-ranked journals. Each was drawn at random from the studies a laboratory had the equipment and expertise to repeat [10]. Fourteen of the 25 repeats found a significant effect in the same direction as the original. Seven of them, 28% of the total, also found an effect of a size compatible with the original, which was the project’s test of a successful replication. In 22 of the 25 the effect was smaller the second time, and the median shrinkage was 75%.

Twenty-five studies cannot stand for a field. Many of the repeats simply doubled the original sample. The authors say that left them with less statistical power than planned, so some real effects will have been missed. And the project covered biomechanics, psychology, physiology, nutrition and injury prevention, in experiments a volunteer laboratory could fit in. A training study that runs for months is far harder to repeat, and I know of no project that has repeated a set of them.

The shrinkage is the simulation’s result appearing in real data. The simulated small trials that reached significance reported almost twice the true effect, because they were the lucky ones, and a repeat is a second draw that has not been selected for luck. When a single small study reports a striking effect, the reasonable working assumption is that the true effect is a good deal smaller than the published one. B

Individual results

Many papers plot each participant’s change and discuss who responded and who didn’t. Measurement noise can produce those apparent differences.

Greg Atkinson and Alan Batterham made the problem clear with a simulation [11]. They created an imaginary trial in which every person’s true response to a treatment was exactly the same, added ordinary day-to-day measurement variation, and plotted the results. The plot showed what looked like strong responders, weak responders and non-responders. All of the difference between individuals was noise.

Their rule is that individual differences in response can be claimed only by comparison with a control group. If the changes in the training group are no more spread out than the changes in people who did nothing, there is no evidence that anyone responded differently from anyone else. Very few studies, they note, make that comparison.

This is the statistical reason behind the caution in Chapter 2 about non-responders, and it applies to your own training too. One good or bad test result is one draw from your own day-to-day variation.

One study, up close: a trial that gets most of it right

The two-year Dallas trial in Chapter 2 shows how to apply these questions to a study [12].

What kind of evidence? A randomised experiment. A statistician allocated the volunteers in blocks, balanced for sex.

Who was studied? Sixty-one healthy, sedentary adults aged 45 to 64, chosen from 262 who were screened. The trial excluded people with high blood pressure, a body mass index of 30 or more, or a habit of regular exercise. The authors say that volunteers willing and able to take on an intensive programme may not represent everyone, and that most of them were white.

What was compared? Training against a control group that was also given something to do: yoga, balance and stretching three times a week for the same two years. Both groups wore heart-rate monitors, and each person in either group had an exercise physiologist following their progress. A control group that is simply sent home knows it is the control group. This one got the same attention as the trainers, which removes one explanation for any difference.

What was measured? The main outcome was named before the trial began: the stiffness of the left ventricle. It was worked out from a catheter in the heart while the amount of blood returning to it was lowered and then raised. That is a capacity and not a performance, but it is measured about as directly as is possible in a living person. The cardiologist who measured the heart’s volume did not know the pressures. VO2max was measured by collecting the air each person breathed out.

How many, for how long? The researchers calculated in advance that they needed 21 people in each group. They recruited 34 and 27, and 28 and 24 finished the two years. The training group completed 88% of the sessions it was set, each one recorded by a heart-rate monitor [12].

How big, and how sure? VO2max rose by 5.3 mL/kg/min in the training group, an 18% gain, with a confidence interval from 4.15 to 6.40. In the controls it changed by −0.3, with an interval from −1.3 to 0.7. The first interval is nowhere near zero and the second sits across it. The result for stiffness, the main outcome, is less emphatic: the difference between the groups had a p-value of 0.04. The gain in fitness is beyond reasonable doubt, and the change in the heart cleared the conventional bar narrowly [12].

Could expectations have produced it? Everyone knew which group they were in, because nobody can be blinded to two years of intervals. That matters little for a pressure reading from a catheter. It matters more for VO2max, which depends on a person being willing to go to their limit.

Choices after the data were in? The trial was registered, with one main outcome, and overseen by an independent monitoring board. A comparison of men and women is labelled as unplanned, and the authors say it “should be interpreted with caution”. The analysis covers the 52 who finished and not all 61 who were randomised, which can flatter a treatment if the people who drop out are the ones it didn’t suit. Six left the training group and three the control group. The paper also states that the data will not be shared with other researchers.

Has anyone repeated it? Not at this length. The authors describe it as the longest randomised trial of structured training in healthy middle-aged adults.

The programme mixed easy sessions, sessions near the threshold, four-minute intervals and strength training. The trial shows that this combination changed the heart, but cannot tell us how much each kind of training contributed.

One comparison in 61 people took two years, a staff of exercise physiologists and catheters in 52 hearts, twice. There are few training trials like it for that reason, and most of the evidence in this book is weaker.

The questions

  1. What kind of evidence is it: mechanism, observation or experiment?
  2. If an experiment, were people allocated at random?
  3. Who was studied, and are they like you?
  4. What did the comparison group do, and what was held equal?
  5. Was the outcome a marker, a capacity or a performance, and if a performance, a time trial or a time to exhaustion?
  6. How many people, for how long?
  7. How big was the effect in real units, and how wide was the range of uncertainty?
  8. Could the participants’ expectations have produced the result?
  9. Was the analysis fixed in advance, or does the result depend on a subgroup, a pooling or one outcome out of many?
  10. Has anyone repeated it?

The last question is the one that most often settles the matter. One small study is one draw. When several independent groups, using different volunteers and different protocols, find the same thing, the luck averages out, and that is what a grade A means in this book.

Most of the studies in this book are small, short and done on people fitter or less fit than you. That still leaves useful evidence. Hold the well-supported claims firmly, treat the rest as reasonable bets, and know which is which.

What survives
  • A small study with a striking result has probably overstated it. B
  • Ask who was studied, for how long, and what they were compared with.
  • Hold the well-supported claims firmly, treat the rest as reasonable bets, and know which is which.

Chapter 5: Intensity, properly defined

Draft · 4,580 words · 27 October 2026

In 2006 Stephen Seiler and Glenn Kjerland published the training records of 11 nationally competitive junior cross-country skiers in Norway. Over 32 days the skiers had logged 384 sessions, and the researchers sorted the endurance sessions into three zones by heart rate. Three-quarters fell in zone 1 and 17% in zone 3. Zone 2 got 8%. The paper’s summary ended by remarking that elite endurance athletes seem to “train surprisingly little” at that middle intensity [1].

In 2025 a panel of 14 sport scientists and coaches published a paper called What is “Zone 2 training”? It set out how to do Zone 2 sessions and what to expect from them. Many people now say this kind of training should fill a large share of an endurance athlete’s week [2]. Seiler was one of the authors.

He had not changed his mind. The zone 2 of the 2006 paper lies between two physiological thresholds. The Zone 2 of the 2025 paper lies below the lower of them. A coach who tells you to stay out of zone 2 and a podcast that tells you to live in Zone 2 may be describing the same week of training.

Most arguments about training intensity have this problem somewhere in them. “Threshold” has at least two meanings and dozens of ways of being measured. “Easy” is often set as a percentage of a maximum heart rate that was itself guessed from the rider’s age. Before Part II can ask what easy riding does, the words need fixing to something in the body.

The three intensity domains

Exercise intensity divides into three domains: moderate below the first threshold, heavy between the first threshold and critical power, and severe above critical power. A 2017 experiment at the University of Exeter shows how differently the body behaves in each [3].

Eleven recreationally active men rode to exhaustion at a constant power in each domain, on separate days, with muscle biopsies taken from most of them. In the moderate domain, at 20 W below their first threshold (113 W on average), they lasted three and a half hours. Their blood lactate barely moved from its starting level. When they stopped, the glycogen in their thigh muscle was down by 83%. The likeliest reason they stopped is that they had run out of fuel [3].

In the heavy domain, at an average of 231 W, they lasted 43 minutes, and the individual times ran from 20 minutes to 67. Twice the power had cut the time by four-fifths [3].

In the severe domain they did several rides at different powers, and lasted between 2 and 14 minutes. Every rider reached his maximum oxygen uptake on every one of those rides. The chemistry inside the muscle at the point of stopping did not differ measurably whether the ride had taken 2 minutes or 14: not its acidity, its lactate or its store of phosphocreatine. Above critical power the riders stopped at a fixed chemical limit, and how hard they were riding decided only how soon they reached it [3]. B

Earlier work found the same pattern across species and kinds of exercise [s1,s2]. The domains are well established; finding their boundaries in an individual is harder.

How it works: lactate, and why breathing changes

Muscle breaks glucose down in two stages. The first, glycolysis, is fast, needs no oxygen and ends in a molecule called pyruvate. The second takes place in the mitochondria, uses oxygen, and extracts most of the energy. When glycolysis runs faster than the mitochondria take up pyruvate, the surplus is converted to lactate. This happens all the time, at rest included. Lactate then moves out of the fibre that made it and into the blood. Other fibres, the heart and the liver take it up, and burn it or turn it back into glucose. The physiologist George Brooks, who spent a career establishing this, calls the traffic the lactate shuttle: lactate is a fuel being passed between cells, and a signalling molecule as well [s3].

The concentration in the blood is therefore a balance. It is the rate at which lactate appears minus the rate at which it is removed, and it says little about either on its own [s4]. At rest and during easy riding the two are equal and the level sits near its baseline, around 1 mmol/L in most people. At the first threshold, production begins to outrun removal. The level rises and then settles at a new, higher balance. Push further and you reach an intensity at which it can no longer settle: lactate climbs for as long as the effort lasts.

Breathing follows. Lactate leaves the muscle together with hydrogen ions, which would make the blood more acidic if nothing absorbed them. Bicarbonate in the blood absorbs them, and that reaction releases carbon dioxide. The extra carbon dioxide has to be breathed out, so above the first threshold breathing rises faster than oxygen uptake does. That is the first ventilatory threshold, and it is why holding a conversation gets harder at about the point where lactate begins to rise. At the second threshold the buffering falls behind, the blood starts to acidify, and breathing rises again, now faster even than carbon dioxide output. A laboratory with a gas mask can see both breakpoints without taking any blood.

Karlman Wasserman connected breathing to lactate in 1964, in a paper with a colleague on detecting what its title called the threshold of anaerobic metabolism in cardiac patients [s5]. His explanation was that the working muscle had run short of oxygen and switched to making energy without it. The method survived and the explanation did not. Lactate rises because glycolysis speeds up as the work gets harder, and muscle with all the oxygen it needs still produces it [4][s4]. A 2021 review of the argument, with Brooks and Poole among its authors, carries the subtitle “50+ years of controversy” [4]. The name is still in everyday use. When you see “anaerobic threshold”, read it as a threshold of some kind, and find out which.

Above the first threshold, holding a fixed power becomes progressively more costly. Below it, the oxygen cost is fixed, and heart rate and breathing level off within a few minutes. Above it, oxygen use creeps upward for many minutes. Physiologists call this the slow component of oxygen uptake. It happens because the muscle becomes less efficient as it tires, and recruits fast-twitch fibres that use more oxygen for the same work [s6].

The first threshold

It has many names: first lactate threshold (LT1), first ventilatory threshold (VT1), gas exchange threshold, aerobic threshold. They describe the same transition seen through different instruments. Where studies have used both lactate and breathing on the same riders, the two agree reasonably well. In 14 well-trained cyclists the power at the lactate threshold and at VT1 did not differ significantly. The average gap was about 14 W, though, and the correlation between the two was 0.72, which leaves room for larger gaps in individuals [s7]. In 50 trained cyclists tested in Germany, in a study this chapter returns to, VT1 came at 200 W on average and the first rise in lactate at 199 W [5].

There is more than one way to read each instrument. A 2009 review found 25 separate lactate threshold concepts in the literature and sorted them into three families: fixed concentrations, the first rise above baseline, and methods aimed at the highest steady state [s8]. The first-rise family alone includes “0.5 mmol/L above baseline”, “1.0 above baseline” and several curve-fitting methods, and they give different answers from one set of blood samples [6].

Where the first threshold sits is a personal matter. Danilo Iannetta and colleagues in Calgary tested 100 men and women and found it at anything from 45% to 74% of VO2max. By heart rate it ran from 60% to 90% of maximum, and by power from 23% to 57% of the peak reached in a ramp test [7]. Seventy per cent of maximum heart rate was in the moderate domain for some of those people and in the heavy domain for others. Their conclusion was that prescriptions based on fixed percentages of a maximum “do not adequately control the metabolic stimulus”. B

The threshold also moves. Training raises it: Chapter 1 gave the figures, from around 60% of VO2max in untrained people to 75–90% in elite athletes [s9]. And it falls during a long ride. In a study from Auckland that Chapter 9 describes in full, two hours of easy riding lowered the power at VT1 from 217 W to 196 W [s10]. A number from a fresh laboratory test describes the first hour of a ride better than the fourth.

The second threshold

The upper boundary has more names and less agreement: second lactate threshold (LT2), second ventilatory threshold (VT2), respiratory compensation point, maximal lactate steady state, onset of blood lactate accumulation, critical power, functional threshold power, and, again, anaerobic threshold.

The oldest practical version is a fixed number. In the 1970s and 1980s physiologists, most of them German, took 4 mmol/L of blood lactate as the mark of the highest sustainable intensity [8]. In 1979 Wilfried Kindermann’s group had seven national-level cross-country skiers run on a treadmill for at least 30 minutes at the speed that an earlier test had matched to 4 mmol/L. Their lactate rose to nearly that level and then stayed there for the rest of the run [s11]. A rule that is still in use rested, at the start, on seven skiers.

It didn’t hold up as a universal number. The lactate level at which a person’s steady state tops out varies widely between individuals and between sports [8]. So the definition moved from a concentration to a procedure. The maximal lactate steady state (MLSS) is found by riding for 30 minutes at a constant power, on four or five separate days at different powers. The threshold is the highest power at which blood lactate rises by less than 1 mmol/L between the tenth minute and the thirtieth.

A 2018 study from Victoria University in Melbourne shows how far the shortcuts miss [6]. Seventeen trained cyclists had their MLSS measured the long way: it averaged 264 W. They also did stepped tests with stages of four different lengths, and the researchers calculated 14 different lactate thresholds from each. The fixed 4 mmol/L rule was 14 W to 41 W too high. The same 17 riders had 56 lactate thresholds between them, depending on the method and the length of the stages, and the authors judged many of the traditional methods not valid.

MLSS has its own critics. Andrew Jones and colleagues argued in 2019 that it is bound to underestimate the true boundary [8]. If the trial powers are 30 W apart and you take the highest one that passed, you will be about 15 W low on average. A lactate meter has an error of 0.2 to 0.4 mmol/L, in a test that turns on a difference of 1.0.

Their candidate for the real boundary is critical power, which Chapter 1 described: the power the curve of your best efforts flattens towards. In the critical power model the boundary is defined by performance, and the physiology follows: just below it oxygen uptake and lactate stabilise, and just above it they climb to their maximum. A 2020 review of every common method concluded that there is some evidence for the first lactate and ventilatory thresholds as the lower boundary. For the upper one it found little evidence for anything except critical power [9]. The authors of the 2019 paper are the researchers most associated with critical power. Their opponents point out that a rider can hold their measured critical power for only 20 to 30 minutes, which is short for something described as sustainable. Jones’s group reply that a measured critical power is accurate to a few per cent at best. So a rider asked to ride at it has about an even chance of being slightly above it, where W′ sets a time limit [8].

Most cyclists meet the second threshold as functional threshold power, or FTP. The term comes from Andrew Coggan, who defined it as the highest power a rider can hold, in roughly a steady state, for about an hour. He offered a field test: ride as hard as you can for 20 minutes and take 95% of the average [10].

Reading the research: agreement on average is not agreement for you

Two studies have compared FTP with the maximal lactate steady state, and they reached opposite conclusions.

The Brazilian paper also reported a correlation of 0.91 between the two, which it called nearly perfect. The Canadian group brought ten of its riders back after seven months of training. Their MLSS had risen by 12 W and their FTP had not risen [12].

The two papers are closer than their conclusions. Beside the 1.4%, the Brazilian abstract reports a third number: the 95% limits of agreement, which were plus or minus 9.2%. Limits of agreement describe individuals. They say that for 95% of riders like these, FTP will fall within about 9% of their MLSS in either direction. For a rider whose steady state is truly at 250 W, that is an FTP anywhere from roughly 230 W to 275 W. Among the less trained riders in the group the limits were plus or minus 11.8% [11].

A correlation of 0.91 doesn’t contradict this. Correlation asks whether riders with a high MLSS also have a high FTP, and across a group that runs from modest club riders to very fit ones, they will. It would still be 0.91 if every rider’s FTP were 30 W too high.

When a paper says a cheap test is valid against an expensive one, the average difference tells you whether the cheap test is biased. The limits of agreement tell you how wrong it can be for one person, and the correlation tells you least.

Three zones, five zones, seven

The three-zone scheme puts zone 2 between the thresholds, in the heavy domain. The framework goes back at least to a 1980 paper by James Skinner and Thomas McLellan [s12]. Seiler adopted it for his studies of how athletes distribute their training, and most research on the subject has used it since [13].

Coaches wanted finer divisions. The scale used by the Norwegian Olympic federation has five zones. Its zones 1 and 2 both lie below the first threshold, zone 3 is the band between the thresholds, and zones 4 and 5 lie above the second [13]. Its Zone 2 is given as 72–82% of maximum heart rate, or a blood lactate of 1.5 to 2.5 mmol/L [5]. Most heart-rate zone systems in apps and bike computers have five zones of this general kind, and this is the Zone 2 of the podcasts.

Coggan’s power levels, widely used in power-meter software, number seven and are all set as percentages of FTP. Level 2, “endurance”, is 56–75% of FTP. Above it come “tempo”, “lactate threshold” at around FTP itself, and three more levels [10]. These zones are easy to calculate, which is why software uses them. But the first threshold appears nowhere in the calculation. The top of Level 2 is wherever 75% of your FTP happens to be. In Iannetta’s 100 volunteers the first threshold ranged from 23% to 57% of peak ramp power and the upper steady state from 44% to 71% [7]. With ranges that wide the gap between a person’s two thresholds is unlikely to be a fixed proportion. A zone system built from one anchor has to assume that it is.

When Seiler reported that elite athletes do about 80% of their training at low intensity, he was counting sessions. A session with 20 minutes of hard intervals in it counts as a hard session, though most of its minutes are easy. In 2014 his group measured how much this matters, using 570 sessions by 29 elite cross-country skiers at a training camp [14]. Counted by session, 87% were zone 1, 11% zone 2 and 2% zone 3. Counted by minutes of heart rate in each zone, the same training was 96%, 3% and 1%. Someone who trains “80/20” by sessions and someone who trains “95/5” by time may be doing the same thing.

What Zone 2 means now

The 2025 panel was convened because the term had spread without a definition. Its 14 members agreed that Zone 2 training “should preferably be performed at intensities located immediately below the first lactate or ventilatory threshold”, and that it can be done as continuous, variable or interval sessions [2]. They expected a broad range of adaptations from it, and added that these “might not be unique” to Zone 2 and could come from riding slightly harder or slightly easier. The definition is expert opinion and carries no more weight than that, but it is the nearest thing to an agreed meaning, and this book starts from it. C

The panel left one choice open, between lactate and breathing [2], and the book makes it. From here on the top of Zone 2 is the first lactate threshold. That is the last intensity before blood lactate rises 0.5 mmol/L above the rider’s own baseline, in a test with stages of at least four minutes. Lactate is what the case for Zone 2 was built on, and a rider can measure it with a handheld meter. A rise above your own baseline also carries over between people better than a fixed figure such as 2 mmol/L. The breathing threshold is its closest relative and on average falls close to it. Chapter 6 gives the reasons in full, along with the evidence that the choice is a practical one: no study shows lactate to be the better boundary of the two.

In practice the label is attached to many other things. The Canadian review that criticised the Zone 2 fashion listed the definitions it found in use: below the first lactate threshold, taken as 2.0 mmol/L; below the first ventilatory threshold; below the intensity of peak fat burning; under 45% of VO2max [s13]. It also pointed out how much the same definition varies between people. The top of Zone 2 can be 24% of VO2max in a sedentary person, which is a walk, and 80% in an endurance athlete, which may be 300 W.

One study, up close: nine markers, fifty cyclists

In 2025 Benedikt Meixner and colleagues, working from the University of Würzburg, asked what happens when you apply the common definitions of Zone 2 to the same riders [5].

They recruited 50 cyclists, 30 men and 20 women, all with more than three years of regular riding. Their average VO2peak was 54 mL/kg/min: trained amateurs [5]. Each came to the laboratory twice within a week. The first visit was a ramp test to find maximum oxygen uptake and peak power. The second was a step test, starting at 100 W and rising by 25 W every three minutes. A mask measured breathing gases, and a drop of blood was taken from the earlobe at the end of each stage. From the step test the researchers calculated the power at which each rider reached nine markers: three lactate concentrations, a rise of 0.5 mmol/L above baseline, VT1, 65% of VO2peak, peak fat burning, and 72% and 82% of maximum heart rate, the edges of the Norwegian Zone 2.

On average the markers ran from 125 W to 224 W. Three of them agreed: VT1 at 200 W, the first rise in lactate at 199 W, and 82% of maximum heart rate at 202 W. A lactate of 2.0 mmol/L came at 211 W and 2.5 mmol/L at 224 W, both above the first threshold for the average rider. Peak fat burning came far lower, at a median of 125 W, and the authors put it at roughly a quarter below VT1 as a share of peak power. On these averages, Zone 2 set by fat burning and Zone 2 set by 2 mmol/L of lactate are 86 W apart. The second is no longer below the first threshold [5].

The Norwegian scale’s two definitions disagree with each other. Its heart-rate band, 72–82% of maximum, ran from 148 W to 202 W in these riders. Its lactate band, 1.5 to 2.5 mmol/L, ran from 194 W to 224 W. The two bands share 8 W, and the lower lactate figure comes from only 41 riders. The other nine never showed a lactate below 1.5 mmol/L at any point in a test that started at 100 W, so for them the lactate version of the zone has no lower edge [5].

For individuals the picture is looser still. VT1 sat at 81% of maximum heart rate on average, with a standard deviation of 3.9 percentage points. Roughly a third of riders were therefore outside the range 77.5–85.3%. The authors note that a difference of five percentage points is about 10 beats a minute [5].

The study’s headline finding needs care. The abstract reports “substantial variability”, with coefficients of variation between riders of 6% to 29% depending on the marker. Those coefficients were calculated on raw watts and raw beats per minute. Riders differ in fitness, and in this group peak power itself varied by 19% and maximum heart rate by 5.7%. A marker that sat at an identical percentage of every rider’s maximum would still show variation of about that size. Most of the 6–29% is the spread of fitness in the sample, and it says little about whether the markers are good or bad. The stronger evidence is in the table of averages and in the agreement analysis, which the paper shows only as charts [5].

The study establishes that the common definitions of Zone 2 pick out different intensities in the same rider. Nobody did any training, so it cannot show which makes the better ceiling for an easy ride. It used one laboratory, one step protocol and riders mostly in their twenties and thirties. The authors declared no funding and no conflicts of interest. B

Power, heart rate and feel

A zone can be written in watts, in beats per minute or as a feeling, and each is a different kind of measurement. Power is what you put in. It responds instantly and takes no account of the day you are having. Heart rate is one of the body’s responses. It lags behind a change in effort, and it drifts upward over a long ride for reasons Chapter 9 explains. The domains are defined by the body’s response, so neither reading is the thing itself.

The Auckland study shows the two readings coming apart. After two hours the power at the first threshold had fallen by 21 W, and the heart rate at the threshold had risen from 142 to 151 beats per minute [s10]. Setting out at the threshold power from the fresh test, a rider would have been 21 W above the threshold by the end. A rider who held the heart rate from the fresh test would have finished further below the threshold than intended.

Perceived effort does better than its reputation. In the 2006 study the skiers also rated each session on a scale of perceived exertion of the kind Gunnar Borg introduced [s14]. Sorted by those ratings, the sessions came out within two percentage points of the heart-rate figures in every zone [1]. Over a month of training, the athletes’ own ratings and their heart rate monitors gave the same account. Only the monitors needed batteries. Chapter 6 covers the talk test, which turns the same sense into a method.

The terms as this book uses them

  • The first threshold is the first lactate threshold (LT1): the intensity at which blood lactate first rises above the rider’s own baseline, taken as a rise of 0.5 mmol/L in a test with stages of at least four minutes. Breathing first rises out of proportion to oxygen uptake at about the same point, the first ventilatory threshold (VT1). Where a study measured the threshold from breathing, the text says so.
  • The second threshold is the highest intensity at which the body can still reach a steady state. Where a study measured critical power, MLSS or FTP, the text names the measure, because they are not interchangeable.
  • Easy, or low intensity, means below the first threshold: the physiologists’ moderate domain and zone 1 of the three-zone model. Physiologists call this intensity moderate and riders call it easy, and the book uses the riders’ word.
  • Zone 2, capitalised, means the upper part of that easy range, immediately below the first threshold, as the 2025 panel defined it. When a study uses the three-zone model, its zone 2 appears here as “between the thresholds”.
  • Between the thresholds is the heavy domain. Riders call parts of it tempo, sweet spot and threshold; the book uses those words only for a session a study itself gave that name.
  • Hard, or high intensity, means above the second threshold, in the severe domain.

Check which boundary a study, coach or app means, and whether it was measured or calculated from a percentage. Several studies in Part II used percentages of a maximum. Iannetta’s figures mean that some volunteers were probably not training in the domain the paper’s title names.

What survives
  • The top of Zone 2 is the first lactate threshold, by expert agreement rather than experiment. C
  • A fixed percentage of maximum heart rate puts different people in different domains. B
  • The common definitions of Zone 2 pick out different intensities in the same rider. B

Chapter 6: Finding your zones

Draft · 5,884 words · 27 October 2026

I’m too squeamish for a home lactate test. I wish I could do one, and that’s why proxies are good for me. I set my own Zone 2 from a percentage of maximum heart rate, taken from the zones Strava suggested from my highest recorded heart rate.

Most riders have never had their threshold measured either. They ride to a heart-rate zone that a watch worked out from their age, or a power zone that an app worked out from a 20-minute test. Both are guesses at where the lactate threshold probably lies.

The top of Zone 2 is the first lactate threshold. During easy riding, lactate production and clearance balance near the rider’s baseline, around 1 mmol/L in most people [s1]. As power rises, production begins to outrun clearance and the level steps up. A lactate test finds that point. The talk test, chest-strap methods and percentages of maximum heart rate all estimate it, with different degrees of success.

Why the boundary matters

Below the first threshold, oxygen uptake, heart rate and lactate level off within a few minutes of a change in power. Above it, the oxygen cost of holding the same power creeps upward for many minutes as the muscle tires and recruits less efficient fibres [s2].

In the Exeter experiment of Chapter 5, men riding 20 W below their first threshold lasted three and a half hours, and stopped when the glycogen in their muscles had nearly run out. Between the thresholds they lasted 43 minutes [s3].

Recovery also changes across the boundary. In 2007 Stephen Seiler and colleagues had nine highly trained runners do four sessions on separate days. They ran an hour below the first threshold, two hours below it, an hour that included 30 minutes between the thresholds, and an hour of hard intervals above the second. After each session the runners lay down, and for four hours the researchers followed their heart rate variability, a marker of how far the nervous control of the heart has been disturbed. After the easy sessions it was back to normal within 5 to 10 minutes, and two hours had cost no more than one. After the session between the thresholds it took about 30 minutes, as it did after the hard intervals. The authors called the first threshold a “binary” one for recovery: what counted was which side of it the session had been on [1]. B

The study used nine runners, one marker of recovery and a boundary found from breathing. It gives a reason to pay attention to the first threshold, rather than proof of a sharp recovery boundary for every rider. The 2025 panel expected much the same adaptations a little above Zone 2 as a little below it [2]; the recovery cost is the reason to keep an easy ride below the line.

Why lactate

The 2025 panel placed Zone 2 immediately below “the first lactate or ventilatory threshold” and left the choice between the two open [2]. This book chooses lactate. The top of Zone 2 is the last intensity before blood lactate rises 0.5 mmol/L above the rider’s own baseline, in a test with stages of at least four minutes. The breathing threshold, and every other method in this chapter, is treated as a way of estimating that point.

The first reason is that lactate is what the case for Zone 2 was built on. The argument made on podcasts descends from work such as a 2018 paper by Iñigo San-Millán and George Brooks. They measured blood lactate and fat burning during exercise in professional endurance athletes, moderately active people and patients with metabolic syndrome. The professionals burned more fat and carried less lactate. Within each group, too, the two measures moved in opposite directions, with correlations stronger than −0.9. The authors proposed blood lactate as an indirect reading of how well a person’s mitochondria are working [3]. If the advice is to ride at the highest intensity that keeps lactate down, the way to know you are following it is to measure lactate.

The second is that a rider can measure it. The first ventilatory threshold needs a mask, a gas analyser and somebody to read the result, and readers differ. In 1983 four exercise physiologists, working independently, marked the threshold on the breathing data from eight people’s tests, and for a given person their answers spanned 16% on average [s4]. A lactate test needs a drop of blood and a meter.

The third is that the rule is a rise above your own baseline, not a fixed figure. The Zone 2 of the podcasts is often given as “lactate below 2 mmol/L” [s5], and a fixed figure fails in two ways. Baselines differ between people. In the 50 cyclists of Chapter 5, 2.0 mmol/L arrived at 211 W on average, 12 W beyond the first rise. Nine of the riders never recorded a value below 1.5 at any power [4]. And handheld meters tend to read lower than laboratory analysers [5][s6]. A meter that reads low reaches a fixed 2.0 later, and so sets the zone too high. A rise measured against the same meter’s own baseline survives both problems.

A 2020 review found some evidence for both lactate and breathing as measures of the lower boundary [6]. In the one study here that tested the same cyclists twice, the breathing threshold was slightly more repeatable [7]. Between the two tests it moved by a standard deviation of 13 W, against 19 W for the lactate threshold.

The two do not always coincide. In three studies of trained cyclists that measured both, the lactate threshold came out level with the breathing threshold in one, 14 W above it in another and 24 W above it in the third [4,7,8]. Nobody has run the trial that would settle it, with one group training to a ceiling set by lactate and another to a ceiling set by breathing. The choice is made on lineage and practicality. C

The rule also needs stages of several minutes, because lactate takes time to pass from muscle into blood. In a test that climbs quickly the blood lags behind the legs. When the power was raised by 25 W every minute, a rise of 0.5 mmol/L above baseline did not appear until 260 W. That was level with those riders’ maximal lactate steady state, at 255 W, so the rule found the second threshold instead of the first [7]. With stages of three to ten minutes, the same rise appeared 30 to 40 W below the maximal lactate steady state, and moved by only 10 W between the shortest stages and the longest [s7]. This book uses four.

Measuring it

A laboratory lactate test is a step test. The rider starts easy and the power goes up every few minutes. At the end of each stage a drop of blood is taken from an earlobe or a fingertip and read on an analyser, and the values are plotted against power. For the first several stages they stay close to level, and then they begin to climb. That early level is the baseline, and the first threshold is read where the curve passes 0.5 mmol/L above it, the rule used in the Würzburg and Leuven studies [4,8].

The same test can be done at home with a handheld meter, test strips and the kind of spring-loaded lancet that people with diabetes use. The meter is accurate enough, just. When three handheld meters were checked against laboratory analysers, the typical error on repeated readings of the same blood at low concentrations ran from 0.1 mmol/L for the best to 0.5 for the worst [5]. Five models tested later were generally within 0.5 [s6]. Against a rise of 0.5 that is not a comfortable margin, so a single high reading should not be believed until the next stage confirms it. The Leuven laboratory described below took a second sample whenever the first rise appeared, for the same reason [8].

Take the baseline as the average of the early stages, not the lowest reading. One stray low reading moves an average less than it moves a minimum, and with a meter’s error, stray readings happen. The papers that use the rule do not agree on this: one averaged the early stages [7], the Würzburg group’s label for its baseline points to the lowest reading of the test [4], and others do not say [8][s7]. An average is never lower than the minimum, so on some curves it places the threshold a stage later than the lowest-reading version would. Don’t start again because early readings differ by a tenth or two, or because a second stage reads lower than the first: that is within the error of the meter.

Technique matters as much as the meter. Sweat contains lactate, and a drop of blood that picks some up from the skin will read high. The skin is washed, dried and wiped before each sample, and the first drop is discarded. These are standard laboratory habits, and I have no figures for how much each one matters at home.

One test fixes the threshold to within perhaps 10 or 20 W, so do a second on another day. Even in a laboratory the answer moves. Fourteen trained cyclists did the same test twice. Their lactate threshold shifted by 2 W on average, and the differences had a standard deviation of 19 W. So for about a third of the riders, the second test put the threshold more than 19 W from the first [7]. That test sampled blood only every 50 W, which will have widened the scatter.

The test gives two numbers to ride by: the power at the threshold and the heart rate at it.

Breathing, and the talk test

The nearest relative of the lactate threshold is the first ventilatory threshold (VT1). Chapter 5 gave the link: lactate leaves the muscle with hydrogen ions, buffering them releases carbon dioxide, and breathing rises to clear it. A laboratory reads VT1 through a mask. At home the only instrument for it is speech.

The talk test is credited to a Professor Grayson, who in 1939 is said to have advised British mountaineers to climb no faster than they could speak. The paper that repeats the story gives no source for it [s8]. The modern version comes from Carl Foster’s group at the University of Wisconsin–La Crosse. During a test of rising intensity, at the end of each stage, the person recites a set passage aloud and is asked whether they can speak comfortably. “Yes” makes it a positive stage, anything uncertain makes it the equivocal stage, and “no” makes it negative.

It works because speech and hard breathing compete. To talk, you have to let air out slowly and under control, and you can’t do that while breathing hard. In 1981 two British physiologists had six people run at five steady speeds and, in the fifth minute at each speed, read a 100-word passage aloud, which took about half a minute. At every speed their ventilation while reading fell to about 55% of what it had been, and when they stopped it overshot by 14% before returning to normal within 30 seconds. The authors concluded that the demands of speech take precedence over the demands of gas exchange [s9].

A talking rider is therefore breathing about half as much as the effort calls for and making it up between sentences. Below the first threshold there is room for that. Above it the extra carbon dioxide has to be breathed out, the drive to breathe rises out of proportion to the work, and half a minute at half ventilation becomes uncomfortable. That is the likely reason comfortable speech ends near the threshold. It is an inference from the two sets of findings, and no study I have read shows the steps in order.

The uncertain stage lands near the threshold, a few beats high. Foster’s group checked the test against the ventilatory threshold in 2004. Sixteen healthy volunteers did tests of rising intensity on a treadmill and on a cycle ergometer, once with their breathing gases measured and once with the talk test. The authors concluded that the equivocal stage was “almost exactly equivalent” to the threshold on both machines, and that negative stages were consistently above it [9]. The figures in the paper’s summary are less tidy. On the bike the threshold came at 82% of peak heart rate and the equivocal stage at 87%. Neither that difference nor the smaller one on the treadmill was statistically significant. But with 16 people, a gap of five percentage points can be real and still fail to reach significance, as Chapter 4 explained. For someone with a maximum of 180, that is about 9 beats.

The test also moves when the threshold moves, which is the stronger kind of evidence. The same group lowered people’s thresholds by having them give blood and raised them with training, and both times the last positive stage of the talk test shifted to match [10]. When the intensity was a little above the threshold, speech took more than two minutes on average to become uncomfortable. The errors leaned one way: people tended to pass the test when they were in fact above the threshold.

In trained cyclists, two studies agree on where the uncertain stage falls and disagree on which stage to use. In 18 highly trained cyclists the equivocal stage matched VT1, at 148 beats per minute (bpm) against 150. The negative stage matched the second ventilatory threshold, at 176 bpm against 177 [11]. In 12 highly trained cyclists in another laboratory the equivocal stage came at 147 bpm, almost to the beat. But the last positive stage came at 129, far below the threshold, and the negative stage at 156, and the authors concluded that the negative stage was the one to use [12]. The difference is in the question. The first study called a stage negative when the rider “could definitely not talk”. The second called it negative when the rider answered “no” to whether he could speak comfortably, which happens much sooner. The talk test’s answer depends on the wording of its question, so choose the words once and keep them.

Stages need to be longer than two minutes. Earlier talk-test studies had used two-minute stages. Speech takes longer than that to become uncomfortable just above the threshold [10], so a short stage can end before the rider has found out. Sixteen active people did a test of rising speed and then ran for 30 minutes at the pace of each talk-test stage. All of them completed the half hour at the last positive stage. At the equivocal stage three could not, and at the negative stage only two could [s8]. An intensity just under the first threshold can be held for hours, so for some of those runners the uncertain stage had been well above it.

Taken together, the equivocal stage is the best single estimate of the breathing threshold. It tends to run a few beats high, more so with short stages, and the last clearly comfortable stage lies on the safe side of it. All of these studies took breathing as the reference. Only one reports lactate: in the 18 trained cyclists, blood lactate at the uncertain stage was 1.3 mmol/L, against 1.6 at VT1, which places that stage at or just before the first rise [11]. For a book that defines Zone 2 by lactate, the talk test is a proxy for a proxy, and most of the evidence comes from one research group. It remains the best-supported method that costs nothing. B

Heart rate variability

The newest home method needs only a chest strap, and it is less reliable than the app makes it look. A heart at rest does not beat like a metronome. The gaps between beats vary, and the variation has structure: long and short gaps follow one another in patterns that repeat across time scales. As exercise gets harder the structure dissolves and the variation becomes random. An index called DFA alpha 1, from a technique named detrended fluctuation analysis, puts a number on this. It sits around 1.0 in very light exercise and falls towards 0.5, the value for pure noise, at high intensity [13].

In 2021 a group led by Bruce Rogers proposed that the midpoint, 0.75, marks the first threshold. The value was chosen on theory, as halfway between order and noise. They tested it in 15 men running on a treadmill and it held: VT1 came at 152 bpm on average and the heartbeat threshold at 154, with a correlation of 0.97 [13]. Free phone apps now calculate the index live from a chest strap.

That correlation deserves the suspicion Chapter 5 recommended. The 15 men were aged from 19 to 52, and their heart rate at the threshold ran from 108 to 183 bpm. Across a spread that wide, almost any two measures that rise with effort will correlate. The limits of agreement are the better guide, and they ran from 12 beats one way to 8 the other [13]. Twenty beats from end to end is about the width of a heart-rate zone.

A 2024 pooled analysis looks more encouraging than it is. Across 22 studies the average difference between the heartbeat threshold and the laboratory one was trivial, and the pooled correlation was 0.85. The body of the paper reports that about 90% of the variation between those studies reflected real differences in what they found. A new study could expect a correlation anywhere from 0.06 to 0.99 [14]. The trivial average comes from studies that erred in both directions.

One study, up close: a chest strap against the laboratory

In 2026 a group at KU Leuven in Belgium tested the method on a bike, against lactate as well as breathing [8].

Behind the average were errors as large as a whole heart-rate zone for individual riders. The pooled analysis also found that the heartbeat threshold agreed better with lactate than with breathing [14].

All 21 riders were young men, and each did only one test, so the method’s repeatability was not tested [8]. Four-minute stages suit lactate sampling and may blur the ventilatory threshold, which is easier to see in a smooth ramp. The work was funded by the university and the authors declared no conflicts of interest. Check a live phone reading against another method before using it to set the top of Zone 2. B

Reading the research: validated against what?

A validation study compares a cheap method with a reference and reports the gap. The gap belongs to both of them. If the reference is itself uncertain, part of the error charged to the cheap method was never its fault, and no cheap method can be shown to be more accurate than the reference is.

The Leuven study lets a reader see this because it measured two references. Against breathing, the heartbeat threshold was 17 beats out and the difference was statistically significant. Against lactate it was 8 beats out and the difference was not. Had the group collected only breathing, the paper would have reported a method that fails. Had they collected only lactate, it could fairly have reported one that agrees with the laboratory on average. Studies in this field differ in which reference they use, and the pooled analysis found that the choice changes the result [14].

Check which laboratory measure was used as the reference, and how repeatable it is. The talk-test studies used breathing, while this book defines Zone 2 by lactate. Even the laboratory answer moves: by a standard deviation of 19 W in the retest of 14 cyclists, and by 16% between the four physiologists of 1983 [7][s4]. The people reading the reference should also be kept blind to the home method’s result, as they were in Leuven. A threshold found by eye is easy to nudge towards a number the reader already knows.

A lactate threshold from a single test is uncertain by 10 or 20 W, and lactate and breathing were about 10 beats apart on average in Leuven [7,8]. A home method that lands within 10 beats of the lactate threshold has done about as well as the laboratory does against itself.

Percentages, drift and feel

A percentage of maximum heart rate is the commonest stand-in and the weakest, because it stacks two guesses, and both are wide.

The first guess is the maximum. The formula 220 minus age was never derived from a study. Two physiologists who went looking for its source in 2000 traced it to a remark in the caption of a figure in a 1971 review [15][s11]. It has had a long career for a caption. The best modern equation, fitted to 3,320 healthy Norwegian adults, has a standard error of 10.8 bpm, which puts about one adult in three more than 11 beats from the prediction [16].

The second guess is the percentage. In 100 adults with a measured maximum, the first lactate threshold lay anywhere from 60% to 90% of it [17]. The rule printed on gym machines and built into many apps puts Zone 2 at 60–70% of maximum. In the 50 trained cyclists of Chapter 5 the first threshold averaged 81% [4], so for the average rider among them the top of that band was about 20 beats too low.

Percentages of VO2max do no better. When 21 fit men rode for an hour at 60% of their VO2max, their blood lactate averaged 2.1 mmol/L and ran individually from 0.7, a resting level, to 5.6 [s12]. Phil Maffetone’s 180 formula leaves the maximum out. It is 180 minus age, with adjustments of 5 or 10 beats for health and training history. Its author’s page cites no study that compares it with a measured threshold [18], and I could not find one.

The drift test has the right physiology and no validation. Coaches often recommend it: ride for an hour at a steady power and compare your average heart rate in the second half with the first. A rise of less than 5% is taken to mean the power was at or below the first threshold. Over a long steady effort heart rate does creep upward while the volume of blood pumped with each beat falls [s13], and above the first threshold the oxygen cost creeps as well. But I could find no study that tests the 5% rule against a measured lactate threshold. And heat, dehydration and the length of the ride all raise drift for reasons unconnected to the threshold, as Chapter 9 describes. A failed test may only show that the room was warm. C

Nose breathing marks nothing in particular. Cyclists often pass on the cue that if you can keep your mouth shut, you are in Zone 2. In 30 adults exercising at rising intensity with a mask over the nose, 20 changed from breathing through the nose alone to nose and mouth together at an average of 105 W. Four breathed through the mouth from the start and five never opened it. What related most closely to each person’s switch point was how hard breathing felt and how much work the nose demanded [19]. For nine of those 30 people the switch could not have marked a threshold of any kind.

Feel finds the zone but not its edge. In 2008 a group of exercise psychologists led by Panteleimon Ekkekakis had 30 young adults do 15-minute treadmill sessions below, at and above their own ventilatory threshold. They rated repeatedly how good or bad they felt. Above the threshold their pleasure fell, and it fell in much the same way across the group [20]. Zone 2 is, roughly, the hardest riding that still feels good. But a later review found that the heart rates people settle at when asked to hold a given feeling vary too much for the feeling to find the top edge [21]. C

A step test for the turbo trainer

In ERG mode a smart trainer holds a set power whatever your cadence, which helps keep the stages consistent. This protocol combines lactate sampling with the talk test; without a meter, you can use the talk test alone. I have assembled it from the studies above. Nobody has tested it as a package.

  1. Pick a day when you are rested, and ride in a cool room with a fan. Heat and fatigue both raise heart rate at a given power.
  2. Warm up for 10 minutes at a very easy power. With a meter, take a first sample at the end.
  3. Start well below where you expect Zone 2 to be and ride four-minute stages, adding about 15 W each time. Four minutes, because lactate needs time to reach the blood [7][s7] and because speech takes more than two minutes to become uncomfortable just above the threshold [10].
  4. In the last 40 seconds of each stage, note your heart rate, then say the same passage aloud: about 100 words that you know by heart, the length used in the 1981 breathing study [s9]. Ask yourself the same question every time: could I speak comfortably? Answer yes, not sure, or no, and settle the wording before you start [12].
  5. With a meter, take a blood sample at the end of each stage, from clean dry skin, discarding the first drop.
  6. Your baseline is the average of the early stages, before the readings begin a steady climb. Expect those readings to differ by a tenth or two, and do not be surprised if the second is lower than the first. The first stage that reads 0.5 mmol/L or more above the baseline is over the threshold, provided the next stage reads higher still. A lone high reading is more likely a bad sample [5].
  7. The top of your Zone 2 is the heart rate and power of the stage before that rise. Without a meter, it is the last stage with a clear “yes”, and the “not sure” stage is roughly the threshold [9,10].
  8. Stop one stage after the rise is confirmed, or at the first “no”. The test goes nowhere near your maximum.
  9. Repeat it on another day. The lactate threshold moved by a standard deviation of 19 W between two tests in trained cyclists [7], and heart rate at a fixed effort varies by several beats from day to day [s14].

A rider who does both gets a check on each. If the last comfortable stage and the last stage before the lactate rise are the same or adjacent, the result can be trusted further than either alone. If they are three stages apart, something went wrong with one of them.

If you have a heart condition, or take medication that alters heart rate such as beta blockers, ask a doctor before testing or training by heart rate. The talk test asks for no maximal effort, and it has been used with cardiac patients [s15].

The second threshold

Zone 2 needs only the first threshold. The hard sessions of Part III need the second, and lactate is a harder way to find it. As Chapter 5 described, the maximal lactate steady state takes four or five 30-minute rides on separate days. The practical routes are tests of performance, and the two home methods above both do better here than at the first threshold.

Chapter 5 covered the 20-minute test: FTP matched the laboratory steady state on average in one study, overshot it in another, and can be 9% out for one rider [s16,s17]. Critical power can also be found without a laboratory, as Chapter 19 describes. All-out efforts of 3, 7 and 12 minutes will do, or a rider’s best efforts of those lengths in ordinary riding [s18].

The talk test reaches the second threshold too. In the 18 trained cyclists, the stage at which they could definitely not talk matched the second ventilatory threshold, and their blood lactate there was 4.2 mmol/L [11]. The heartbeat index did better here than at the first threshold. In Leuven its 0.5 value came within 1 beat and 2 W of the second lactate threshold on average, with limits of 17 beats and 54 W either side [8].

A rider who wants percentages as a cross-check should measure a maximum heart rate on the bike and not predict one. A properly measured maximum is accurate to about two beats [15]. Older riders, untrained riders and anyone with a heart condition should not go looking for one without medical advice.

If FTP is the only number you have

Many riders have only an FTP, because that is the number their software asks for. It can set a Zone 2 ceiling, as long as the ceiling is treated as a first guess.

The usual way is Coggan’s levels, which stop Level 2 at 75% of FTP [s19]. On average that sits below the first threshold, not at it. In 17 trained cyclists tested with four-minute stages, the first lactate rise came at 229 W and the maximal lactate steady state at 264 W [22]. So the first threshold was about 87% of the steady state. FTP has come out level with the steady state in one study and about 7% above it in another, as Chapter 5 described [23,24]. Put together, my arithmetic places the average first threshold at roughly 80 to 87% of FTP. For a rider with an FTP of 250 W, Level 2 stops at about 190 W, and the average threshold sits somewhere around 200 to 220 W.

Those are averages from small groups, and for one rider each step adds its own error. FTP can be about 9% out against the steady state [24], and the gap between the two thresholds is unlikely to be a fixed proportion (Chapter 5). So start at 75% of FTP, which is cautious for the average rider in these studies, and use the talk test to find how far above it you can ride while still speaking comfortably. C

For the hard sessions FTP is more useful, because it is an estimate of the second threshold itself. Threshold intervals belong a little below it, since it may read high. For the sessions near VO2max, Chapter 11’s advice stands: a percentage of FTP is a starting point, and the power to ride is the highest you can hold for the whole set.

Keeping the numbers right

Heart rate at the threshold stays put through a season and the power moves, so the power is what needs rechecking. In 2000 Alejandro Lucía and colleagues tested 13 professional road cyclists three times in a season: in November during their break, in January, and in May when they were racing. The power at their thresholds rose as they got fitter. The heart rates hardly moved. At the lactate threshold they averaged 154, 152 and 154 bpm across the three tests, and at the second ventilatory threshold 178, 173 and 176 [s20]. The authors concluded that one test at the start of the season is enough to set a professional’s heart-rate targets for the year.

Those were professionals with many years of training behind them, and nobody has shown the same for a rider in a first season, whose heart may be changing faster. For an established rider, the heart rate at the lactate threshold, once found, should last. Recheck the power every couple of months, and after illness or a long break. No study sets the interval; that one is a reasonable guess.

Day to day, heart rate wobbles by about 5 beats, and within a long ride by more. Forty-four people did the same submaximal running test at the same time on five consecutive days. Their heart rates spread by about 5 bpm at the stage where they were most consistent, near 90% of maximum, and by more at the easier stages [s14]. In the Auckland study that Chapter 9 describes, two hours of easy riding raised the heart rate at the first threshold by 9 bpm and lowered the power by 21 W [s21]. A ceiling written as a single number of beats claims more precision than any of these measurements has.

A lactate meter stays at home, and the numbers it gave you are what you ride to. Of the stand-ins, the talk test is the one that goes out on the road. If you are riding at your Zone 2 heart rate and can’t finish a sentence comfortably, the number is wrong for that day.

What survives
  • Lactate is this book’s reference; even a laboratory test is uncertain by 10 to 20 W.
  • The talk test is the best-supported method that costs nothing. B
  • A heart-rate app can be 30 beats out for one rider. Check it before you ride to it. B
  • With only an FTP, 75% of it is a cautious Zone 2 ceiling to start from. C
