Part IIThe easy part

Chapter 7: What easy riding does to the body

Draft · 5,852 words · 27 October 2026

The winter in the Introduction is the reason this book exists. It was four or five easy rides a week on a trainer in the garage, then a climb up Sa Calobra more than two minutes faster than I had ever ridden it. I put it down to Zone 2 and the mitochondria it was said to build. The training studies in this chapter do not bear that out, and they point to a plainer explanation.

Since about 2019 a great deal has been claimed for easy riding: that it is the best way to build mitochondria, that it trains fat burning and lactate clearance, and that its upper edge, Zone 2, has effects no other intensity does. That is a lot to ask of a pace at which you can hold a conversation. The training studies support a simpler account. Easy riding provides a small stimulus that can be repeated in large amounts.

A professional can train for most of the day; an amateur with a job and a family may have a handful of hours a week. Easy riding has a different place in those two weeks.

What an easy ride asks of the muscle

A muscle is a bundle of fibres, each a single long cell, and the fibres are not all alike. What sets them apart is the kind of myosin they build, the protein that produces force. Human limb muscle makes three kinds, which gives three named fibre types: type I, called slow-twitch, and two fast-twitch types, IIA and IIX [s1]. Slow fibres contract more slowly, are rich in mitochondria and are slow to tire. Fast fibres produce force quickly and tire sooner.

The two kinds differ in colour, because slow fibres hold more myoglobin, the red protein that stores oxygen in muscle. A chicken shows it at the table. The legs, which carry the bird all day, are dark meat, and the breast, which powers a few seconds of flapping, is white. Human muscles are not sorted that way. Slow and fast fibres lie mixed together through the same muscle, in an arrangement that looks random, and a thin slice has to be stained before the types can be told apart under a microscope [1][s2]. A fibre takes its type from the nerve cell that drives it [s3], and each nerve cell drives many fibres of one type, scattered among the fibres of its neighbours.

The mix varies widely from person to person. Chapter 1 described 19 trained cyclists whose thigh muscle ran from 32% slow fibres to 76% [s4].

How far training can change the mix is not settled [1]. In any case a fibre’s type is separate from its contents: the mitochondria inside it, which are the subject of this chapter, increase with training without the type having to change [1].

The nervous system calls on these fibres in a fixed order. Slow fibres are used first, and fast fibres are added as the force required goes up, or as the slow fibres tire. The classic demonstration was published in 1974. Philip Gollnick, Karin Piehl and Bengt Saltin had people ride at intensities from 30% of VO2max upward, took samples of thigh muscle, and stained them for glycogen, the muscle’s store of carbohydrate. A fibre that has been working uses up its glycogen and stains pale. At every intensity below VO2max the slow fibres emptied first, and the fast fibres began to empty only as the ride went on. After three hours at low intensity a large amount of glycogen was still in the muscle, nearly all of it in fast fibres [2]. At 75% of VO2max, by contrast, a later study found the slow fibres and the IIA fibres working together from the first minute [s5].

Chapter 2 ended on the rule that a fibre adapts only if it was disturbed. An easy ride disturbs the slow fibres. It reaches the fast ones only if it goes on long enough for the slow ones to run down.

The disturbance is also small. Below the first threshold the cell’s chemistry settles into a steady state, so the energy sensor AMPK, which responds to a shortfall, has little to respond to. Chapter 2 described the Dublin experiment in which a ride at 40% of VO2max did not activate AMPK and raised the messenger RNA for PGC-1α less than half as far as a ride at 80% [s6]. In 2025 four Canadian physiologists gathered the measurements of this kind that they could find for exercise at Zone 2 intensity. Their review, Much Ado About Zone 2, concluded that the signals are small, inconsistent, or both [3].

Duration seems to help, up to a point. In the studies that review lists, AMPK activity was unchanged after two hours of easy exercise and raised at three and a half. The message for PGC-1α rose after 60 and 90 minutes in one study and not after 30, and did not rise after 90 in another. Two to three and a half hours of easy exercise also lowers muscle glycogen, and low glycogen is itself a signal to AMPK [3].

How intensity and duration combine was mapped in rats in 1982. Gary Dudley and colleagues trained rats on treadmills for eight weeks on 19 different schedules, covering six running speeds and several daily durations at each. They then measured a mitochondrial protein, cytochrome c, in each type of muscle fibre. At any one speed, running for longer each day produced more adaptation up to a ceiling and then no more. The height of the ceiling was set by the speed. The faster the running, the higher the ceiling and the shorter the daily run needed to reach it. The least-used fast fibres did not adapt at all until the speed reached about 80% of VO2max, and above that their response rose steeply [4].

Those were rats, and their minutes and speeds do not translate to a cyclist. The shape is what matters, and the human evidence below is consistent with it. More easy riding adds adaptation at a diminishing rate, the rate depends on how easy it is, and some fibres are barely touched by it.

What it builds

One study, up close: 353 training studies

The largest test of what continuous riding builds over a training programme was published in 2025 by Knut Sindre Mølmen, Nicki Winfield Almquist and Øyvind Skattebo, working in Norway [5].

They searched three databases for every study that had trained people and measured their muscle before and after. Of 5,224 records, 425 papers met their criteria. The analysis of mitochondria used 353 studies, containing 506 separate training groups and 5,650 people. For each group they recorded how long, how often and how hard the training was, and how fit the people were at the start. The outcome was the percentage change in the muscle’s mitochondrial content, pooled from five markers: the volume of mitochondria seen under an electron microscope, and four mitochondrial enzymes.

Each group’s training was put in one of three classes. Sprint training meant all-out efforts of 4 to 90 seconds. High-intensity training meant work above the second threshold. Everything continuous below the second threshold went into a single class that the authors call endurance training, at low or moderate intensity [5].

All three raised mitochondrial content, and by similar amounts: 23% for continuous training, 27% for high-intensity training and 27% for sprints, differences that were not statistically significant. Gains were visible after two weeks. Training six times a week produced more than four, and four more than two. Age, sex and disease made no difference to the response [5].

Per hour of training the three were far apart. High-intensity training raised mitochondrial content about 1.7 times as much per hour as continuous training, and sprints about 3.9 times as much. The same held for VO2max, where sprints were about 4.9 times as efficient per hour as continuous training [5].

Capillaries told a slightly different story. The number of capillaries around each fibre rose by 15% with continuous training, 13% with high-intensity training and 10% with sprints, with no significant difference. Capillary density, the number per square millimetre of muscle, rose more with continuous training (13% against 7%), which the authors put down to the fibres themselves growing less. Most of the gain had arrived within four weeks [5].

The authors sorted the groups into untrained (an average VO2max of 35 mL/kg/min), moderately trained (49) and well trained (62). The untrained gained most. Well-trained people gained about 7% in mitochondrial content, averaged over every kind of training. Expressed per hour, well-trained people showed no measurable gain from continuous training or from high-intensity training, and a gain only from sprints. Their capillaries did not change significantly with any training, and nor did their VO2max per hour [5].

What the analysis says about easy riding in particular is limited, first of all by its own categories. The continuous class runs all the way up to the second threshold, so it mixes easy riding with riding between the thresholds. The 23% belongs to that mixture. The analysis cannot say how much of it easy riding alone would produce, and the Canadian review makes the same objection [3].

The studies are short and small in dose. The average programme of continuous training lasted 11 weeks in untrained people and seven in the others, and in untrained and moderately trained people it added up to about 36 hours of training in total. A cyclist riding eight hours a week does that in a month. The authors say their findings describe mainly the first response to a change in training [5].

And the well trained are barely represented. Of 270 groups doing continuous training, 14 were well trained, with 104 people between them. Nearly two-thirds of all the measurements came from untrained people, 36% of their groups had a disease, and three-quarters or more of the participants in every class were men [5]. The authors did not test for publication bias, which they acknowledge. They declared no funding and no conflicts of interest.

The analysis establishes that continuous riding below the second threshold builds mitochondria and capillaries in people who are not yet well trained. It does so about as much per programme as harder training, and much less per hour. A For riders who are already well trained it found no measurable gain from more of it, on thin evidence. B

Studies that kept the riding easy

The studies that kept training clearly below the first threshold are small, but they separate easy riding from the broader continuous class.

At low volume, four weeks produced no measurable gain in mitochondrial content. In a 2016 study from David Bishop’s laboratory, 29 men did 12 sessions of sprints, four-minute intervals, or continuous riding below the lactate threshold for 20 to 36 minutes. Citrate synthase, the usual marker of mitochondrial content, did not change in any group, and the mitochondria’s capacity to use oxygen rose only after sprints [6].

At equal work, easy training does not raise the ceiling. A Norwegian trial assigned 40 moderately trained men to one of four ways of running, three days a week for eight weeks. The four were slow running at 70% of maximum heart rate, steady running at 85%, and two kinds of interval. The total oxygen consumed was matched between groups. VO2max rose by 5.5% and 7.2% in the interval groups, significantly more than in the other two, and the heart’s stroke volume rose by about 10% after intervals [s7]. The summary of the paper gives no figures for the slow group.

With enough hours, easy training does improve some things as well as hard training does. In a Finnish trial that Chapter 9 describes, 35 sedentary or recreationally active adults did ten weeks of either easy riding, averaging 6.8 hours a week, or intervals, averaging 1.6 hours. Durability, the ability to hold a steady effort for three hours without drifting, improved by about the same amount in both groups. VO2max rose only in the interval group [s8]. The easy group needed four times the hours to match the interval group on one measure and did not match it on the other.

In athletes who are already elite, easy training holds what they have. Twenty elite junior cross-country skiers trained 12 to 15 hours a week for five months, one group mostly at 60–70% of VO2max and the other mostly at 80–90%, close to the lactate threshold. The harder group improved more in a 20-minute run and raised their speed at the lactate threshold by 3.2%. The easier group’s threshold speed did not change, and neither group’s citrate synthase did [s9,s10].

The study furthest from ordinary training is a ski expedition. In 1983 six people skied 30 kilometres a day with backpacks, six days a week for eight weeks, at about 45% of VO2max. In their arms, which were doing work they were not used to, citrate synthase rose by 90% and the number of capillaries per fibre by 40%. In their thighs nothing changed. The authors concluded that long duration is not, by itself, enough to make the leg muscles adapt [s11].

What counts as easy is relative to what the muscle is already used to. The skiers’ legs were already trained for work at walking pace, so hours a day of it gave them nothing new to adapt to. Their arms had never worked so hard, and for them the same expedition was a training programme. The Canadian review presses this point hardest. It cites an earlier analysis by Bishop’s group which suggests that exercise below about 60% of a person’s maximum work rate is not expected to raise mitochondrial content at all [3][s12]. An older pooled analysis of 34 studies agrees. Sedentary people raised their thresholds at any training intensity. People who were already trained showed gains that were not statistically significant, and tended to respond better to high intensity [s13].

Capillaries follow the same pattern. A 2022 analysis of 57 training groups found that in sedentary people, capillaries per fibre grew 21% more after moderate continuous training than after low-intensity training, and 54% more after high-intensity intervals. In people who were already trained, no kind of training added any [s14].

I know of no study that adds easy hours to a trained cyclist’s week and measures the muscle, or that compares riding at the top of Zone 2 with riding lower at the same hours. The evidence that exists says that easy training builds a great deal in the untrained, and that in the trained, at the volumes and durations anyone has studied, it maintains more than it builds. B

Four claims

That Zone 2 is the best way to build mitochondria

It is not. Per hour, continuous riding builds less mitochondrial content than harder riding, and the continuous riding in that comparison was harder than Zone 2 on average [5]. The signals from a single easy session are small [3]. In the one four-week study that isolated riding below the threshold, mitochondrial content did not move [6]. No trial supports the claim described in the Introduction, that easy riding is the single most effective way to build mitochondria.

The opposite claim, that easy riding does nothing for mitochondria, is also wrong. Continuous training raised mitochondrial content by nearly a quarter across 270 training groups [5]. In a muscle that is not yet used to it, enough of it clearly works. The Canadian review’s conclusion is carefully limited: Zone 2 has not been shown to be the optimal intensity, and people with little time should put harder riding first. It is about the general population, and says of athletes that the question is open [3].

That Zone 2 is where you burn the most fat

From the saddle. I ride at the top of where I think my Zone 2 is, partly because I think that is the “fat max”. Managing my weight is definitely a goal, so that’s why I do the top of Zone 2. But is that really fat max? Could I protect my hard rides by riding even easier?

Fat burning rises with intensity to a peak and then falls as carbohydrate takes over. Where the peak sits depends on what you have eaten. Asker Jeukendrup’s laboratory tested 33 trained endurance athletes and found that peak fat burning and the first rise in lactate came at the same intensity, 63% and 61% of VO2max [7]. That laboratory’s practice was to test after an overnight fast, though the paper’s summary does not say so of this study. When it gave 11 trained people 75 g of glucose 45 minutes before the same test, the peak rate of fat burning fell by 28%. The intensity at which it occurred fell from 60% of VO2max to 52% [8]. In the 50 cyclists of Chapter 5, who had been told to eat a carbohydrate meal three hours beforehand, fat burning peaked at 56% of VO2max and the first threshold came at 70%. The gap was 75 W and 16 beats per minute [9].

Peak fat burning may sit near the Zone 2 ceiling when fasted and lower after eating. Feeding is my explanation for the difference between studies, but their test protocols differed too. The peak is broad: in moderately trained cyclists, fat burning stayed within 10% of its peak from 55% to 72% of VO2max [s15]. When 15 men were tested twice, each man’s peak moved by 16–21% [s16].

For body fat, where the peak sits matters much less than it seems. Sixteen adults each spent three days in a sealed room that measured everything they burned. On one day they rested, on one they did 400 calories of exercise at 40% of VO2max, and on one they did 400 calories at 70%. Over the full 24 hours, the fat they burned did not differ between the three days [10]. A review by the same group concluded that exercise of an hour or less has little effect on fat burned over a day [s17]. The likely reason is that the body settles its fuel account over the day, so that a ride which burned mostly fat is followed by hours that burn a little less. B

Training trials agree. A pooled analysis of 31 studies found no difference in body fat between people assigned to intervals and people assigned to steady moderate training, and neither produced a loss the authors considered clinically meaningful [11]. Training at fat max does reduce weight in people with obesity, by about 4 kg across 11 trials of 8 to 20 weeks [s18]. The summary of that analysis does not say what the comparison groups did.

What differs between the top of Zone 2 and the bottom is the energy. On the averages of the 50 cyclists, the first threshold is 75 W above the fed-state fat max [9]. An hour at the higher power burns roughly 270 calories more, against a difference in fat burned during the ride of probably a few grams. A rider who wants to lose weight has a reason to ride at the top of Zone 2, and the reason is the energy.

That Zone 2 trains the clearing of lactate

The idea comes from the 2018 paper described in Chapter 6, in which professional endurance athletes carried less lactate and burned more fat than moderately active people or patients with metabolic syndrome [s19]. Its reasoning is sound as far as it goes. Mitochondria are where both fat and lactate are burned. A muscle with more mitochondrial capacity can meet a given power while burning more fat and letting less lactate build up, which is the explanation Chapter 2 gave for why trained riders have higher thresholds. So the lactate and fat-burning curves from an exercise test are a window on how much mitochondrial capacity a person has. The authors call a body that switches easily between fuels metabolically flexible.

The step from there to a training prescription is the weak one. The paper compared three groups of different people at one moment. It did not train anybody. Professionals differ from patients in years of training of every kind, in how much of it they do, and in whatever made them professionals in the first place. A comparison of that sort cannot say which of those produced the difference. It is a description of what a very fit body looks like, and it is used as if it were evidence about how to build one.

The one training study I found that measured the machinery directly points the other way. In the elite skiers described above, the researchers also measured MCT1, the transporter that carries lactate into muscle fibres to be burned. After five months of mostly easy training it had fallen by 12%. In the group that trained near the lactate threshold it was unchanged, and theirs was the group whose threshold speed improved [s10]. The study had 20 skiers, and the summary does not say how they had trained before, so the fall may reflect a step down from harder training. It does not support the idea that easy riding is what builds lactate clearance. C

That easy miles teach the body to run on fat

The performance version of the fat claim says that long easy rides train the muscles to burn fat, and that a rider who burns more fat saves glycogen and lasts longer. On this view, that is what the professionals’ hours are for. The first step is right: training does shift the fuel mix towards fat. The rest has little support. Intervals shift it as well, and burning more fat has not by itself made anyone faster.

The shift is one of the oldest findings in the field, and Chapter 2 gave the reason for it: with more mitochondria, the muscle meets the same power with more fat. In 1986 Holloszy’s laboratory put nine men through a strenuous 12-week programme and tested them at the same power before and after. The share of their energy that came from fat rose from 35% to 57%, and they used 41% less muscle glycogen [12][s20]. A

Easy riding is not the only way to get it. In 2008 Martin Gibala’s laboratory gave active but untrained young adults six weeks of either all-out 30-second sprints or steady riding. The sprints took about an hour and a half a week, the steady riding about four and a half hours. In the same one-hour test afterwards, both groups burned more fat and less glycogen, with no difference between them, although the steady group had done ten times the work [13][s21]. In trained cyclists the evidence is thinner. In the same Cape Town laboratory as the trials in Chapter 12, eight cyclists riding about 300 km a week swapped 15% of it for 12 sessions of five-minute intervals over six weeks. Afterwards they burned less carbohydrate at the same power [14]. That study had no control group, and I found none in trained riders that compared easy and hard training on this measure. B

The Cape Town study also shows that a fitter rider does not win by saving glycogen. The cyclists’ 40 km time trial went from 42.0 to 43.0 km/h. They rode it at 327 W instead of 291 W and at a higher share of their peak power, so they burned more carbohydrate, about 5.1 grams a minute instead of 4.3 [14]. At the old pace the fitter rider runs more on fat. In a race they go faster, and back onto carbohydrate [s22]. B

A laboratory test of fat burning adds little to what a test of fitness already shows. In 17 trained cyclists and triathletes in New Zealand, peak fat burning tracked a marker of mitochondrial content closely and predicted a 30-minute time trial ridden after two hours. But once their VO2max, threshold power and efficiency were known, it explained only 2.6% more of the differences between riders. The authors suggested that more mitochondria may underlie both [15]. In Ironman triathletes, whose races last more than nine hours, it had a modest link with finishing time that VO2max did not explain [16]. In elite road cyclists, how much fat they burned did not predict how much power they lost over four hours (Chapter 9). C

The most direct test is to raise fat burning further than training can, which a high-fat diet does. In 2017 Louise Burke’s group at the Australian Institute of Sport put elite race walkers through three weeks of hard training on one of three diets. On the high-fat diet their fat burning rose sharply, to 1.57 grams a minute during two hours of walking. The walkers on high or periodised carbohydrate improved their 10 km race times by 6.6% and 5.3%. The high-fat group did not improve, and walking at race pace cost them more oxygen, since fat needs more oxygen than carbohydrate for the same energy (Chapter 9) [17][s23]. B

The professionals’ hours probably raise their fat burning along with everything else, but nothing shows that this is why the hours work. Fat burning is better read as a sign of fitness than as a separate quality to train. Whatever makes a rider fitter raises it, and the harder a rider races, the more of the energy comes from carbohydrate, which is why Chapter 13 is about eating it.

Reading the research: who chose the studies?

Two reviews run through this chapter, and they sound as if they disagree. One says that continuous training builds as much mitochondrial content as intervals. The other says Zone 2 is not the best way to build mitochondria. They rest on much the same body of studies.

They are different kinds of document. The Norwegian analysis is a systematic review. Its authors wrote down in advance which databases they would search and which studies would qualify, screened 5,224 records, and report how many they excluded and why [5]. Another team following the same rules should arrive at nearly the same set of studies. The Canadian paper is a narrative review, and says so: its authors did not run a systematic search, and drew on reference lists, on papers they knew, and on articles shared through social media [3]. A narrative review is an argument made by experts. It can be right, and this one mostly is, but the reader has no way to know which studies were left out.

It also helps to ask what question each was answering. The Norwegian authors asked how much each kind of training changes muscle, per programme and per hour. The Canadian authors asked whether Zone 2 is the optimal intensity for people who are inactive or doing about two and a half hours of exercise a week. “Not shown to be optimal” is a much weaker statement than “shown not to work”, and the paper is often quoted as if it had made the second.

And look at who is writing. One of the Canadian authors declares an advisory role and shares in a longevity company whose services relate in part to exercise. Much of that author’s career has been spent showing what short hard sessions can do [3]. That does not make the review wrong. The Norwegian authors declare no interests and did not test for publication bias. They also put easy and moderate riding in one category, which happens to be the choice that decides what their headline number means for Zone 2. Both papers need reading past the summary. What survives is the ground they share: easy riding builds mitochondria, and harder riding builds more per hour.

What easy riding is good for

Easy riding is worth its hours when recovery, rather than time, limits how much you can train.

In Seiler’s runners, the heart-rate-variability marker returned to normal within 5 to 10 minutes of an easy session, against 30 minutes after harder sessions [s24]. Chapter 12 examines how many hard sessions a rider can absorb in a week. Easy riding lets you add work around them.

So easy riding is how a rider with time turns that time into training. The Norwegian authors found that training load, the product of volume and intensity, was the best predictor of the gain in mitochondrial content [5]. Easy riding is the only way to raise the volume very far. This is why the athletes of Chapter 8 do so much of it. It does not follow that a rider with four hours a week should spend them the same way.

Easy riding may also build things that short studies cannot see. Chapter 2 described changes to the heart over months and years; nearly every trial here lasted weeks. Only mechanism and the habits of elite athletes support the case that years of easy volume build an engine that intervals alone cannot. No trial has run long enough to test it. C

How easy, and how long

This book’s rule for an easy ride is that it should carry as much work as it can without taking anything from the hard sessions. For a rider on six to ten hours a week that means the top of the easy range, Zone 2. At equal hours it is more work, more energy burned and a larger disturbance to more of the muscle than riding lower. The ski expedition shows what can happen when the intensity is too low for a muscle that is already trained. No trial has compared the top of the range with the bottom.

The best evidence against the rule is that Olympic champion skiers do most of their easy training well below Zone 2. Chapter 8 gives their figures, and my reason for thinking they follow the same rule with different numbers. They fit about 15 easy hours a week around their hard sessions [s25]; a seven-hour rider has five or six, with a day or more between hard sessions. C

If the ride is truly below the first threshold, Seiler’s runners suggest that riding easier still buys very little extra recovery [s24]. Nine runners and one marker of recovery are enough to show a direction and not much more.

The risk at the top is of being over the threshold without knowing. Chapter 6 put the uncertainty of a ceiling found without a lactate test at about 10 beats [s26], and the threshold itself falls during a long ride [s27]. A margin of a few beats under the estimated ceiling costs little and covers both.

The better way to protect a hard session is to arrive at it fuelled. Riding near the top of Zone 2 uses more carbohydrate than riding lower: in the 1974 study, glycogen was used 2.7 times as fast at 64% of VO2max as at 31% [2]. Chapter 13 covers how to replace it. That last step is my inference. No study here tested whether eating more or riding easier does more for the next day’s intervals.

On duration, the mechanism favours long rides over many short ones. Nothing more precise can be said. The signalling studies suggest that an easy ride has to last well over an hour before the sensors register much [3]. The glycogen staining suggests that fast fibres join in only late in a long ride [2]. And the rat study shows a ceiling beyond which more minutes add nothing [4]. None of that tells a cyclist whether one three-hour ride is worth more than three of an hour. It does suggest that a week of 45-minute easy rides is the form of easy riding with the least to recommend it on mechanism. I say that as someone who spent a winter doing exactly that and got faster.

From the saddle. Before that winter I’d been doing mainly high-intensity sessions, mostly racing online on Zwift, and rather inconsistently. At the weekends I rode with friends, and those rides were generally high intensity too. It came to maybe three or four hours a week. That winter it was about three to five hours a week. I generally felt better, and I fell ill less often with coughs and colds.

My hours changed little, from three or four a week to three to five. What changed was the regularity: four or five sessions every week, a frequency at which the Norwegian analysis found larger gains [5]. Since the evidence favours harder riding per hour, I think regularity explains my improvement better than the lower intensity. One rider and one climb cannot establish that. Easy riding was simply something I could do week after week and feel better for.

Who it is for

A new or returning rider gains from easy riding in almost any form, because a muscle that is not used to training adapts to nearly anything. Most of the 23% in the Norwegian analysis was measured in people like that [5].

For anyone riding to manage their weight, the hours and the power matter and the fuel mix does not.

A trained rider with only a few hours a week gets the least from it. The muscle is already used to the stimulus, the hours are too few for volume to do its work, and per hour every harder kind of riding does more. For that rider easy riding fills the days between the hard sessions, and the hard sessions are where most of the training is.

That reading comes from studies that were mostly not designed to sort riders this way, and Part III tests it against the trials that compared easy riding with intervals directly. C

A trained rider with many hours can use easy riding to add work once the hard sessions are in place. That is the position of the best endurance athletes in the world, who do most of their training easy, year after year.

What survives
  • Easy riding builds mitochondria and capillaries in the untrained, as much per programme as harder training but less per hour. A
  • In well-trained riders, more easy riding has not been shown to build more. B
  • Easy hours add work without taking anything from the hard sessions. C
  • Any training, intervals included, shifts the fuel mix towards fat; burning more fat has not made anyone faster. B

Chapter 8: Why elite athletes ride easy

Draft · 4,395 words · 27 October 2026

Eleven Norwegian cross-country skiers and biathletes kept a diary of every training session in the year that led to the best result of their careers. Each had won at least one individual Olympic or world championship gold medal. Researchers at the Norwegian Olympic Federation later added the diaries up. The athletes had trained for 770 hours each on average, in 470 sessions, which is about 15 hours a week across the whole year. Of the time they spent on endurance training, 91% was below the first lactate threshold [1].

These records are usually read as a recipe: four easy sessions to one hard one, or 80/20. I think that takes the wrong number from the diaries. The same athletes logged about 1.3 hours a week above the first threshold in every phase of the year, spread over two or three sessions. Their easy training rose to 15 hours a week in summer and fell to 10 in the racing season [1]. The hard training looks like a fixed dose within an amateur’s reach, with easy hours added around it. If that reading is right, a seven-hour rider should copy the hard dose rather than the ratio. The diaries alone cannot establish it.

What the records show

Across sports, elite athletes do about four easy sessions for every hard one, and counted by time the easy share is higher still. Stephen Seiler, whose 2006 study of junior skiers opened Chapter 5, summarised the descriptive studies in 2010, which covered athletes of national and international standard training 10 to 13 times a week. They converged, he wrote, on about 80% of sessions at low intensity and about 20% built around hard work such as intervals. They appeared to “self-organize” towards a high volume of training with hard sessions applied carefully [2]. As Chapter 5 explained, that 80% is a share of sessions, not of time. Counted in minutes the same training comes out nearer 90 or 95% easy, because most of a hard session is warm-up, recovery and cool-down [s1]. The eleven champions show both figures at once: 77% of their sessions were easy, and 91% of their time [1].

From here on a distribution is written as three percentages of training time: below the first threshold, between the thresholds, and above the second. The champions’ was 91 / 3 / 5.

Other sports show the same first number. Thirty-six German junior rowers of national and international standard rowed at 95 / 2 / 3 over a 37-week season [3]. World-class distance runners cover at least 80% of their distance at low intensity all year round [s2].

Where the records disagree is in how the remainder is split. A distribution with more time above the second threshold than between the thresholds is called polarised, and one with more between them is called pyramidal. When Thomas Stöggl and Billy Sperlich reviewed the published records in 2015 they found that most described a pyramid. Polarised distributions turned up in three studies of cross-country skiers and one of marathon runners [4]. The name that became attached to elite training describes a minority of the elite training on record.

Road cycling doesn’t fit so neatly: professional cyclists spend far more of their time between the thresholds than the 2 to 3% of the rowers and the champions in the figure. Thirteen professionals followed through a season spent 11 to 17% of their riding there [8,4], and eight who wore heart rate monitors through a Tour de France spent almost a quarter of the race there [5]. The shape is still a pyramid: a 2025 study of 28 riders from the sport’s top division found one in every phase of the season [s3].

The figure’s two other cycling groups sit at the extremes. The 30 under-23 professionals in the bottom row do not fit the pattern at all [9]. Only 17 to 19% of their riding time was below the first ventilatory threshold, and 51 to 63% was between the thresholds. The German team-pursuit squad sits at the other end, at 94 / 4 / 2 for a track event that lasts about four minutes [6,4].

Part of the difference comes from the counting. Fifteen well-trained road cyclists had the same ten weeks of training sorted three ways. By heart rate it was 87 / 9 / 4. By power it was 80 / 9 / 12. By the riders’ own rating of each session it was 45 / 30 / 25 [s4]. The rest, I suspect, comes from the sport. A skier or runner training alone chooses the pace, and a cyclist in a road race or a group has it chosen for them.

How easy the easy hours are

The champions’ easy training was mostly below Zone 2. The Norwegian federation’s scale has five zones, and Chapter 5 placed its zones 1 and 2 both below the first threshold. In the champions’ version zone 1 ran up to 73% of maximum heart rate, with blood lactate under 1.2 mmol/L. Zone 2 ran from 74 to 83%, with lactate of 1.3 to 2.0 mmol/L. That Zone 2 is the band this book calls Zone 2, the upper part of easy. The champions spent 86.0% of their endurance training time in zone 1 and 5.3% in Zone 2; in the summer preparation phase that was 14.3 hours a week against 0.9 [1].

For professional cyclists I found no record separating the easy hours this way. Tadej Pogačar gave his own account in a September 2024 podcast interview, as the reigning Tour de France champion [10]. As it was reported, he put his Zone 2 at 320 to 340 W and said that on flat roads he will ride in it for five hours. He added that by the end the power has slipped to about 300 W [11,12]. He weighed about 65 kg at that year’s Tour [10], which puts his Zone 2 at roughly 5 W/kg. The 14 trained cyclists and triathletes of Chapter 9, who rode about nine hours a week, reached their first threshold at 217 W [s5]. He judges the zone, he said, from heart rate, power, speed and how he feels [10].

An interview is not a training record, and his Zone 2 is whatever his team’s testing says it is. Taken at face value, it has the Tour de France champion doing his long rides in Zone 2, where the skiers do theirs below it.

Alistair Brownlee, the only triathlete to have won two individual Olympic titles, gave a similar account in September 2026, and his easy riding was much slower. As the episode’s notes give it, he trained about 35 hours a week at his peak and up to 40. Of that, 15 to 18 hours or more were on the bike, and only one or two were hard. His easy rides averaged about 200 W, from a rider with an FTP of over 400 W [13]. Those rides were at half his FTP or less, below the 56% of FTP at which Chapter 5 put the start of Coggan’s level 2 [s6]. His easy runs were at 5 minutes a kilometre, and his best 10 km works out at 2 minutes 51 a kilometre. Everyone who came to train with him, he said, was surprised by how slowly he went most of the time. He gave his reason too: to do “the maximum volume possible and protect the really hard sessions, the vast majority of that volume had to be as easy as possible” [13]. His test of an easy session was that he came back from it feeling better than when he set out.

I think the skiers, the triathlete and the cyclist are all following the same rule with different numbers. Chapter 7’s rule for an easy ride is that it should carry as much work as it can without taking anything from the hard sessions. For a rider on six to ten hours a week, that means Zone 2. In summer the skiers fitted 15 easy hours a week around their hard sessions, in ten sessions, working their arms as well as their legs [1]. An hour near the top of the easy range burns carbohydrate far faster than an hour lower down [s7]. For them the intensity that leaves the hard sessions untouched is a low one, and Brownlee, on 35 hours, said as much. Pogačar’s account suggests that on a bike a professional can make five hours of Zone 2 a regular part of his week. A rider with seven hours, and a day or more between hard sessions, has more room than either and gives up work by riding lower. Nothing in these records tests that reading, and the skiers’ figures come from diaries in which the athlete assigns each part of a session to a zone. C

How the pattern came about

A 2023 review of a century of distance-running training traced most practices to trial and error [14]. From the 1930s to the 1950s the leading runners trained on intervals: Emil Zátopek, the Czech Olympic champion, ran sessions of 40 or 60 repetitions of 400 metres. In the 1960s the New Zealand coach Arthur Lydiard argued against the hard interval programmes. He built his runners’ preparation on 10 to 12 weeks of mostly easy continuous running, aiming at 100 miles a week. His athletes Peter Snell and Murray Halberg won four Olympic gold medals between them from 1960 to 1964. By the 1970s and 1980s many international runners had combined Lydiard’s volume with interval sessions. The pattern of hard days and easy days is usually credited to the Oregon coaches Bill Bowerman and Bill Dellinger [14].

Rowing left numbers. Twenty-eight Norwegian rowers won international medals between 1970 and 2001, and 21 of them answered a detailed questionnaire about how they had trained. Between the 1970s and the 1990s the medallists’ easy training went from 30 hours a month to 50, and their training at race pace and above fell from 23 hours a month to about 7. Their total volume rose by a fifth. Over the same period their VO2max rose by 12% and their six-minute ergometer performance by almost 10% [15].

Dutch speed skaters made the same move without the extra hours. Across ten Olympic cycles from 1972 to 2010 the programmes of the medal winners went from 40 / 40 / 20 to about 80 / 12 / 8, with no trend in the total hours trained [4][s8].

All of this is observation, and it points one way: athletes and squads did better as their training became bigger and easier. It cannot show that the training was the cause. Over the same decades altitude camps were added to the rowers’ winters [15], and equipment, coaching and the number of people competing for a seat will have changed as well. A medal table also holds only the athletes a training system suited. The rower who broke down on 1,100 hours a year is not among the 28. C

Why it might work

The champions’ steady hard dose suggests a limit to how much hard training they could usefully do. Their two weekly hard sessions rose to three before a championship, about 100 sessions a year [1].

Recovery is the likely reason for the ceiling. In Seiler’s highly trained runners of Chapter 6, heart rate variability was back to normal 5 to 10 minutes after an easy session and about 30 minutes after a harder one. In less trained people the harder sessions took far longer to recover from [s9]. Seiler’s 2010 review found no convincing evidence that giving already well-trained athletes more hard training produced lasting gains [2]. One group in the trial described later in this chapter did 27 interval sessions in nine weeks [16]. It gained less than a group that did 14 alongside far more easy training, and lost 3.7% of its body weight on the way.

Once the hard training is at its ceiling, the only training left to add is easy, which was Chapter 7’s argument. What the added hours do is less certain, and the candidates are all long-term. They raise the total training load, which was the best predictor of mitochondrial content in the largest analysis of the question [s10]. They may build the things that change over years and that short studies miss, the capillaries and the heart of Chapter 2 and the durability of Chapter 9. The reason coaches most often give is that the hours teach the body to run on fat. That did not survive Chapter 7: intervals shift the fuel mix as well, and burning more fat did not make athletes faster. Reviews of elite training have also suggested that long easy sessions and short hard ones reach the muscle by different routes. One is the calcium signal of many thousands of contractions, the other the energy signal of a few very hard minutes. A programme with both would then get more than either gives alone [14][s11]. Nobody has shown that they add up in the way the suggestion needs. C

The polarised idea makes a second claim, with less support: that training between the thresholds should be kept small, because it costs as much to recover from as harder training and achieves less. Seiler’s runners support the first half: a session between the thresholds took the same 30 minutes to recover from as intervals above the second [s9]. The records give the second half little support. Most elite distributions are pyramids [4]. And the Norwegian runners who have lately won Olympic and world titles follow a model built on the middle. It has three or four interval sessions a week at a blood lactate of 2 to 4.5 mmol/L, checked with a meter during the session. There is one session near VO2max, and the week holds 150 to 180 km of running in all. One of the authors of the paper that describes it is Marius Bakken, the 5,000-metre runner who worked the method out on himself in the late 1990s. His reason was that holding lactate down let him do much more fast running in a week than harder intervals had allowed [14].

In 2022 the journal Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise printed two papers back to back. One, with Seiler among its authors, was titled “Polarized Training Is Optimal for Endurance Athletes” [17]. The other was titled “Polarized Training Is Not Optimal for Endurance Athletes” [18].

The pyramid, the polarised week and the Norwegian threshold model share a very large volume of easy training and a hard part controlled closely enough to be repeated every week for years. Where exactly the hard part sits looks to me like the smaller choice. C

Selection is the remaining explanation. These are full-time athletes who train eight to ten times a week, and the men among the champions had a VO2max of 85 mL/kg/min [1]. What suits a person selected for the work is weak evidence for what suits anyone else.

What the trials found

No trial has assigned Olympic champions to a training programme. Stöggl and Sperlich wrote that neither elite athletes nor their coaches like to have training altered for an experiment [16]. The trials that exist used club and national-level athletes, for six weeks to five months.

The one crossover trial in cyclists favoured polarised training. In 2013, twelve trained men did two six-week blocks in random order, with four weeks of detraining between. One was polarised, at 80 / 0 / 20 on 6.4 hours a week; the other was threshold-heavy, at 57 / 43 / 0 on 7.5 hours a week. Their 40 km time trial improved after both blocks. Peak power rose by 8% after the polarised block against 3%, and power at the lactate threshold by 9% against 2%. Time to exhaustion at a hard fixed power rose by 85% against 37% [19].

One study, up close: four ways to train for nine weeks

The largest of the early trials was run by Stöggl and Sperlich in Salzburg and published in 2014 [16].

Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionPolarised training gave the greatest improvements in most of the key measures of endurance. Threshold and high-volume training gave no further improvement.

The distributions are counts of sessions. The polarised group is described as 68 / 6 / 26, which means that 14 of its 54 sessions were interval sessions. Each held 16 minutes of hard effort. By my arithmetic from the paper’s table, that is under four hours of intervals in 104 hours of training, less than 4% of the time [16].

The groups did not train for the same number of hours: over the nine weeks the polarised group trained 38 hours more than the interval group [16]. Only the comparison with the high-volume group is free of that difference.

That comparison has a problem of its own. Before the trial every athlete had been training the high-volume way, with at most two threshold sessions a week, and none had been doing intervals regularly. The high-volume group therefore carried on as before, and the authors say that this may be why it did not improve. The polarised group kept its volume and was given something new. What the trial shows most securely is that adding two interval sessions a week to a high-volume programme raised VO2peak in athletes who had not been doing intervals. It does not show that a ratio was responsible.

Nothing was raced, and the authors list the absence of a time trial as a limitation.

Four of the seven athletes who dropped out came from the threshold group, and among those who stayed in it the change in VO2peak ran from a gain of 4% to a loss of 20% [16]. A fifth of a trained athlete’s VO2peak does not disappear in nine weeks of training three threshold sessions a week. Illness or a bad test is a likelier explanation, and in a group that had lost four of its members one such result moves the average a long way.

The headline number is also very large. The authors themselves wrote that an 11% rise in nine weeks in athletes of this standard “has to be put in perspective” [16]. Chapter 4 explained why the largest results from the smallest groups are the ones most likely to shrink when the experiment is repeated.

Reading the research: an effect that shrank

Three pooled analyses of polarised training have been published, each larger than the last.

The 2025 analysis was by the author of the 2019 one, working with the people who had run many of the trials, Seiler among them. It found no difference in VO2max either [22]. The 2024 analysis still found VO2peak favouring polarised training, by 0.24 of a standard deviation, with an interval that only just excluded zero. That advantage appeared only in programmes shorter than 12 weeks and in highly trained athletes. The authors pointed out that the highly trained athletes were in the short studies, so the two could not be told apart [21].

Pooling three small trials doesn’t remove the selection problem in Chapter 4. The trials most likely to be published are the ones with large effects, so an early meta-analysis can inherit their exaggeration. As more trials accumulated here, the time-trial advantage disappeared.

The same caution applies to what the later analyses found in subgroups. The 2025 paper reports that competitive athletes gained more VO2max from polarised training and recreational athletes more from pyramidal [22]. Chapter 4 listed the subgroup among the signs that a finding may not last, and this one has not yet been tested by a trial designed to look for it.

Cyclists have a pooled analysis of their own. Published in 2025, it took in 41 studies of trained cyclists, with 797 riders in 81 training groups. Training improved VO2max and time trial performance. Programmes classed as polarised did no better than those that were not. Longer programmes did better than shorter ones, and the volume of training, by the week or in total, showed no relationship with the size of the gain [23].

Among programmes that are mostly easy and contain some hard work, no way of dividing the hard work has been shown to make athletes faster than another over 4 to 16 weeks [21,22,23]. B Whether one does better over years is unknown, because nobody has run the trial. C

The programmes shared a large amount of easy training with some hard work. The evidence gives little reason to choose between polarised and pyramidal versions of that mix.

Six to ten hours a week

The athletes in the records train 15 to 20 hours a week [1,15]. Most readers of this book train less than half of that.

At an amateur’s hours, the mix made little difference in the two trials that tested it, both in recreational runners. Thirty of them trained for ten weeks at about 77 / 3 / 20 or 46 / 35 / 19. The first group improved its 10 km time by 5.0% and the second by 3.6%, a difference that was not statistically significant [s12]. Thirty-eight more trained for eight weeks at 77 / 3 / 20 or 40 / 50 / 10, with the two programmes matched for training load. Both groups improved by similar amounts, and the group that did more of its running between the thresholds got there in 24.8 hours of training against 29.9 [s13]. Nothing here says the mix matters much at these volumes, and one trial says the threshold-heavy mix saves time.

The better way to use the elite example is to copy the amount of hard training and ignore the ratio. The champions did about 1.3 hours a week above the first threshold, in two or three sessions [1]. In a seven-hour week that much hard training is 19% of the time. For the champions in summer it was 8%. A seven-hour rider who trained to that percentage would do about half an hour of hard riding a week, far less than the champions did themselves.

Volume still counts for those who are adapted to it. When 18 male professionals were confined to indoor trainers for seven weeks in 2020, their training fell by a third, to about 12 hours a week with 2 of those hours at high intensity. Most readers of this book would call that a training camp. Every one of them lost power over 5 and 20 minutes, by between 1% and 19% [s14]. Those riders had also lost racing, the road and their routines, so the lost hours cannot be isolated. It is still a warning against reading this chapter as an argument that hours do not matter.

For a rider on these hours, the elite example says to decide the hard sessions first and let the easy riding, and the percentages, follow. Chapter 17 builds the week that way.

Elite practice lends little support to Zone 2 in particular: most of the champions’ easy hours were below it [1]. The case for riding near the top of the range remains Chapter 7’s practical judgement for riders with fewer hours.

What survives
  • Champions spend about 91% of their training time below the first threshold. C
  • Their hard training is a steady dose of about 1.3 hours a week. C
  • No way of dividing the hard work has beaten another over 4 to 16 weeks. B
  • Copy the volume and the steady hard dose, not the ratio. C
