Chapter 9: Durability

Draft · 5,304 words · 27 October 2026

175 kilometres alone

The final stage of the 2026 Tour de Luxembourg ran 177 km from Mersch to the Limpertsberg district of Luxembourg City. Mathieu van der Poel rode clear in the opening kilometres and stayed clear to the line. He said afterwards that it hadn’t been the plan. He had found himself alone and assumed the chasers would come back. With 45 km to go, when the bunch swept up the riders who had been pursuing him, he still had three and a half minutes in hand, and he won by 1:04 from Mikkel Honoré [1].

Tadej Pogačar has made a habit of the same thing from shorter range. At Strade Bianche in March 2024 he attacked on the Monte Sante Marie gravel sector with 81 km left and won by 2:44. At the World Championships in Zürich that September he rode the last 50 km alone and held off Ben O’Connor by 34 seconds [2].

Van der Poel’s lead came down by almost two and a half minutes in the last 45 km [1]. That could be a rider fading or a bunch finally racing for the finish. His power files haven’t been released, so nobody outside his team can say how much he faded.

VO2max, the fraction of it you can sustain, and efficiency are usually measured on a fresh rider. Four or five hours into a race, what matters is how much of that capacity remains. I have felt the difference well below the level of a World Championship.

From the saddle. In 2025 I rode a tour of the Pyrenees. On the fourth day I was really struggling, while one of my friends in particular seemed to be getting stronger. He’s an ex-professional golfer and spends a lot of his time on the golf course.

Most durability research concerns a single long ride, so it cannot yet explain our fourth day in the Pyrenees. It has begun to measure why some riders fade more than others.

What durability is, and what to call it

In 2021 a group led by Ed Maunder in Auckland argued that physiologists had been profiling athletes in the wrong state. Stephen Seiler, whose work on training intensity runs through this book, was among the authors. Lab tests are done rested. The qualities those tests measure shift during long exercise, and they shift by different amounts in different people. Maunder and his colleagues proposed the word durability for this, and defined it as when, and by how much, an athlete’s physiological characteristics deteriorate during prolonged exercise [3].

Three years later Andrew Jones made the stronger claim. He is the Exeter physiologist whose lab worked with Nike’s two-hour marathon project. He argued that this quality belongs in the Joyner and Coyle model as a fourth factor alongside the original three, and he called it physiological resilience: the ability to resist functional decline under stress [4]. The two terms describe the same thing. This book uses durability, because that is the word cyclists and coaches have adopted. It is also easier to say on a climb.

The most direct way to measure durability is to test a rider fresh, tire them, and test them again. The clearest examples come from Jones’s own lab. In one study, 16 men did a three-minute all-out test fresh, and again after 40 minutes, 80 minutes and two hours of steady riding [5]. The test estimates critical power, the boundary described in Chapter 1 above which every effort has a time limit, and W′, the small reserve of work available above it. Critical power was 260 W fresh, 268 W after 40 minutes and 260 W after 80 minutes. After two hours it was 236 W, a fall of 9%. W′ went sooner: it was down 18% by 80 minutes and 23% by two hours. So the reserve you draw on for attacks and short climbs drains first, and critical power stays put for a surprisingly long time and then drops.

The riders in that study were competitive amateurs with an average VO2peak of 52.5 mL/kg/min, much like the readers of this book and nothing like van der Poel. And the two-hour ride that cost them 9% of their critical power averaged 164 W, about 64% of their VO2peak at the start [5]. That is a steady endurance ride just above the top of Zone 2. Nobody was being broken.

Riders differed far more than the average suggests. Across three studies from the same lab, the fall in critical power after two hours averaged about 10%, but individual riders ranged from under 1% to about a third [4]. B On a fresh critical power of 260 W, that is the difference between losing a watt or two and losing more than 80.

A second way needs no lab. Researchers with access to professional riders’ power files look for each rider’s best efforts over set durations. Then they look again at the best efforts produced after a given amount of work has already been done that day. The work is counted in kilojoules per kilogram of body weight, the same kilojoules a bike computer shows. For a 70 kg rider, 45 kJ/kg is 3,150 kJ, roughly four and a half hours at an average of 195 W.

A third is to watch what drifts during a long steady effort: heart rate climbing at constant power, or the oxygen cost of that power creeping up. This is the version you can observe on your own rides, and the thresholds that define your training zones drift too.

In 2022 Maunder’s group took 14 trained cyclists and triathletes, people training about nine hours a week, and measured the power at their first ventilatory threshold (VT1), which marks the top of Zone 2. Then the riders did two hours at 90% of that power, an average of 194 W, and the threshold was measured again [6]. It had fallen from 217 W to 196 W, a drop of 10%. Individual falls ranged from about 9 W to 44 W. The heart rate at the threshold had moved the other way, from 142 to 151 bpm.

After two hours of riding in Zone 2, then, the top of Zone 2 was 21 W lower and 9 bpm higher than the fresh test said [6]. A rider holding fixed power drifts towards the threshold from below. A rider holding fixed heart rate sees their power sink. One caution: the riders had fasted overnight and drank only water, and the authors expect the shift to be smaller in someone who has eaten and is taking in carbohydrate. There was also no control trial in which the riders simply sat for two hours between tests, although it is hard to see why sitting would lower a threshold by 10%. B

How it works

Rising oxygen cost and falling oxygen delivery both help explain why sustainable power declines. Neither yet explains why one rider loses 1% and another 30% [4,7].

Start with what critical power is. Below it, oxygen uptake rises when you start riding and then settles. Above it, oxygen uptake keeps climbing until it reaches VO2max and you have to stop. Critical power is the highest power at which uptake can still settle. It follows that critical power will fall with anything that raises the oxygen cost of each watt, or lowers the amount of oxygen the body can deliver. Nothing need have gone wrong in the usual sense of the word.

Take the cost first. In the two-hour rides from Jones’s lab, the power was held constant and oxygen uptake was not. In one study the same power went from 64% to 68% of VO2peak over the two hours [5]; in another, from 65% to 72% [8]. The rider’s computer shows the same number throughout while the body works progressively harder to produce it.

Part of this is fuel. As a ride goes on and carbohydrate stores run down, the muscles burn proportionally more fat. In the second of those studies, carbohydrate use fell from 1.77 to 1.17 grams a minute while fat use rose from 0.68 to 1.08 [8]. Fat is the larger store by far, but it needs more oxygen than carbohydrate does to produce the same amount of ATP [7]. Jones and his colleague Brett Kirby estimate that the change in fuel accounts for roughly 30% of the rise in oxygen uptake over two hours.

A second contributor is which muscle fibres are doing the work. Chapter 1 introduced type I fibres, the slow, efficient ones. They are recruited first and do most of the work at moderate power. As those fibres tire or run low on glycogen, the nervous system has to call on fibres further up the recruitment order to keep the power constant. Those type II fibres can produce the force, but they use more ATP and more oxygen to do it [7]. The power on the screen is unchanged while a more expensive set of fibres is producing a growing share of it. The reviews favour this as the explanation for much of the rest of the rising oxygen cost. It is well supported as a general principle of how muscle is recruited. Nobody has measured how much of the fall in critical power it accounts for in any particular rider.

Delivery is the other side. Over a long ride you lose fluid as sweat, which lowers blood volume. Your core temperature rises, and the skin, which needs blood to shed heat, competes with the working muscles for it. The heart fills a little less with each beat and beats faster to compensate. This is cardiovascular drift, the slow rise in heart rate at constant power that everyone who rides with a heart rate monitor has seen. In the Auckland study heart rate rose 8.2% over two hours at constant power [6]. If the drift goes far enough, the maximum amount of oxygen the heart can deliver falls, and VO2max, the thresholds and critical power can fall with it [7].

Heat makes all of this worse, and it is the mechanism I have felt most directly, as Chapter 15 describes. Part of what feels like fading legs is the circulation.

These changes compound: critical power falls as each watt costs more oxygen and less oxygen can be delivered.

Then there is glycogen. The oldest explanation for fading late in a ride is that the muscles run out of stored carbohydrate, and nobody doubts that glycogen matters in long exercise. What Jones’s lab found is that it doesn’t neatly explain the fall in critical power. They took muscle biopsies from 14 men before and after two hours of riding. Glycogen fell by about 65% and critical power by about 11%. But the riders who lost the most glycogen were not the riders who lost the most critical power: the correlation between the two was 0.19, which is close to none [8].

That result is often repeated as “it’s not about glycogen”, which goes further than the data. The authors themselves point out that a biopsy samples a tiny piece of one muscle, and that a real relationship could be hidden by that alone. A study of 14 people is also too small to detect a relationship of moderate size reliably, a problem the Reading the research box in this chapter returns to. The fair summary is that in these data, glycogen loss did not predict who faded most. The same study found that the rise in oxygen cost did not predict it either. The two most obvious explanations both fail to account for the differences between riders, and the question is open. C

Carbohydrate during the ride is a clearer story. When the riders in the earlier study repeated the two-hour ride drinking 60 grams of carbohydrate an hour, their critical power afterwards was 254 W [5]. On a placebo it was 236 W, and fresh it was 260 W. Carbohydrate removed most of the fall. It did so without sparing muscle glycogen, which dropped by almost the same amount in both trials. Blood glucose and the rate of carbohydrate burning late in the ride were higher with the drink. The authors’ reading is that a steady supply of glucose from the blood kept the working fibres going.

This also suggests why training might improve durability, and here the chapter moves from evidence to inference. If the trouble starts when type I fibres tire and more costly fibres take over, then anything that lets type I fibres carry the load for longer should delay it. That means more capillaries around them, more mitochondria inside them and a greater capacity to burn fat. Those are among the adaptations to endurance training described in Chapter 2. It is a plausible chain of reasoning, and it is the reasoning behind the long easy ride.

What the professionals show

Professional cyclists are the best-studied group in this field, for a practical reason. They race with power meters, their teams keep every file, and a season of racing contains maximal efforts made at every stage of fatigue.

The study with the most riders comes from a Spanish group led by Manuel Mateo-March [9]. It used data collected between 2013 and 2021 from 112 male professionals: 66 from the WorldTour, the sport’s top division, and 46 from ProTeams, the division below. It reports anonymous groups, so it cannot tell us about van der Poel or Pogačar individually. For each rider the researchers found the best power ever recorded for durations from 10 seconds to two hours. Then they found the best for the same durations after 15, 25, 35 and 45 kJ/kg of work that day.

Power fell at every duration as the work mounted up. After 15 kJ/kg the losses were between 1.6% and 3.0%, depending on the duration. After 45 kJ/kg they were between 6.0% and 9.7% [9].

The comparison between divisions is what made the study widely cited. Fresh, the WorldTour riders and the ProTeam riders were hard to tell apart: their best power did not differ consistently. After 45 kJ/kg the WorldTour riders had lost 4.7% to 8.8% and the ProTeam riders 7.6% to 11.6%. The gap showed mainly in efforts of five minutes and longer [9]. On these figures, what separates the top division from the second is less what riders can do in the first hour than what they can still do in the last.

A smaller study found the same pattern inside a single race. During the 2020 Vuelta a España, eight WorldTour and seven ProTeam riders were compared week by week. Fresh, the WorldTour riders were better only over 30 minutes. After 35 kJ/kg they were better over 30 seconds, one minute, five minutes, 20 minutes and 30 minutes [s1]. That study is as close as the research comes to my fourth day in the Pyrenees, and with 15 riders it is a small one. B

In a lab study of trained amateurs described later in this chapter, three hours at 169 W came to 24 kJ/kg [10]. The professionals’ 45 kJ/kg is nearly double that. It describes the closing stages of a long professional race, a state few amateurs ever ride themselves into.

The “fatigued” figures are the best efforts a rider happened to make late in a ride. Nobody asked him to make them. A rider produces a maximal five-minute effort after 45 kJ/kg only if the race makes it worth doing. That means being in the front group on the last climb. A domestique who has finished his work for the day rides in at whatever pace gets him to the bus. Better riders are more often in the finale, so they have more chances to record a high number late on. Some of the gap between divisions may be opportunity. This is my own reading of the method, and I have not seen the size of the effect estimated.

A second complication is that kilojoules are a blunt measure of how tired someone is. Two thousand kilojoules ridden steadily in the bunch and 2,000 that include repeated attacks are different days. A group led by Peter Leo counted only the work done above critical power. In under-23 riders, power for efforts of a minute or longer fell significantly after 5 kJ/kg of it, while professionals held on until 7.5 kJ/kg [s2]. A 2026 systematic review of 21 studies reached the same conclusion more generally: hard work does more damage per kilojoule than easy work [11]. It found losses of 10% to 20% reported after as little as 2.5 to 15 kJ/kg of high-intensity riding. For anyone comparing their own files, the lesson is to compare like with like. Power after three steady hours and power after a three-hour chain gang are answers to different questions.

Whether durability can be read off an ordinary lab test is disputed. In the amateur riders tested in Jones’s lab, the fall in critical power was unrelated to VO2max or to critical power when fresh [7]. In 10 young professionals studied by James Spragg and colleagues, the change in critical power after a set of hard efforts correlated very strongly with VO2max, threshold power and efficiency [12]. The correlations ran from 0.74 to 0.89. Ten riders is a very small group for claims of that kind, and the Reading the research box below explains why those numbers deserve less trust than they seem to. A Danish study found the opposite in 12 elite and professional road cyclists fed 100 grams of carbohydrate an hour. None of the same measures taken fresh, peak fat burning among them, predicted how much six-minute power they lost over four hours, and nor did the fat they burned along the way [13]. With 12 riders, it is hardly larger. For now the fair statement is that nobody knows whether durability is a separate quality or mostly a reflection of being fit.

What trains it

No long-term trial has set out to find which training best improves durability. Jones and Kirby’s 2025 review describes the data as “scant”: one 10-week training trial in beginners, one strength-training study in trained cyclists, and comparisons of trained with untrained, faster with slower, and professionals with under-23s [7].

Take the comparisons first. Over an hour at the same relative intensity, trained runners drift less than active adults who don’t run. In one study of 20 people, the relative intensity rose by 2.6% in the trained group and 8.3% in the others [s3]. Faster runners lose less running economy over 90 minutes than slower ones, 2.4% against 4.5% in a study of 44 men [s4]. The same study, as Jones and Kirby describe it, found that among runners of similar ability, those who regularly ran for longer than 90 minutes held their economy better than those who didn’t [7]. Professionals fade less than under-23s. Each comparison points the same way, and none can separate cause from effect. People who are naturally durable may find long sessions easier and so do more of them.

Spragg’s group came closer by following 30 under-23 professionals through a season. Riders who spent more time below the first threshold improved their two-minute power when fatigued, and riders whose training became more polarised improved their fatigued 12-minute power [14]. The correlations were around 0.4. A correlation of that size is loose, and it is still observation: nobody was assigned to ride more easy hours.

The one trial that assigned people to easy or hard riding comes from Finland. Pekka Matomäki and colleagues took 35 sedentary or recreationally active adults and gave them 10 weeks of either low-intensity riding, averaging 6.8 hours a week, or high-intensity intervals, averaging 1.6 hours a week [15]. Before and after, each did a three-hour ride at an easy fixed power while the researchers tracked how much heart rate, energy cost and other measures drifted, and when the drift began.

Durability improved in both groups, and by about the same amount. In the low-intensity group the average drift went from 7.7% to 6.3% and its onset moved from 106 to 131 minutes, changes that fell just short of statistical significance. In the interval group the drift went from 8.8% to 5.4% and the onset from 108 to 137 minutes, both significant [15]. There was no significant difference between the groups.

In that trial, training of either kind made beginners more durable. Four times the hours of easy riding bought no more durability than the intervals did. And the changes were small. It can’t tell you what happens in a rider with five years of training behind them, or over a year instead of 10 weeks. The reviews’ main suggestion is precisely that durability comes from volume accumulated over years [7]. A 10-week trial cannot test that idea. B for the claim that training improves durability in untrained people.

My friend in the Pyrenees spends a lot of his time on the golf course. If he walks his rounds, that is many hours a week of very low-intensity exercise, kept up for years. It fits the volume-over-years idea, though a single golfer proves nothing.

The study in trained cyclists was of strength training. Bent Rønnestad’s group in Norway had 11 well-trained cyclists add heavy leg strength training twice a week for 12 weeks while nine carried on with endurance training alone [s5]. Afterwards each rode for just over three hours at an easy pace and then did a five-minute all-out effort. The strength group’s power in that effort rose from 371 W to 400 W. The control group’s didn’t change. It is one study of 20 riders, but it is an intervention in trained cyclists, measured late in a long ride, and the thing that worked was heavy weights. It belongs here as a reminder that the long ride is not the only candidate.

The case for the long easy ride rests on the mechanism, the comparisons between groups and Spragg’s season of data. No trial in trained riders has tested it. I think it is a reasonable bet. C

Fuelling is a different matter, because there the trials exist.

From the saddle. One thing I try to do is out-fuel the riders I’m riding with. I can be a bit of a greedy pig, but that often helps keep me at the front of the group and gives me a strong finish in sportives.

The study from Jones’s lab described earlier found that 60 grams of carbohydrate an hour removed most of the fall in critical power over two hours [5]. A larger and more recent trial tested whether more is better.

One study, up close: carbohydrate dose and critical power

In 2026 a group at Liverpool John Moores University recruited 16 trained cyclists and triathletes, 15 men and one woman. Their average age was 35 and their average VO2max 51.8 mL/kg/min. All trained more than five hours a week [10]. They are a fair match for the readers of this book.

Each rider’s critical power was measured fresh with a three-minute all-out test. Then, on three separate days at least six days apart, each rode for three hours at 95% of the power at their gas exchange threshold, which is the top of Zone 2 by another name. It averaged 169 W [10]. Straight afterwards they did the three-minute test again. On one day they drank only water, on another a drink supplying 60 grams of carbohydrate an hour, and on the third 120 grams an hour, as a mix of maltodextrin and fructose. The order was randomised and balanced, so that any effect of doing the rides first or last was spread evenly across the three conditions. This is a crossover design: every rider is compared with themselves, which removes the differences between people that swamp small studies.

The riders were well fed going in. For 24 hours before each ride they ate a supplied diet containing 8 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight, and they had a set breakfast [10]. Nobody started short of glycogen.

Fresh, critical power averaged 277 W. After three hours on water it was 236 W, a fall of about 15%. With 60 grams an hour it was 257 W, a fall of about 7%. With 120 grams an hour it was 266 W, a fall of about 4%. Each step was statistically significant. W′, the reserve above critical power, dropped by a similar amount whatever the riders drank [10].

The first step did most of the work: going from nothing to 60 grams an hour saved 20 W, and doubling it saved 9 W more. Stomach complaints were mild at every dose, though fullness and cramping scored higher at 120 grams than on water. And during the three-hour rides themselves, oxygen cost and efficiency did not differ between the drinks, so the carbohydrate was not working by making each watt cheaper. The riders on the highest dose could simply get closer to their VO2max in the final test [10].

The paper describes no attempt to disguise which drink was which, so the riders presumably knew when they were on water. A three-minute all-out test depends on how hard someone is willing to go. Fifteen of the 16 were men. Carbohydrate was supplied by a supplement company, although the funding came from a public research foundation. Critical power was estimated from a single short test, and the authors themselves think the method may have understated the fall. And it measured one all-out effort after one ride. So it shows carbohydrate protecting late-ride power on the day, and leaves open whether fuelling well in training makes you more durable in the long run. B

Reading the research: correlation and small samples

Spragg’s season-long study found that riders who spent more time below the first threshold improved their fatigued two-minute power, with a correlation of 0.43 [14]. Squaring a correlation gives the share of the variation it accounts for. Here that is 18%, which leaves 82% to everything else. Then there is the direction. Easy riding might build durability. Or the riders able to pile up easy hours might be those who are already durable, or simply healthy and uninjured that year. Or a third thing might drive both, such as a coach who prescribes more volume and better fuelling. An observational study can’t choose between these, however carefully it is done. Only assigning riders to different training can.

Spragg’s lab study found correlations as high as 0.89 between riders’ lab measures and the change in their critical power [12]. That looks close to proof. It came from 10 riders. With a sample that small, the true value could plausibly lie anywhere from about 0.6 to 0.97, by the standard calculation of a 95% confidence interval. For the weakest of the reported correlations, 0.74, the plausible range runs from about 0.2 to 0.93. The same arithmetic applies in the other direction to the glycogen result earlier in the chapter. A correlation of 0.19 from 14 riders is compatible with a true value anywhere between about −0.4 and 0.65, which covers everything from a moderate negative relationship to a strong positive one [8]. With 10 or 14 people, chance alone can produce a large correlation or hide a real one.

When a paper reports a correlation, look for the number of people before the size of r. Below about 30, treat a striking correlation as a reason to run a bigger study. What survives from this chapter’s correlations is a pointer, not a proof: over a real season, the riders who did more easy riding improved their power when fatigued.

What to do with it

Start by finding out how much you fade, because the range between riders is so wide that the average tells you little about yourself.

The simplest test needs a power meter and two rides. On the first, after a warm-up, ride as hard as you can for a fixed time: Spragg’s group used two, five and 12 minutes [14], and five or 12 suits most amateurs. A week or so later, do the same effort at the end of a ride of two and a half to three hours at your usual endurance pace, eating and drinking as you normally would. The percentage you lose is a rough measure of your durability. Keep the route, the fuelling and the temperature as similar as you can, and expect the result to move by a few per cent from one attempt to the next for no reason at all.

You can also watch drift without a hard effort. On a long ride at steady power, compare your average heart rate in the last half hour with the half hour after you warmed up. In the Finnish trial, untrained people drifted by 5% to 9% over three hours at an easy pace [15]; in the Auckland study, trained riders who had not eaten drifted 8.2% in two [6]. Heat and dehydration push the number up on their own, so compare cool day with cool day.

For Zone 2 training, the Auckland result has a direct consequence. If you ride at the very top of your zone by power, the top comes down to meet you, and after two hours you may be above it. If you hold a heart rate ceiling set from a fresh test, your power will sink further than it needs to, because the heart rate at the threshold rises as you tire [6]. Neither method is right late in a long ride. A reasonable rule of thumb, which no study has tested, is to set power 10 to 15 W under the top of the zone for rides over two hours, and to eat.

Eat on anything longer than about 90 minutes, which is roughly where critical power began to slide in Jones’s lab [5]. Sixty grams of carbohydrate an hour gets you most of the protection in the trials above. More helps a little further if your stomach accepts it, and that is worth practising in training before trying it in an event [10].

Then there is the long ride itself. Keep doing it. The mechanism is plausible, and the comparisons of durable and less durable athletes point to accumulated volume. Apart from fuelling and, on one study, the weights room, nothing else on offer has better evidence. But hold the belief at its proper strength. Suppose the next few years bring a trial showing that an hour of intervals builds as much durability in trained riders as it did in the Finnish beginners. That should change your mind, and it will change this chapter.

What survives
  • Over a long ride, riders lose anything from under 1% to about a third of their critical power. B
  • Carbohydrate during the ride protects late-ride power. B
  • The long ride is a reasonable bet for durability, not a proven one. C

Chapter 10: Beyond performance

Draft · 3,654 words · 27 October 2026

Between 1991 and 2014 the Cleveland Clinic put 122,007 patients through a treadmill test, and in 2018 its cardiologists checked how many of them had since died [1]. In the quarter of patients least fit for their age and sex, 23.7% had. Among the 3,570 whose fitness put them in the top 2.3%, the figure was 2.6%. After adjusting for age, smoking, diabetes, heart disease and the rest, the least fit carried five times the risk of death of the fittest. The authors wrote that being unfit was as dangerous as smoking or diabetes, or more so [1].

Figures like these are why Zone 2 is sold as medicine as well as training. Fitness predicts lifespan better than most things a doctor measures, steady riding builds fitness, and so an hour in Zone 2 is presented as an hour added to a life.

Fit and active people do live longer. How much of the difference comes from training, rather than the kind of person who becomes fit, is not known. The one long randomised trial found no significant reduction in deaths from adding supervised training to advice to follow activity guidelines. Trials do show that training lowers blood pressure and blood sugar. In the surveys, most of the lower risk arrives with the first few hours a week, well below a six-to-ten-hour rider’s volume. The health evidence gives that rider no reason to favour Zone 2 over intervals.

Fit people live longer

The Cleveland figures have limits that the headline leaves out. Fitness was not measured directly but estimated from the speed and slope of the treadmill when each patient stopped. And the patients were people sent for a test, mostly to look for heart disease or explain symptoms. The analysis left out the 38,828 patients who had a drug-based stress test instead of exercising, and those switched to one because they could not keep going [1].

The comparison with smoking also deserves a second look. The fivefold difference sets the least fit quarter against the top 2.3%, which is not the same kind of comparison as smokers against non-smokers. The smaller step, from just below average fitness to just above it, carried a hazard ratio of 1.41, exactly the figure for smoking [1]. A hazard ratio is how many times more often one group died at any point in the follow-up than the other, so 1.41 means 41% more. That smaller step is the one more readers could actually take, and it is still a large difference.

Surveys of activity tell the same story more modestly, because activity is a looser measure than fitness. In 2015 a group from the US National Cancer Institute pooled six cohorts in the United States and Europe: 661,137 adults, followed for a median of 14 years, who between them had 116,686 deaths [2]. They used the American guidelines as a yardstick: a minimum of 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week. People were grouped by how many multiples of that minimum they reported in their leisure time.

Even activity below the minimum went with 20% lower risk than none. At one to two times the minimum the figure was 31%, at two to three times 37%, and at three to five times 39%. After that the curve went flat: five to ten times the minimum also gave 39% [2]. People who reported ten times or more had 31% lower risk than the inactive, and the authors found no evidence of harm at that level. Their summary was that meeting the minimum gave nearly the maximum benefit [2].

Riding hours can be placed on that curve, roughly. A MET is the body’s resting rate of energy use, about 3.5 millilitres of oxygen per kilogram per minute. Take a rider with a VO2max of 55 mL/kg/min, close to the amateurs in the trials of Chapters 15 and 16. At 60% of it, which is near the first lactate rise in the two studies of Chapter 7’s fat-max figure, that rider uses about 33 mL/kg/min, or 9.4 METs. An hour of that is 9.4 MET-hours against the surveys’ weekly minimum of 7.5 [2]. So six hours a week is about seven and a half times the minimum, and ten hours about twelve and a half. A rider on six to ten hours is somewhere between the flat part of the curve and the far end of the data, where few of the people surveyed were. The surveys asked about walking, gardening, running and the like, and gave each activity a standard value, so this is a placing, not a calculation the study made.

The lowest intensities carry an association too. A 2019 analysis pooled eight cohorts in which 36,383 people wore movement sensors instead of describing their own activity. Over about six years, the most active quarter had 73% lower risk of death than the least active. Light activity on its own, the kind involved in slow walking and housework, followed the same pattern: 40%, 56% and 62% lower risk in the second, third and fourth quarters [3]. Time spent sitting ran the other way, with 2.63 times the risk in the most sedentary quarter.

Cycling has its own figures. In UK Biobank, 263,450 people who said how they travelled to work were followed for five years. Those who cycled had 41% lower risk of death from any cause than those who drove or took public transport, after adjustment for the usual factors. Those who walked had lower risk of heart disease but no significant difference in deaths overall [s1].

That fit and active people live longer is one of the most consistent findings in epidemiology. That the training is the reason is a separate claim. C

Reading the research: marker or cause

The question is as old as the field. In the 1950s Jeremy Morris and his colleagues in London found less coronary heart disease among the conductors of double-decker buses than among the drivers. The conductors climbed the stairs all day; the drivers sat. The group also found less among postmen than among civil servants at desks [s2]. Morris knew the obvious objection, that heavier and less healthy men might choose the driver’s seat. His group went on to study the physique of busmen from the sizes of the uniforms they were issued [s3].

The Cleveland authors could not tell whether high fitness picked out patients who were going to live longer anyway or made them live longer [1]. Illness, habits and inheritance could each contribute to the association.

The first is illness. People who are already becoming ill, before any diagnosis, walk less far on a treadmill and also die sooner. Leaving out the patients who could not exercise removes the most obvious cases and leaves the hidden ones in.

The second is habit. People who exercise also tend to smoke less, eat differently and go to the doctor, and adjustment catches only what was recorded.

The third is inheritance. Chapter 2 described how differently people respond to the same training, and some of the fitness a person has is fitness they were born with. If the same genes that make a person fit also protect them in other ways, fitness would predict a long life without training having anything to do with it.

Twins offer a test of the third. Finland has followed same-sex twins born before 1958 for decades, and asked about their exercise in 1975, 1981 and 1990. Across individuals, those who kept up vigorous exercise through all three surveys had 45% lower risk of death to 2013 than those who never did. After adjusting for education, smoking, alcohol, weight, work and health, the figure was 27% [4]. Then the researchers found the pairs in which one twin exercised throughout and the other never did. Among non-identical twins, who share about half their genes, the active twin had 42% lower risk. Among identical twins, who share all of them, there was no difference at all: a hazard ratio of 1.00 [4]. For the twin on the sofa, it is the best news in this chapter. An earlier analysis of the same cohort, over a shorter run of years, had found the same pattern [s4].

The identical-twin result rests on 34 pairs, and its 95% confidence interval runs from about half the risk to about twice it [4]. Thirty-four pairs cannot show that exercise does nothing. They are, though, the nearest thing in the observational data to a controlled comparison, and the benefit that every other analysis shows does not appear in them. The authors suggest that some of the same genes influence how much people exercise, how fit they are and how long they live. C

A hazard ratio compares groups that differ in many ways; it does not directly measure what happens when someone changes their behaviour. Fitness reliably marks out people who live longer. The trials below can tell us more about what training itself changes.

A trial of exercise and death

The only way to settle the question is a randomised trial. Death is rare enough that a trial needs thousands of people, years of follow-up or a population old enough to die in useful numbers. Researchers in Trondheim chose the third.

One study, up close: Generation 100

In 2012 they invited every resident of the city aged 70 to 77, 6,966 people, to five years of training, and 1,567 agreed [5].

Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionModerate training and intervals together had no effect on deaths compared with following the guidelines, with a trend towards fewer deaths after intervals than in the other two groups.

The confidence intervals show how little five years could settle. Against the control group, the interval group’s best estimate was 37% fewer deaths, with an interval running from 67% fewer to 20% more. The moderate group’s was 24% more, from 27% fewer to a little over twice as many [5].

The trial had the problem that every long exercise trial has: the control group would not sit still. At five years 69% of them still met the guidelines, about one in five had taken up interval training on their own, and only about half of each exercise group kept to its programme. The volunteers were also healthier than their neighbours. Deaths in the control group ran at less than half the 10% expected over five years among Norwegians of that age. The authors accept that a population this active may have had little room to gain [5]. A null result in people who were all exercising is not evidence that exercise does nothing.

Five years of supervised training added no measurable survival benefit for healthy, active 70-year-olds beyond following the guidelines. B The moderate sessions, at about 72% of peak heart rate and rated somewhat hard, were the nearest the trial came to steady Zone 2. Nobody measured whether they were below each person’s first threshold. The interval group ended with higher peak oxygen uptake than both others and better scores for physical and mental quality of life [5]. There were no heart problems during supervised sessions. The three injuries were fractures from falls on slippery ground, two of them in the moderate group.

What training does to the risk factors

Blood pressure falls with endurance training. A 2013 analysis of 93 randomised trials involving 5,223 healthy adults found an average fall of 3.5 mmHg in systolic and 2.5 mmHg in diastolic pressure [6]. The size depended on where people started. It was 8.3 and 5.2 mmHg in people with high blood pressure and about 2 in those slightly above normal. In people with normal pressure, systolic pressure fell by less than a millimetre, a fall that could have been zero. A

Blood sugar falls too. In 47 trials of people with type 2 diabetes, structured exercise lowered HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar over the previous two or three months, by 0.67 percentage points against controls [7]. Amount mattered: programmes of more than 150 minutes a week lowered it by 0.89 points and shorter ones by 0.36. Advice to exercise, without a programme, changed nothing unless it came with dietary advice. A

On intensity, the trials in patients lean the other way from the Zone 2 argument. In ten trials of 273 people with heart disease, high blood pressure, metabolic syndrome or obesity, interval training raised peak oxygen uptake by 3.03 mL/kg/min more than moderate continuous training. The authors describe that as almost double the gain [s5]. In 50 studies of interval training, insulin resistance fell more after intervals than after continuous training, by a small to moderate margin [8]. Both sets of trials were small and short, and their authors call for longer ones. B

Lower blood pressure and blood sugar give a reason to expect fewer heart attacks and strokes. These trials did not count those events, so they cannot tell us how much the risk fell.

Zone 2 as medicine, weighed

The case for Zone 2 as medicine starts from metabolic disease, in which the muscles burn fat poorly and let lactate build up. If Zone 2 is the intensity that best trains a muscle to burn fat and clear lactate, the argument goes, it must be the best exercise for metabolic health, and through that for a long life.

The observation about diseased muscle comes from the 2018 comparison in Chapters 6 and 7, which trained nobody [s6]. The Canadian review concluded that Zone 2 had not been shown to be the best intensity for either mitochondria or fitness [s7]. Nor do the trials above show it to be better: intervals did at least as well on fitness and insulin resistance, and the mortality trial’s non-significant trend favoured intervals.

What the argument gets right is that steady exercise is effective medicine. It lowers blood pressure and blood sugar, it is safe for nearly anyone, and it can be done in amounts that hard training cannot, which matters because the diabetes trials found that amount counted. For a person starting from nothing, with a heart condition, or who simply will not do hard sessions, steady riding is a sound prescription. That is a long way from saying it is a special one. C

Heart rhythm and arteries in lifelong athletes

Tour de France riders give the most extreme cycling data. Of the 786 French riders who started the race at least once between 1947 and 2012, 208 had died by 2012. Their death rate was 41% lower than that of Frenchmen of the same age, with fewer deaths from both cancer and heart disease [9]. The authors could not separate the effect of the riding from the selection of unusually healthy young men, or weigh it against the effects of very heavy training and doping.

The costs show up in the heart’s rhythm and its arteries. The study covered 52,755 people who completed the Vasaloppet, Sweden’s 90 km cross-country ski race, between 1989 and 1998. Those who had finished five or more times had 29% higher risk of atrial fibrillation than those who had finished once. Atrial fibrillation is an irregular rhythm of the heart’s upper chambers. They also had about twice the risk of an abnormally slow heart rhythm [10]. There was no link with the dangerous rhythms that cause cardiac arrest. The finding is stated for men.

In 284 men around 55 years old who played sport competitively or for recreation, CT scans looked for calcium in the coronary arteries. They found it in 68% of those with the most lifelong exercise, more than 2,000 MET-minutes a week, against 43% of those with under 1,000 [11]. But the most active men’s plaques were more often fully calcified and less often of the mixed kind, which the authors describe as a more benign composition. At the 9.4 METs of the example rider above, 2,000 MET-minutes a week is about three and a half hours of riding. So every rider this book is written for is in that top group.

The most active endurance athletes, then, have more atrial fibrillation and more calcified plaque, and they still lived longer than the general population in the Tour data and longer than the inactive in the surveys. For a rider on six to ten hours the balance looks favourable. A rider who notices palpitations, or a heart rate that behaves strangely, should see a doctor, not a training book. C

Colds

In the winter described in Chapter 7, when I rode more often and mostly easy, I fell ill less often with coughs and colds.

In 2011 David Nieman’s group followed 1,002 adults through 12 weeks of autumn and winter. People who did aerobic exercise five or more days a week had 43% fewer days with cold symptoms than those who did it once a week or less. The third who rated themselves fittest had 46% fewer than the least fit third, after adjusting for seven other factors [12]. The study was observational, and fitness was self-rated.

The same researcher’s earlier work raised the opposite worry, that a marathon or very heavy training leaves the immune system open to infection [s8]. That idea is now disputed. Those infections were self-reported. When a later study swabbed elite athletes who reported symptoms, only 11 of 37 episodes turned out to be infections; the rest may have been allergy, asthma or airways irritated by hours of heavy breathing [13].

So regular exercise goes with fewer colds, and big events and very heavy training may go with more, for reasons that may have little to do with the exercise. No study I found compared easy riding with intervals for infections. My winter fits the first finding, and it also fits the fact that I was riding more often. C

Weight

Chapter 7 dealt with the question of which fuel a ride burns and concluded that for weight it matters little. What matters is how much energy the riding uses. In the Midwest Exercise Trial, 141 overweight young adults exercised five days a week for ten months, burning either 400 or 600 calories a session, without being asked to change their diet. Among those who completed nearly all their sessions, weight fell by 3.9 kg and 5.2 kg, while the control group gained 0.5 kg [s9]. Across 50 studies of interval training, weight fell by 1.3 kg against controls [8]. Exercise alone takes off a few kilograms over months, in proportion to the work done, whatever the intensity. B

What to do with it

The large surveys place a rider on six to ten hours well into the part of the curve where more activity buys no more lower risk, or beyond the end of the data. Whatever exercise does for lifespan, that rider has most of it already, and nothing in the evidence says that the split between Zone 2 and intervals changes it. If the one trial points anywhere, it points to the intervals.

For someone riding mainly for health, the first few hours of weekly activity carry most of the association with a longer life, and the risk factors improve with any intensity. C In Generation 100, about half of each exercise group was still doing its programme after five years [5]. The best exercise for health is the one a person will keep doing.

What survives
  • Training lowers blood pressure and blood sugar. A
  • Most of the link between activity and a longer life comes with the first few hours a week. C
  • For health, Zone 2 is not shown to be special. C
  • The best exercise for health is the one you keep doing.

Part IIIThe hard part

Chapter 11: Designing intervals

Draft · 4,338 words · 27 October 2026

Harder intervals are not always better intervals. In 2013 Stephen Seiler’s group in Kristiansand tested this in recreational cyclists, much like the readers of this book. For seven weeks, three groups added two interval sessions a week to their easy riding: four efforts of 4, 8 or 16 minutes. A fourth group just rode easy. Nobody was given a target power. Each effort was ridden as hard as the rider could sustain for its length, so the longer the interval, the lower the intensity [1].

One study, up close: four ways to spend two sessions a week

Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionIntensity and accumulated duration interact. Accumulating 32 minutes of work at about 90% of maximum heart rate gave greater gains than accumulating 16 minutes at about 95%, although it felt easier.

The 4 × 8 group improved twice as much as any other. Its riders worked less intensely than the 4 × 4 group but accumulated twice as many hard minutes [1]. Going longer still, to 4 × 16, meant settling at about the second threshold and brought a smaller gain.

For a rider with two hard sessions a week, the finding is clear: doubling the work at a slightly lower intensity did more than squeezing half the work in at the very top. The trial was small, with eight or nine riders in each group, and it lasted seven weeks. But the 4 × 8 advantage didn’t come from one measure. That group’s gain was the largest in each of the three, and in a ride to exhaustion as well. The 4 × 4 riders rated their sessions much harder than the others did, and the authors could not rule out that they were still tired at the final tests. The easy-only group, who rode about a fifth more than before, gained 4.2%: seven weeks of riding more improves a rider whatever the sessions [1].

What works is enough intensity to be near your limit, held for enough minutes to add up to a substantial session. In trained cyclists long intervals have worked well, and so have 30/15s, sets of 30 seconds hard and 15 seconds easy [1,2]. Pick one or two formats you will ride hard, pace each set so you can finish it, and progress by adding work at that effort. B

What a hard session does: time near VO2max

Interval sessions are usually compared by how long they keep a rider near VO2max. Close to it, the heart is pumping as much blood as it can, and nearly every muscle fibre in the legs is working, the fast fibres as well as the slow. The usual argument is that this is the strongest signal the heart and the muscles receive. In a 2007 trial from Trondheim, two interval programmes raised the amount of blood the heart pumped per beat by about 10% [3]. In a 2017 Canadian study, ten active men trained one leg with intervals and the other with continuous cycling, matched for work. A marker of mitochondrial content rose further in the interval leg [s1]. Most studies count the minutes above 90% of VO2max, though the line is a convention.

The idea comes from one experiment. In 2000 Véronique Billat’s group put eight long-distance runners on a 400 m track with portable gas analysers and had them run two hard sessions [4]. In one they alternated 30 seconds at the speed that just brought out their VO2max with 30 seconds at half that speed. In the other they ran without stopping, at a speed halfway between their threshold and that top speed. Both sessions left about the same lactate in the blood. The stop-start session kept the runners at VO2max for 7 minutes 51 seconds, the continuous one for 2 minutes 42.

The reason lies in how slowly oxygen uptake moves. It does not jump to its new level when hard work starts. It rises over a minute or two, so a short effort ends before the body’s oxygen use has caught up with the demand. Above critical power (Chapters 1 and 5) it then keeps creeping upward until it reaches VO2max or the rider stops. That is how Billat’s continuous runners got there without running at their top speed. Oxygen uptake also falls slowly when the effort stops. Fifteen seconds of easy pedalling is too short for it to drop far, so a session of 30 seconds hard and 15 easy holds it high through the recoveries as well as the efforts [s2].

Twenty-five years of interval research has been organised around Billat’s result. A 2006 review of the running studies turned it into a recipe of efforts and recoveries lasting 15 to 30 seconds each. It also asked for more experiments on what such sessions build before competitive runners were advised to use them [s2].

Reading the research: a correlation inside a trial

Nobody has shown that time near VO2max is what produces the adaptation, rather than something that goes with it, such as the total amount of hard work. Until 2024 nobody had even measured oxygen uptake in every session of a training programme and then asked whether it predicted the result [5].

The main analysis was a regression across all 22; the authors also split the riders into halves by the average share of VO2max they reached [5].

Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionImprovements in endurance were positively related to the share of VO2max reached during interval training, and that share was the measure that best reflected how much each rider adapted.

VO2max was measured during the programme as well as before and after, so each session was compared with a current figure. The share of VO2max proved more repeatable from session to session than the share of maximum heart rate [5].

It cannot show that reaching a higher share caused the bigger improvements, and the table shows why. Every rider rode the same session at the same share of their own 40-minute power. Whether a rider reached 86% of VO2max or 80% was therefore a property of the rider, not of the session. The two halves were different groups of people before the training began, and they trained differently while it ran. The higher half rode two hours a week more, most of it in the lowest zone, and it started with a lower VO2max, which leaves more room to improve. The authors acknowledge that the extra volume “could have affected the results”, and judge that the share of VO2max was “most likely” responsible [5]. That judgement is reasonable, but it is a judgement, not a result.

Despite taking place inside a training programme, this was an observational comparison: the riders who did better also differed in other ways. Testing the cause would require random assignment to sessions that differ only in how close to VO2max they keep riders. I found no such trial. C The practical case rests on the randomised comparisons in this chapter, which favour accumulating work close to the top of what a rider can sustain.

Other routes to a bigger engine

Comparisons of whole programmes support a narrower claim: that intervals raise VO2max more than continuous training, by a modest margin. A 2015 analysis pooled 28 controlled studies in 723 healthy adults [6]. Intervals beat continuous training by 1.2 mL/kg/min on average, about 3% for a recreational rider, with a larger gap in less fit people and in longer programmes.

Intervals are not the only route. In 2024 a Canadian group randomised 84 young adults to six weeks of training in one of four intensity domains, each set from the person’s own thresholds [7]. Continuous riding in the upper part of the band between the thresholds raised VO2max by 5.4 mL/kg/min. That was nearly as much as intervals in the severe domain, at 6.2. All-out sprints, whose long rests leave little time near VO2max, raised it by 4.7. Riding below the first threshold, matched for work, raised it by 1.8, not significantly different from doing nothing.

Closest is not automatically best either. Seiler’s 4 × 4 riders worked nearer their ceiling than the 4 × 8 riders and gained half as much [1]. In people who are not very fit, almost any hard enough training raises VO2max, and time near it is one route among several. In trained riders the trials that improved VO2max mostly used intervals close to it, which is consistent with the idea without proving it. C

As a yardstick, though, it works. Between two sessions of the same length and effort, the one that keeps you closer to the ceiling for longer is probably the stronger stimulus for the heart and the oxygen system.

Long intervals

Four to eight minutes is the oldest and best-tested range. The best-known version is the Trondheim group’s 4 × 4 minutes, at 90% to 95% of maximum heart rate with three minutes of easy recovery. It has been used in heart patients as well as athletes [8].

Ride the different lengths in whatever order suits you. The largest trial of long intervals in cyclists, published in 2016, gave 63 riders 24 sessions over 12 weeks [9]. They rode 4 × 16, 4 × 8 and 4 × 4 minutes, all as maximal efforts, on top of a large amount of easy riding. One group rode four weeks of each, longest first; a second rode them shortest first; a third mixed all three throughout. Every group improved its 40-minute power, peak power and VO2peak by 5% to 10%, and the order made no difference.

30/15, and the catch

The session called 30/15 is three sets of 13 repetitions of 30 seconds hard and 15 seconds easy, with three minutes between sets [10]. That is 19.5 minutes of hard work in about 35 minutes. Fifteen seconds is long enough to decide that the next 30 seconds are impossible, which is about when they start.

In trained cyclists it has done at least as well as long intervals. In 2015 Bent Rønnestad’s group in Norway had 16 cyclists add two hard sessions a week to their easy training for ten weeks. One group rode 30/15s, the other 4 × 5 minutes, each as hard as they could sustain. VO2max rose 8.7% in the 30/15 group against 2.6% in the long-interval group. Every performance measure, from 30-second to 40-minute power, moved in favour of the short intervals [2]. A three-week version in 18 elite cyclists found no difference in VO2max, but 20-minute power rose 4.7% with the 30/15s and fell 1.4% with the long intervals [10].

At the same average power, the short format keeps a rider near VO2max for longer. In 2024 a Norwegian group had 11 women and 8 men ride 6 × 8 minutes at the same average power, either steady or as 30/15s. The 30/15 version gave 1,123 seconds above 90% of VO2max against 879, and the women responded as the men did [11].

The catch is that riders on the road do not ride at a fixed power. In 2025 twelve well-trained cyclists and triathletes rode 3 × 13 × 30/15 and 6 × 5 minutes twice each: once at powers the researchers set, and once as hard as they could manage [13]. At the set powers the 30/15 session won easily, with 420 seconds above 90% of VO2max against 178. Ridden all-out, both sessions gave far more, 1,130 seconds and 1,016, and the difference was no longer statistically significant. How hard a session is ridden changes its time near VO2max more than its format does.

So the Rønnestad trials support a narrower claim than their headline numbers. Both are small, both come from the group that designed the session, and both compared it with long intervals paced by the riders, which are hard to pace well. Thirty-fifteens make a large dose of work near the top easier to reach. That is a real advantage for anyone who struggles to hold a hard long interval, but a well-paced long-interval session may do much the same [2,13]. B

Whatever the format, the sessions that kept riders near VO2max longest were big ones. The best in the figure gave 15 to 19 minutes above 90% of VO2max. They were 6 × 8 minutes, 6 × 5 minutes and three sets of 13 × 30/15, each with 20 to 50 minutes of hard work in it [11,13].

A large 2026 review agrees with the figure, although at first sight it seems not to. Across 239 sessions in 86 studies, efforts of two minutes or more gave 555 seconds above 90% of VO2max on average, against 336 for efforts of 30 seconds or less [15]. But the review counted a set of 30/15s as short intervals, and its authors point out that a set behaves more like one long effort. Its long-interval sessions also held about twice as much hard work. And where studies compared steady and varied power within the same session, the 30/15 comparisons above among them, varied power gave 165 seconds more. Short efforts strung together with short recoveries behave like a long interval, and varying the power inside an effort adds time near the ceiling rather than costing it. C

Threshold intervals

Threshold intervals sit in the band Chapter 5 called “between the thresholds”, where many amateurs spend much of their training. They typically last 8 to 20 minutes, just below the second threshold, and are easier to recover from than anything harder. In the review Chapter 12 describes, the heart’s nervous control took 24 to 48 hours to recover from a single session, against 48 hours or more after harder intervals [s3].

Their strength is the share of VO2max a rider can sustain. In 2025 a Norwegian group gave 22 young, well-trained cyclists a week of six threshold-interval sessions, and two months later a week of five sessions of 30/15s. Both weeks raised 15-minute power by similar amounts. But the threshold week raised power at a lactate of 4 mmol/L about twice as much, 4.5% against 2.1%. Only the threshold week raised the share of VO2max the riders could hold there. VO2max rose a little after both weeks, with no significant difference between them. Every rider did the threshold week first, so the comparison was not randomised [16].

Seiler’s cyclists showed no such advantage. His 4 × 16-minute group settled at a lactate of 4.9 mmol/L. It gained about as much as the 4 × 4s, in VO2peak and in threshold power alike, and half as much as the 4 × 8s [1].

The pattern fits Chapter 1’s model. Threshold work trains the fraction of VO2max a rider can sustain, and work near VO2max trains the ceiling itself. A rider whose VO2max is already high relative to their threshold has more to gain from the first; one whose ceiling is low has more to gain from the second. For most amateurs on six to ten hours, who have one or two hard sessions to spend, the trials favour giving at least one of them to intervals near the top. C

Sprints

Sprint interval training usually means repeated efforts of about 30 seconds, all-out, with three or four minutes of rest. Its appeal is time. In 2006 Martin Gibala’s group in Canada gave sixteen active young men six sessions of sprints over two weeks, about two and a half hours of training in all. They gained as much in a time trial and in their muscles’ oxidative capacity as men who did about ten and a half hours of continuous riding [s4].

For a rider who already trains, sprints come off worse than long intervals. A 2020 analysis of six trials in moderately trained people found no overall difference in time-trial performance. But intervals of four minutes or more beat sprints by 2%, and raised maximal aerobic power more [17]. A 2023 trial in 81 well-trained women, running, was starker. After eight weeks of three sessions a week, only 4 × 4 minutes raised VO2max, by 7.3%. Two sprint protocols raised anaerobic capacity instead, and improved a 300 m sprint more [18]. The 10 × 30-second all-out sprints also caused eight injuries, six of them hamstring strains, each bad enough to stop training for at least a week. The other two protocols caused none. That trial was on a treadmill, and I found no comparable count of injuries from sprinting on a bike.

Sprints raise VO2max in untrained people, improve sprinting, and save time. For a trained rider aiming at long efforts they are the weaker choice. B

Most readers of this book ride events that last an hour or more, and sprints train something those riders rarely need. Criterium racers have a reason to include them that the VO2max trials do not capture, and so does anyone who wants to win the sprint for the village sign.

Riding the sessions

For self-paced sessions, aim for the hardest effort you can sustain across the whole set. When twelve well-trained runners chose their own pace for repeats of one to six minutes, they rated every session at about 17 on the 6-to-20 scale, very hard, whatever the length [19]. Expect the last repetition to be the hardest, and if you finish with something left, raise the power next time. Building surges into long efforts added time near VO2max without making the session feel any harder [12].

On a smart trainer, set the power from recent efforts and raise it when you finish with something left. Smart trainers can hold a set power whatever the rider’s cadence, and many riders do their intervals that way. In the terms of the trials, those are fixed-power sessions. In the pacing study above, the 6 × 5-minute session gave three minutes above 90% of VO2max at the researchers’ powers. Ridden as hard as the riders could manage, it gave seventeen [13]. Part of that gap may come from the particular powers the researchers chose, but the same thing happens to a rider who sets a power from an old test, or a cautious one. A fixed power is a ceiling on the session as well as a floor. C

Judge short intervals by power and effort, not heart rate. Twelve highly trained runners spent less time above 90% of VO2max in 24 × 30 seconds than in 4 × 3 minutes, 201 seconds against 328 [14]. Yet they spent more time above 90% of maximum heart rate, 820 seconds against 545. In short intervals heart rate and oxygen uptake do not move together, and heart rate can make a session look closer to the ceiling than it is.

The recoveries between efforts matter less than the efforts. Nine well-trained runners did 6 × 4 minutes as hard as they could, with recoveries of one, two or four minutes. The length of the rest made little difference to how fast they ran, how much oxygen they used or how hard it felt. Left to choose, they rested for about two minutes [20]. The trials used two and a half to three minutes between long intervals, and a warm-up of about ten minutes [10,8]. I found nothing to suggest that a longer warm-up adds anything.

Most interval trials are of men. The few that compared the sexes found the sessions worked in much the same way. The exceptions came in the women’s sprint trial. One sprint protocol that had raised VO2max in men did not in women, and the all-out sprints injured more women than the same protocol had injured men [11,18]. Chapter 18 returns to women’s training.

From the saddle. I ride two interval sessions a week. One is 5 × 4 minutes at 300 W, with 2 minutes’ rest between them. The other is 10 × 1 minute at 350 W. I know I’m going to suffer in both. If I’m tired from work I might put a session off, or replace it with a longer Zone 2 ride. Writing this chapter showed me that those sessions hold 20 and 10 minutes of hard work, less than the trials here favour, so I’m changing them.

The sessions, in brief

These are the sessions the trials in this chapter used, as a rider might ride them. Each assumes a warm-up of about ten minutes of easy riding with a few short pick-ups, and an easy spin afterwards. Chapter 17 puts two of them into a week.

  1. 4 × 4 minutes, with 3 minutes of easy riding between. Ridden as hard as can be sustained for all four, which in the Trondheim trials meant 90% to 95% of maximum heart rate [8]. Sixteen minutes of hard work; the shortest of the long sessions.
  2. 4 × 8 minutes, with 2 to 3 minutes between, about what Seiler’s runners chose for themselves [20]. The session that beat both 4 × 4 and 4 × 16 in recreational cyclists, ridden at about 90% of peak heart rate [1]. Thirty-two minutes of hard work. A rider who finds 4 × 8 comfortable can add a fifth repetition, as the 22 cyclists in the correlation study did [5].
  3. 30/15: three sets of 13 × 30 seconds hard and 15 seconds easy, 3 minutes between sets [10]. The 30-second efforts are harder than a long interval and the 15 seconds are easy pedalling, not rest. Two sets is a reasonable start.
  4. Threshold intervals: for example 3 × 12 or 2 × 20 minutes just below the second threshold, with 3 minutes between, ridden at about 14 to 15 on the 6-to-20 scale: hard, not very hard. In the 2025 trial that effort put the riders at about 85% of maximum heart rate and a lactate of about 3 mmol/L [16]. Less intense, cheaper to recover from, and better for the fraction of VO2max a rider can sustain than for VO2max itself.
  5. Sprint intervals: 4 to 6 × 30 seconds all-out with 4 minutes of easy riding between. Useful for sprinting and for a rider short of time; the weaker choice for long efforts [17].
What survives
  • Piling up work near your limit beats going harder: 4 × 8 doubled the gain of 4 × 4. B
  • Thirty-fifteens make a large dose of near-maximal work easier to reach. B
  • For long efforts, sprints have weaker evidence than long intervals. B
  • Ride every set as hard as you can hold for all of it.

Chapter 12: How many hard sessions, and how often

Draft · 2,610 words · 27 October 2026

Two hard sessions a week is familiar advice. The champions in Chapter 8 kept a steady hard dose while their easy hours rose and fell [1]. That suggests a ceiling, but does not tell us where it lies for an amateur.

For a rider on six to ten hours, I would start with two hard sessions at least 48 hours apart [2,3]. The frequency trials are small and short, but give little reason to add a third as a routine. How the sessions are spaced, and how easy the riding between them is, matters at least as much as their number. B for two as the default; C for the ceiling

Where two comes from

The number began as a description. Counting sessions by their purpose, Stephen Seiler found that elite endurance athletes in several sports did roughly four easy sessions for every hard one. For an athlete training ten to fourteen times a week, that means two or three hard sessions [4][s1]. The champions’ diaries in Chapter 8 add that it was the hard dose, not the hard share, that held steady [1].

Those records cannot tell us whether two or three sessions worked best, whether more was unsustainable, or whether coaches were following tradition. That requires trials.

Adding hard sessions to easy training

The trials that best match an amateur’s situation add a few hard sessions to a base of easy riding. In two South African trials, trained cyclists added about one and a half or two interval sessions a week to their usual riding. They improved their 40 km time trial within three or four weeks [5,6].

Neither trial tested whether three or four sessions would have brought more.

Trials of frequency

Few trials change only the number of hard sessions, and those that exist are small. Read together, they say that one session a week does little for people who are already fit, and that a third adds little to two.

In a 1999 French study, eight trained runners did one session a week at the speed that brings out VO2max for four weeks, then three a week for four more [7]. One a week improved the speed they could hold at VO2max, through better economy. Three a week improved nothing further, and the noradrenaline in their blood at the end of a maximal test rose from 11.1 to 26.0 nmol/L, a sign of a stress response building.

In 2025 a German group randomised 26 recreationally active people to one, two or three sessions a week of 4 × 4-minute running intervals for six weeks [8]. VO2max barely moved with one session a week, from 53.0 to 53.6 mL/kg/min. It rose from 53.5 to 57.6 with two, and from 48.5 to 51.2 with three. The authors saw no clear extra benefit from the third session and call their results exploratory and imprecise.

Three a week can work. In the Trondheim trial of 2007, moderately trained men raised VO2max by 7.2% in eight weeks on three sessions a week of 4 × 4 minutes [9].

One study, up close: two sessions or four

The most direct test in trained athletes came from Norway in 2020 [3].

Hypothesis
HypothesisTwo longer interval sessions a week would bring greater improvements in performance and physiology than four shorter sessions at the same intensity.
Design
DesignRandomised trial lasting 12 weeks, May to August, on roller-skis. 20 national-level cross-country skiers and biathletes, with a median VO2max of about 68 to 71 mL/kg/min. Every interval was in the Norwegian zone 3, at 82% to 87% of maximum heart rate and 2.5 to 4.0 mmol/L of lactate, so these were threshold sessions, not VO2max sessions. Both groups did 136 minutes of interval work a week; the rest of their training was easy, with at most one other hard session a week [3].
Two sessions a weekFour sessions a week
Finished the study

Spacing
