Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionTwo longer interval sessions a week appear superior to four shorter ones for endurance adaptations and performance, perhaps because the longer gaps between sessions let the athletes recover.

The trial is often quoted as showing that two sessions beat four. The two-session group did improve its time trial, its threshold and its economy, and the four-session group did not change significantly. More of the four-session group also dropped out, mostly through illness, which fits the authors’ suggestion that their sessions came too close together.

Reading the research: a difference in significance

But look again at the time trial. The hypothesis was about the difference between the groups, and the effect size for that difference was 0.17, trivial by the authors’ own description [3]. “Superior” rests on one group’s improvement crossing the line of statistical significance while the other group’s did not. With nine athletes in one group and six in the other, small differences in where each group’s change falls can move it across that line.

The same pattern runs through the frequency literature. In the German runners, the test of whether frequency changed the result gave p = 0.17 for VO2max, so the groups were not shown to differ. Yet the two- and three-session groups’ changes were each significant and the one-session group’s was not [8]. A 2025 meta-analysis of interval training in athletes found effect sizes of 0.69 for two sessions a week and 1.21 for three, against controls [10]. It described three as superior because only that figure crossed p = 0.05. Both effects point the same way, and their uncertainties overlap.

Compare the groups directly. “Group A improved significantly and group B did not” reports two tests, each comparing a group with itself. Showing that A did better than B requires a separate test of the difference between them.

Read that way, the frequency trials agree on something more modest than any single number. One hard session a week builds little in people who are already fit, and two and three build similar amounts over a few weeks. In the one trial of trained athletes, four short sessions did no better than two long ones and may have done worse [8,3]. B

Recovery sets the ceiling

A 2013 review followed the heart’s autonomic recovery, the return of the nervous system’s control of heart rate to its resting state [2]. It took up to 24 hours after easy exercise, 24 to 48 hours after threshold work, and at least 48 hours after high-intensity work, and was faster in fitter people. Seiler’s measurements over the first hours also showed slower recovery after crossing the first threshold [s2].

The review also suggests what is recovering. In the first hour and a half after a session the heart’s nervous control is driven mostly by the acid left in the muscles and blood. Over the following one to two days it tracks slower changes such as the volume of the blood plasma [2]. The authors add a caution that matters for anyone using a heart-rate-variability app: the heart’s nervous system recovering does not mean everything has. Muscle fuel stores and the nervous system’s control of the muscles keep their own timetables, and the review had little data on them.

The arithmetic follows. With at least 48 hours after each hard session [2], a seven-day week holds three at most, Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with no room for a long ride on fresh legs. Two hard sessions leave 48 to 72 hours between them and a weekend free, unless Sunday’s group ride turns out to be the third.

Pushing past that has a cost before it has a benefit. A consensus statement from the European and American sports medicine colleges separates three states. Functional overreaching is a short drop in performance that turns into improvement after rest. Non-functional overreaching is a longer drop that does not. The overtraining syndrome is a prolonged failure to adapt [11]. It also notes that no single marker reliably tells them apart. A 2004 review put the recovery from overreaching at about two weeks and from the overtraining syndrome at months to years, and found no evidence beyond anecdote that the first leads to the second [s3]. Billat’s rising noradrenaline is a small version of the warning [7].

Arranging the same work

Concentrating the work in a short block, followed by recovery, helped trained cyclists. In a 2014 trial, one group did five high-intensity sessions in the first week and one a week for the next three. Another did two a week throughout, with the same volumes of hard and easy riding in total. After four weeks the block group’s VO2max was up 4.6% and its power at a lactate of 2 mmol/L up 10%, while the steady group had not changed [12].

Blocks can also go wrong. The Trondheim group cites two studies in which two weeks of intensified training left competitive cyclists with a lower VO2max and worse performance [13]. A block works when it is followed by recovery, and the recovery is part of the dose.

Compressing the work without a recovery period afterwards delayed the gain. In 2014 a Trondheim group gave 21 young adults 24 sessions of uphill treadmill intervals, 4 × 4 minutes, either over eight weeks or over three [13]. Four days after the last session, VO2max was 10.7% higher in the eight-week group, and the 3.0% in the three-week group was not significant. Twelve days later, after rest, the compressed group had reached 6.1% and the spread-out group had slipped to 7.9%, and the two were no longer significantly different.

And in the largest trial of cyclists the order of the hard sessions did not matter at all. Its 63 riders did 24 interval sessions, two a week, in three different orders, and all improved by 5% to 10% [s4]. Doing the hard sessions consistently mattered more than sequencing them cleverly. B

Threshold sessions count differently

A threshold session is a hard session that is cheaper to recover from, so a week can hold more of them. Recovery took up to 48 hours after threshold work and at least 48 hours after harder work [2], and the sessions in the two-against-four trial were threshold sessions [3]. The Norwegian runners described in Chapter 8 do three or four threshold sessions a week. They check their lactate every one to three repetitions to keep it between 2 and 4.5 mmol/L, and add one faster session and 150 to 180 km of easy running [s5]. Elite distance runners more generally do at least one threshold session and one faster session a week on a hard-day, easy-day pattern [s6].

That holds only if the threshold work is controlled and genuinely below the second threshold. For a rider on six to ten hours, I would count a controlled threshold session as a hard session that is cheaper to recover from. A ride between the thresholds that drifts harder than intended is a hard session that was not planned. C

How little keeps fitness

Keeping fitness takes far less than building it. In 1981 Robert Hickson had twelve young adults train six days a week for ten weeks, cycling and running 40 minutes a day, which raised their VO2max by 20% to 25% [14]. They then cut to four days a week or two, at the same intensity and duration, and fifteen weeks later both groups had kept their VO2max.

In a companion study, the intensity was cut by a third or two thirds while the frequency and duration stayed the same. That lost part of the gain in VO2max, cut endurance at a submaximal pace by 21% and 30%, and returned the heart’s muscle mass to where it started [s7]. A 2021 review of the minimum dose reached the same conclusion [15]. Endurance can be held for up to 15 weeks on as few as two sessions a week, or a third to two thirds less volume, provided the intensity is kept. B

For a busy month or an off-season, I would keep one hard session a week alongside whatever easy riding fits. That is a practical inference from the reduced-training studies, which did not test this exact mix. For a rider new to structured intervals, one well-ridden session is a better start than two half-hearted ones. Older riders who find two leave them flat can reasonably drop to one or stretch the gap. A review of masters athletes concluded that age may slow recovery less than is often assumed, and that a sedentary life explains more of the decline [16]. C

Is the champions’ hour a ceiling?

The trials that improved cyclists put a similar amount of hard work into a week. Seiler’s 4 × 8s, twice a week, came to 64 minutes [17]. The 30/15 sessions of Chapter 11 came to about 39 minutes of hard efforts [s8]. The Trondheim 4 × 4s, three times a week, came to 48 [9]. The champions’ 1.3 hours a week is time in the top three zones as they logged it, which probably includes some of the recovery between repetitions. So their figure and the trials’ are not quite the same measure [1]. But they are the same order: something like 40 minutes to an hour of hard work a week, in two or three sessions.

I read that match as a limit on the hard work a body can absorb, with the champions adding easy hours around it. No trial has tested a larger hard dose over months in amateur cyclists, so the ceiling’s exact height is unknown. In the short frequency trials above, more sessions brought no clear extra gain and some signs of strain. C

The winter in the Introduction was the mirror image of this. Before it I rode hard sessions, irregularly. That winter I rode regularly, and nothing hurt. Chapter 7 put the faster climb down to the regularity. The trials in this part say that a rider with a few hours a week does not have to choose between the two.

What survives
  • Two hard sessions a week, at least 48 hours apart, is the best-supported default. B
  • One hard session plus easy riding is a reasonable fallback for a busy period. C
  • How the sessions are spaced matters at least as much as how many there are. B

Part IVOther ways to get faster

Chapter 13: Fuelling

Draft · 5,514 words · 27 October 2026

In a study published in 1989, researchers from Maastricht followed riders from one of the leading professional teams through the Tour de France, 22 days and about 4,000 kilometres. The riders wrote down everything they ate [1]. Eight riders were asked and five agreed to keep a food diary. One crashed out after four days and a team-mate took over, so four riders have a complete record.

They took in an average of about 5,900 calories a day, and about 7,700 on their biggest day, in the mountains. Almost half of it, 49%, was eaten on the bike. Across 115 hours of racing that came to 94 grams of carbohydrate an hour. The largest single source of their energy was sweet cakes, eaten during the stages. A maltodextrin drink came second and bread third [1].

The usual account today is that professionals have recently learned to eat far more during races, 100 or 120 grams an hour from drinks and gels, and that this helps explain why racing is faster. A 2026 review says the change “has been widely described as a ‘carbohydrate revolution’” [2].

The old diaries were not accurate to the gram, although a nutritionist checked them weekly against team supplies, and drinks came in standard bottles [1]. They still show Tour riders eating a great deal on the bike in the 1980s, much of it cake.

What a ride costs

Three hours at 200 watts costs over 2,000 calories. A gram of carbohydrate supplies about 4 calories, so 60 grams an hour for those three hours puts back 720 calories, about a third of what was spent. At 90 grams an hour it is about half.

Nobody eats as much on the bike as the ride burns, and nobody needs to. The fat stored in the body holds far more energy than even a very long ride uses. What the body runs short of is carbohydrate, which is stored as glycogen in the muscles and the liver in amounts that a few hours of hard riding can empty. The harder the riding, the larger the share of the fuel that is carbohydrate. In one of the trials described below, highly trained cyclists rode at the top of Zone 2 after an overnight fast. They burned a little over 2 grams a minute of their own stored carbohydrate, about 130 grams an hour, on top of what they were drinking [s1].

Professionals in a grand tour are at the far end of this. The researchers on the 1980s Tour estimated that the riders spent about 6,100 calories a day, and their body weight did not change over the three weeks. They ate 12.3 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight a day [1]. Three decades later, investigators weighed everything that nine riders on a WorldTour team ate through the three weeks of the Vuelta a España. They found an average of 12.5 [3]. For a 69-kilogram rider, the average in the Tour study, that is about 850 grams of carbohydrate a day, every day for three weeks.

How it works: the limit is in the gut wall

Carbohydrate eaten on the bike has to leave the stomach, cross the wall of the small intestine into the blood, and be taken up by the muscle. Researchers can follow it by labelling the carbohydrate in a drink with a traceable form of carbon. How much of that carbon comes out in the rider’s breath shows how much of the drink has actually been burned.

Such studies kept finding a ceiling. However much glucose a rider drank, the body burned no more than about 60 grams of it an hour. Intakes of 144 and 180 grams an hour did not raise the figure much [4]. The stomach was emptying fast enough and the muscle could have used more, so by elimination the limit was absorption. Glucose crosses the gut wall through a transport protein called SGLT1, and at about a gram a minute those transporters are working at capacity [4].

Fructose crosses by a different transporter, GLUT5. In 2004 Asker Jeukendrup’s group gave eight trained cyclists drinks containing glucose alone, or glucose with fructose, during two hours of riding. With glucose alone, at either of two doses, the peak rate at which the drink was burned was about 0.8 grams a minute. With the mixture it was 1.26 [s2]. A second route through the gut wall let more sugar through.

Four years later the same group tested whether that mattered for performance. Eight cyclists rode for two hours and then did a time trial lasting about an hour. On a glucose and fructose drink they finished it 8% faster than on glucose alone, and 19% faster than on water [5]. B

This is the basis of the standard advice for long events, which is up to 90 grams an hour from a mixture of sugars. The 2026 review treats 90 grams as the upper limit of established guidelines and anything above it as “ultra-high” [2].

Does more help?

The largest trial of dose was run across four research sites and published in 2013. Fifty-one cyclists and triathletes each rode for two hours at a steady, fairly hard pace and then did a 20-kilometre time trial, on four occasions. Twelve drinks were tested, from 10 to 120 grams of carbohydrate an hour in steps of 10, along with a placebo, and neither the riders nor the testers knew which drink was which [6].

Performance rose with dose, steeply at first. Riders were 1% faster than on placebo at 9 grams an hour, 2% at 19, 3% at 31 and 4% at 48. The curve peaked at 78 grams an hour with a gain of 4.7%, and above that the benefit shrank [6].

The 2026 trial described in the Durability chapter has the same shape. Going from nothing to 60 grams an hour saved 20 watts of critical power after a three-hour ride, and doubling the dose to 120 saved 9 more [7]. That carbohydrate during a ride of two hours or more improves performance is as well established as anything in sports nutrition. A

Above 90 grams an hour the evidence thins quickly. In 2022 a trial compared 120 grams an hour with 90 in eleven highly trained cyclists during three-hour rides. At 120 the riders burned more of what they drank, 1.51 grams a minute against 1.29. But they burned just as much of their own stored carbohydrate as before [s1]. The extra sugar displaced fat as a fuel and spared no glycogen. And a smaller share of it was used. By the 2026 reviewers’ calculation, about 86% of the carbohydrate drunk at 90 grams an hour was burned, and about 76% at 120. That leaves some 30 grams an hour unaccounted for. They suggest much of that is still sitting in the gut [2].

The study most often cited in favour of 120 grams was run during a mountain marathon. Twenty elite runners, who had trained their guts beforehand, were randomised to 60, 90 or 120 grams an hour. A day after the race the 120 group had lower blood markers of muscle damage and reported a lower overall load during the race [s3]. The study did not show that they ran faster [2], and with 20 runners split three ways it had little chance of detecting it if they had.

The 2026 review, by a group based in Auckland, went through all of this. It concluded that intakes above 90 grams an hour remain “poorly evidenced”, with support “largely derived from anecdotal reports and elite athlete practice rather than controlled research” [2]. Two trials from one laboratory compared doses from 60 to about 110 grams an hour and found no significant difference in time-trial performance between them. C

The authors do not dismiss the practice. They point out that people differ. In one study, riders all given 120 grams an hour burned anything from about 1.3 to 1.9 grams a minute, so a few could use nearly all of it and most could not. And they suggest that the real benefit of eating a great deal during a stage may arrive the next day, as better recovery. That would matter in a three-week race, and no laboratory trial of a single ride would detect it [2].

A second review, published the same year by seven British researchers, argues for raising the limit from 90 to 120 grams an hour for trained athletes, because more carbohydrate is burned [8]. It concedes that a definitive study of dose and performance “is yet to be completed”. The reviews disagree about the recommendation, rather than the result: more is burned, but a performance gain has not been established.

Reading the research: what the fast riders eat

In 2012 a group surveyed 221 athletes after Ironman triathlons, a marathon, a long cycle race and professional stage races, asking what they had eaten and what stomach trouble they had had. Intakes ranged from 6 to 136 grams of carbohydrate an hour. In the Ironman races, the athletes who ate more finished faster, and the correlation was a fairly strong one [s4].

It is tempting to read that as proof that eating more makes you faster. The survey can’t show it. The faster athletes in an Ironman are the fitter and more experienced ones. By my reasoning, not the survey’s, they are working at a lower fraction of their capacity at any given speed, which leaves more blood flow for the gut. And they have had years to practise eating in races. Speed may be what allows the eating. The same survey found that higher intakes went with more nausea and flatulence [s4], so the athletes eating the most were not having an easy time of it.

The review on training the gut that this chapter draws on appeared in a journal supplement supported by the research institute of a sports drink company. Its author received a fee for attending the meeting behind it [4]. The carbohydrate in the 2026 dose trial was supplied by a supplement company [7]. That does not make the findings wrong, and the big dose trial was double-blind.

The two 2026 reviews also declare industry relationships. Five of the seven authors arguing for 120 grams have a relationship with one sports nutrition company, and one is employed by it [8]. The lead author of the more sceptical review holds a post with a company selling other supplements [2]. These interests don’t settle the argument, but they belong beside any recommendation to consume more of a product.

From the saddle. On a long ride I eat Precision PF 30 Chews. They’re pretty tasty and I can keep eating them on the move. I’ve found it’s important to start on them early, maybe 20 minutes in, because it gets me into the habit of eating regularly. Gels can upset my stomach. I generally prefer Lucozade Sport to a specialist carb drink, mainly for the taste. It matters to me that the drink tastes good, so that I’m looking forward to drinking it rather than forcing it down.

Is this why racing is faster?

I found no study isolating fuelling’s contribution to faster racing. Nor do the older records establish that riders always ate as much as they do now: they cover two teams in different races, measured by diary in one case and weighing in the other [1,3].

The published hourly figures show a recent upturn, and it is smaller than the word revolution implies. The British review, some of whose authors work with professional teams, says that professional cyclists’ intakes have usually been reported at 60 to 90 grams an hour. It gives Chris Froome’s figures across nine stages of the 2018 Giro d’Italia, which he won: between 52 and 96 grams an hour, with the highest on the hardest day. It also passes on a press report that a stage winner at the 2025 Tour took about 116, and reports that some riders are said to be training their guts to tolerate 200 or more [8]. So if the press figures are right, the leading edge has moved up in the last few years, from the nineties to something over a hundred. The 200 figure is hearsay.

The controlled trials have not shown that going from 90 to 120 makes riders faster on the day [2].

It might still be true by the recovery route. A rider who eats more on Tuesday starts Wednesday with more glycogen, and over three weeks that could add up. Both reviews say as much. The British one suggests that higher intakes help riders match what they eat to what they spend each day, “even if this does not necessarily confer an immediate performance benefit” [8].

It might also be true through consistency. An average from a handful of riders on one leading team says nothing about how many riders in the race ate that much, on how many days, or how well it stayed down. If every rider now eats what only the best-organised did then, the race is faster without the ceiling having moved. Both are reasonable guesses and neither has been tested. C

Can the gut be trained?

The stomach can, and the best demonstration comes from outside sport. Competitive eaters train for weeks by drinking large volumes of fluid and eating progressively larger amounts of the food they will compete on. The stomach learns to stretch further, and a full stomach comes to feel less full. When Jeukendrup reviewed the subject in 2017 the record stood at 69 hot dogs, with buns, in ten minutes [4].

The athletic version is less dramatic and works the same way. In one study he describes, runners practised drinking at a rate that matched their sweat losses during 90-minute runs. Their stomach comfort improved over repeated sessions, although the rate at which the stomach emptied did not measurably change. What changed was how the fullness was tolerated [4].

Diet changes how fast the stomach empties, and the change is specific to the nutrient. Volunteers given an extra 400 grams of glucose a day for three days emptied a glucose drink from the stomach faster afterwards, in a half-emptying time of about 21 minutes against 29. A protein drink emptied no faster than before [4]. Three days was enough.

In animals, feeding more carbohydrate makes the gut wall produce more SGLT1 transporter. Mice had nearly twice as much after two weeks on a high-carbohydrate diet [4]. Nobody has measured this directly in a human athlete, which would require samples of the intestinal wall. The cyclist study below provides indirect evidence.

One study, up close: 28 days of eating on the bike

In 2010 a group at the Australian Institute of Sport led by Gregory Cox tested whether the gut adapts to carbohydrate taken during exercise [9,4].

The high-carbohydrate group burned about a sixth more of the test drink after training, but gained no more speed than the control group. More transporters in the gut wall could explain the extra absorption, as in animals; the study did not measure them.

There are limits on both findings. Eight riders a group is a small study by the standards of Chapter 4. The test drink was glucose alone, so the study cannot say whether training raises the higher ceiling that glucose and fructose mixtures reach. I have read this paper’s abstract and Jeukendrup’s detailed account of it, not the paper itself. And sixteen years later the 2026 reviewers note that its central finding “has not been consistently replicated” [2]. C

Symptoms are another matter

Whether or not practice lets you absorb more, there is better evidence that it makes eating on the move more comfortable.

Two trials in recreational runners, both from Monash University in Melbourne, found that practice cut symptoms by more than half. In the first, 25 runners did a two-hour run eating 90 grams of carbohydrate an hour, practised for two weeks with gels, ordinary food or a placebo, and then did the run again. Gut symptoms fell by about 60% in both carbohydrate groups and by 25% on placebo, so part of the improvement came simply from doing the test twice. The distance covered in an hour’s test afterwards rose by about 5% in the carbohydrate groups and fell slightly on placebo [10][s5].

The second trial was blinded. Eighteen runners practised daily for two weeks with 90 grams an hour or a placebo, without being told which. Symptoms fell by 61% with carbohydrate and 2% with placebo, and breath hydrogen, a sign of sugar reaching the large intestine unabsorbed, halved [10][s6].

A third trial, from the Australian Institute of Sport, did not find this. Elite race walkers and runners, 19 and 18 of them, trained for two weeks on 60 to 90 grams an hour instead of 30. Gut symptoms stayed the same or got worse, and neither breath hydrogen nor the runners’ time-trial performance changed. The authors’ own title describes the effects as “minor” [10].

All three are in a 2023 systematic review, which found eight studies of gut training in total. It concludes that two weeks of repeated feeding reduces gut discomfort and malabsorption, and that stomach emptying does not change. It also notes that no standard protocol exists, that 79% of participants were men, and that most of the studies were in runners [10]. Only one used cycling alone. The review was written by the Monash group, and its senior author is also the senior author of the two trials that found a benefit. That is normal in a small field, and the review reports the contrary trial fairly, but it means the positive case comes from one laboratory.

Practice probably makes eating during exercise more comfortable, at least in recreational runners. B Evidence that it raises carbohydrate absorption rests on one small cyclist study, which found no extra performance gain. C

Carbohydrate sensed in the mouth

One finding does not fit the picture of carbohydrate as petrol. In 2004 nine endurance cyclists did a time trial lasting about an hour, twice. In one they rinsed a carbohydrate solution around the mouth for five seconds at intervals and spat it out. In the other they did the same with water. Nothing was swallowed either time. With the carbohydrate rinse they finished in 59.57 minutes against 61.37, at an average of 259 watts against 252 [11].

An hour is too short for a rider to run out of glycogen, and nothing reached the gut. The researchers concluded that receptors in the mouth detect carbohydrate and that the signal raises what the brain is prepared to ask of the muscles. That is the subject of Chapter 3: effort is regulated centrally, and it responds to information. The 2026 reviewers raise this as one possible reason riders report feeling better on very high intakes. But they note that rinsing works best in fasted riders, and that nobody has shown the effect grows with dose [2]. B

Eating less on purpose

For some years the fashionable idea in sports nutrition ran the other way. Riding before breakfast, or withholding carbohydrate after a hard session, means training with low glycogen, and that amplifies the molecular signals described in Chapter 2. A 2018 review counted the studies: training low increased cell signalling in 73% of them and raised oxidative enzymes in 78%. The same review counted performance, which improved in 37% of studies and did not change in 63% [12].

A meta-analysis in 2021 pooled the nine training studies done in well-trained endurance athletes. Periodically restricting carbohydrate had no overall effect on performance compared with doing the same training well fed [13]. B

This is Chapter 2’s warning in a real case. A larger signal after a session did not become a larger adaptation over weeks, and the likely reason is that riders short of carbohydrate cannot train as hard. The Cox study points the same way from the other side. Its two groups ate very differently around training for a month and improved by the same amount [9]. Within the range those studies cover, how much carbohydrate you eat around training seems to matter less to how fit you get than either camp has claimed.

Cutting carbohydrate out almost entirely is another matter. On a high-fat diet, the elite race walkers in Chapter 7 burned far more fat and missed the improvement that the same training brought the groups eating carbohydrate [14]. B

The greater hazard is eating too little altogether. Athletes who persistently eat less than their training costs develop a recognised syndrome, relative energy deficiency in sport, which affects men as well as women and damages both health and performance [15]. A cyclist trying to lose weight while training hard is an obvious candidate.

Water

For decades the standard advice was to drink enough to keep weight loss during exercise under 2% of body weight, because laboratory studies showed performance falling beyond that. In many of those studies the riders knew whether they had been allowed to drink, and they were tested in still air, which no cyclist outdoors experiences [16].

In cycling time trials, moderate dehydration has cost riders little. A 2011 meta-analysis took only studies that used cycling time trials. It found five, with 39 riders between them. Riders who finished an average of 2.2% lighter performed no differently from riders who had been kept topped up: the difference was 0.06%. Drinking according to thirst gave better results than drinking less than thirst asked for [17].

In 2015 an Australian group repeated the comparison with the riders blinded. Ten cyclists were dehydrated by 3% of body weight and then given back all, a third or none of the fluid through a drip, without knowing which. They then rode a 25-kilometre time trial at 33 °C with a 32 km/h headwind. Performance did not differ between the three conditions [16].

Two years later a British group did the blinding another way, by putting water into the stomach through a tube, and got the opposite result. Seven active men, about 2.4% dehydrated and at 34 °C, did 152 kilojoules of work in a 15-minute test against 165 when hydrated [s7].

So two blinded studies disagree, and they had ten and seven people in them. They differed in ways that could matter: trained cyclists against active men, a strong headwind against less airflow, a time trial against a short all-out test. I would not claim more than this. Moderate dehydration costs a fit rider less than the old advice implied. It probably costs more in heat and still air, which describes an indoor trainer. And thirst is a reasonable guide. C

Drinking too much is the more dangerous error. At the 2002 Boston Marathon, researchers took blood from 488 finishers. Thirteen per cent had hyponatraemia, a blood sodium concentration low enough to be abnormal, and 0.6% had it to a critical degree. The runners at risk were those who had gained weight during the race by drinking more than they lost, and those who took more than four hours. Whether they drank water or sports drink made no difference [s8]. Hyponatraemia can kill. A slow rider on a long cool day who drinks at every opportunity is more exposed to it than to dehydration.

Salt

Electrolyte tablets and salt capsules are sold on two promises: that they prevent hyponatraemia and that they prevent cramp. The evidence for both is poor.

At a 161-kilometre mountain run in California, 94% of the runners surveyed were taking sodium supplements, and 6.6% of the finishers tested still had hyponatraemia. Those who developed it had taken sodium at the same rate as those who did not. What marked them out was over-drinking [18]. Low blood sodium in endurance events comes from too much water, and salt tablets do not correct that.

On cramp, a South African group followed 210 triathletes through an Ironman. Forty-three cramped. Their blood electrolytes and weight changes before and after the race were no different from those of the athletes who did not cramp. What predicted cramp was a faster race pace and a history of cramping [s9]. That points to a muscle pushed beyond what it is trained for, and away from salt.

One randomised trial found a benefit. Twenty-six triathletes took salt capsules or a placebo during a real half-Ironman, and the salt group finished faster [s10]. With 26 athletes split between two groups and a p-value of 0.04, it is the kind of result Chapter 4 advises waiting to see repeated. C

Sodium in a drink does no harm, and a salty drink may be easier to keep drinking. It is not protection against either of the things it is sold for.

Caffeine, ketones, beetroot and cherry juice

Question

What the trials foundVerdict
Caffeine, 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight, about an hour before
Caffeine, 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight, about an hour before46 placebo-controlled trials of endurance time trials: average power up about 3% and finishing time down about 2%; two of the studies found riders slower [19]Works A

A ketone drink after trainingOne trial, nine men a group, in three weeks of deliberate overload: a higher training load, and 15% more power late in a two-hour ride [21]Promising, not yet repeated C

Beetroot juice before a ride80 studies: a clear effect in recreationally active men, none in well-trained athletes with a VO2max of 65 or more, none detectable in women [22]A small gain for a club rider B

Tart cherry juice after a ride19 trials in athletes: muscle strength recovered better and one marker of inflammation fell; no effect on soreness; certainty of the evidence very low to moderate [23]A recovery aid at best C

Caffeine is the best-supported performance aid a cyclist can legally buy, and most cyclists were buying it already. A common belief is that regular coffee drinkers get nothing from it. A Brazilian trial divided 40 trained cyclists by their habitual intake and found the same benefit in light, moderate and heavy coffee drinkers. It also found that a capsule with nothing in it produced about a quarter of the gain that caffeine did, which is worth remembering after Chapter 4 [s11]. For a 70-kilogram rider, 3 to 6 milligrams per kilogram is 210 to 420 milligrams, roughly two to four strong coffees. The cost that matters most to training is sleep.

Ketones became famous through a 2016 paper from Oxford, which reported that a ketone drink changed the muscles’ choice of fuel and improved endurance performance [s12]. The next year ten professional cyclists given a different ketone compound before a time trial were 2% slower, with stomach discomfort and a higher sense of effort [s13]. The pooled trials have since sided with the second result. The sport’s governing body reviewed the evidence in 2025, said it found none that was compelling, and recommended that riders not take ketones, without banning them.

Beetroot juice is taken for its nitrate, which appears to lower the oxygen cost of exercise. The trial that started the interest, in nine club cyclists in Exeter in 2011, found them almost 3% faster over 4 and 16.1 kilometres [s14]. The later trials kept the effect for club riders and lost it in well-trained ones, which makes beetroot juice an odd thing to copy from a professional.

The red drink handed to riders as they cross the line is tart cherry juice, as at least one professional team has explained on its own website [s15]. Tart cherries are rich in plant compounds that reduce inflammation, and the juice also contains sugar, which a rider needs at that moment anyway. There is a reason to be careful with it in training. The inflammation and oxidative stress that follow a hard session are part of the signal described in Chapter 2. In a small study in men, backed by experiments in rats, a gram of vitamin C a day, another antioxidant, hampered the gains from endurance training and suppressed the molecular signals that build mitochondria [24]. Nobody has shown that cherry juice does the same. But the logic of taking it is strongest in a stage race, where the aim is to be recovered by tomorrow, and weakest after an ordinary training ride, where the aim is to adapt.

What to do with it

Scale it to the ride. Under about 90 minutes at an easy pace there is no need to eat on the bike. That is roughly where critical power began to slide in the trial described in the Durability chapter [s16]. For rides of two hours or more, eat from early on.

Sixty grams an hour gets most of what is available. In the largest trial the first 50 grams an hour bought four of the 4.7 percentage points on offer [6]. Sixty grams is roughly two gels and a banana, or a large bottle of sports drink and a bar. Check the labels, because products vary.

Go to 90 only for long, hard days, and only with a mixture of sugars. Above 60 grams an hour, glucose alone is absorbed no faster, and the excess is the likeliest cause of stomach trouble. Products that combine glucose or maltodextrin with fructose are made for this.

Above 90 is unproven. It may help a professional recover between stages. For an amateur doing one ride it has not been shown to add speed, and at lower power outputs less of it will be used. A rider averaging 150 watts spends about 540 calories an hour, and 120 grams of carbohydrate would replace nearly all of it.

Practise. If you plan to eat a lot in an event, eat that way on your long training rides for at least the two weeks before. Two weeks was the dose in the trials that reduced symptoms. Use the same products you will use on the day.

Don’t under-eat to get fitter. Training short of carbohydrate has not improved performance in trained athletes, and chronic under-eating causes harm.

Drink to thirst. On most rides nothing more is needed. Drink more deliberately indoors and in heat, and never so much that you finish heavier than you started.

Don’t rely on salt to prevent cramp or low blood sodium. Pace and training are the better explanation for cramp.

Caffeine works. Three milligrams per kilogram about an hour before a hard effort is the low end of the range that has been tested, and regular coffee drinkers benefit as much as anyone.

Leave the rest to the professionals. Ketones have not been shown to improve performance. Beetroot juice may be worth a small gain to a club rider before a race. Cherry juice is a recovery drink for multi-day events.

Remember what sugar is. The 2026 reviewers warn that a habit of high carbohydrate intake around every session is a different thing from fuelling a race. They cite a study in which about 30% of athletes on a moderately raised carbohydrate intake showed fasting blood glucose in the pre-diabetic range within a month; the change was reversible [2]. Fuel the long and hard rides. An easy hour does not need a gel.

What survives
  • Carbohydrate on rides of two hours or more improves performance. A
  • Caffeine, 3 to 6 mg per kg about an hour before, raises power by about 3%. A
  • Intakes above 90 grams an hour are poorly evidenced. C
  • Fuel the long and hard rides. An easy hour doesn’t need a gel.

Chapter 14: Strength training

Draft · 2,867 words · 27 October 2026

In 1980 Robert Hickson published a study with three groups of volunteers. One lifted weights five days a week. One did endurance training six days a week. The third did both programmes in full. After ten weeks the endurance and combined groups had raised their VO2max by the same amount, about 25% on a bike test. Strength told a different story. The combined group kept pace with the lifters for seven weeks, then stopped improving, and in the ninth and tenth weeks went backwards [1].

The paper’s title called this an interference, and the word stuck. For lifters it was a warning that endurance work costs strength. Many endurance athletes took it to mean that the two kinds of training don’t mix, and stayed out of the gym with a clear conscience.

The study never showed that. Its endurance result was that lifting did no harm: VO2max rose as much with weights as without. Eight years later Hickson tested the question the right way round. Eight runners and cyclists who had stopped improving added heavy leg training three days a week for ten weeks and changed nothing else. Their leg strength rose by 30%. Their VO2max did not change. But they lasted 11% longer in a hard effort of four to eight minutes on the bike, and their time to exhaustion at 80% of VO2max went from 71 minutes to 85 [2].

Eight people, no comparison group and time-to-exhaustion tests leave the result uncertain. But it raised a useful question: could lifting make a cyclist faster without raising VO2max?

What the cycling trials found

Most of the modern evidence comes from Scandinavia, and the largest share of it from one group in Norway led by Bent Rønnestad.

Their first trial took 20 well-trained cyclists. Eleven added heavy strength training to their normal riding, and nine carried on riding only. The lifting was four leg exercises, three sets of four to ten repetitions with a weight that could only just be lifted that many times, twice a week for 12 weeks. The lifters’ thigh muscles grew, their power at a fixed blood lactate level rose, and their average power in a 40-minute all-out test improved. The riders who only rode came close to improving in that test too, falling just short of statistical significance. So the gap between the groups was smaller than the headline suggests. VO2max rose equally in both groups [3].

The same riders were also tested at the end of a long ride, and that result is in the Durability chapter.

A Danish study gave 14 young elite cyclists 16 weeks of endurance training with or without strength work. Short efforts of five minutes improved by 3 to 4% in both groups. Performance in a 45-minute test improved by 8%, and only in the group that lifted [4].

The Norwegian group also repeated its design in women. Nineteen well-trained female cyclists were randomly assigned to 11 weeks with or without heavy strength training. The 11 who lifted improved their 40-minute power, their cycling economy and the fraction of VO2max they could sustain. The eight who did not lift did not change [5].

Not every trial agrees. In 1999 an Australian group randomly assigned 21 trained female cyclists to 12 weeks of heavy squats twice a week or to a control group. The squatters’ strength rose by 36%. Their power in a one-hour test did not change, nor did their lactate threshold or anything measured in their muscles [6]. A 2010 systematic review that admitted only randomised trials in highly trained road cyclists found five, of which two showed no benefit [7].

The Norwegian review offers reasons for two other trials that found nothing: one used light, explosive training instead of heavy loads, and the other lasted only six weeks [8]. It has no such explanation for the Australian one, which used heavy squats for 12 weeks.

The pooled result

A meta-analysis published in 2026 gathered every controlled study it could find of heavy strength training in cyclists, heavy meaning loads of at least 80% of the most a person can lift once. There were 17 studies with 262 participants, 60 of them women, and programmes lasting from 5 to 25 weeks at one to three sessions a week [9].

Lifting had no effect on VO2max, on the power at which VO2max is reached, or on threshold power. It had a small effect on efficiency, the oxygen cost of riding at a given power, and moderate effects on sprint power and on performance in time trials and tests to exhaustion [9].

The authors rate the certainty of all of this as low. Their assessment found a moderate risk of bias across the studies, “mainly due to a lack of group randomisation”, and the pooled estimates are imprecise. Nine studies measured performance, and four of those nine came from the Norwegian group. The authors also state that they registered their protocol after analysing the data [9], which is the opposite of what registration is for.

So the best summary available says that heavy lifting probably makes trained cyclists somewhat faster in efforts from a few minutes to about an hour. The studies behind that conclusion are small, mostly unrandomised and concentrated in a few laboratories. B

How it works

Of Chapter 1’s three original factors, lifting appears to change only efficiency: the pooled results show no effect on VO2max or threshold power. It also improves the muscle’s ability to produce force.

A review by Rønnestad and Iñigo Mujika sets out the mechanisms that have been proposed [8]. Rønnestad led most of the Norwegian trials, so this is the field’s main contributor summarising work that is largely his own. The simplest mechanism is that a stronger muscle uses a smaller share of its maximum on every pedal stroke. The slow-twitch fibres, which are the efficient ones, can then do more of the work before the less efficient fast-twitch fibres have to be called in. The review cites a study in which, among cyclists of equal VO2max, the stronger ones showed less electrical activity in their muscles at a given power.

A second is a change within the fast-twitch fibres themselves. Both the Danish study and the Norwegian women’s study took muscle biopsies and found that lifting shifted fibres from the most fatigable fast-twitch type, IIX, towards the more enduring IIA type [4,5]. In the women, the riders whose fibres shifted most were the ones whose 40-minute power improved most.

A third is in how force is applied. Strength training raised the rate at which the elite Danish riders could develop force by 12 to 20% [4]. In the 25-week Norwegian study the lifters came to produce their peak torque earlier in the pedal stroke, and that change tracked their improvement in 40-minute power [10].

These are proposals supported by correlations in groups of ten to twenty riders. Chapter 2’s caution applies: a change seen in a biopsy alongside a change in performance has not been shown to be its cause.

Reading the research: one group of riders, two papers

The first Norwegian trial and the long-ride result described above have the same design in every detail: 20 cyclists, 11 lifting and nine not, seven men and two women in the comparison group, four leg exercises twice a week for 12 weeks [3,11]. They read as two reports from one group of riders.

One experiment can reasonably produce several papers. Count the independent groups of riders, though, and “several trials from Norway” may amount to fewer experiments than the reference list suggests.

The abstracts of those two papers also say only that the riders “were assigned” to their groups, where the women’s trial says “randomly assigned” [5]. Cyclists who choose to spend a winter in the gym may be the more motivated or the more ambitious, and Chapter 4 described how the same problem undid an early study of pain tolerance. The meta-analysis identified missing randomisation as the main weakness of this whole literature. What survives is the summary above: heavy lifting probably makes trained cyclists somewhat faster, on fewer independent experiments than the reference list suggests.

Will it make me heavier?

In the first Norwegian trial the lifters’ thigh muscles grew, and their body mass did not increase [3]. In Hickson’s 1988 study, leg strength rose 30% with no change in thigh girth or muscle-fibre size [2]. Lean mass in the lower body did increase in the 25-week elite study [s1]; across the meta-analysis, body mass made no difference to the size of the benefit [9].

The Norwegian review summarises the wider literature the same way [8]. Across trials of 8 to 16 weeks in cyclists, runners, triathletes and skiers, added strength training did not increase total body mass, while the muscles being trained grew by about 3 to 6%.

Hickson’s original finding works in the cyclist’s favour here. Heavy endurance training holds back the muscle growth that lifting would otherwise produce [1]. The review gives a likely reason, and it is one Chapter 2 introduced. AMPK, the energy sensor that endurance exercise switches on, suppresses the pathway through which lifting builds muscle protein [8]. On ten hours a week on the bike and two sessions in the gym, a rider is unlikely to gain much muscle. Strength can rise a long way without size, because much of the early gain comes from the nervous system learning to use the muscle that is already there.

Is size the point?

Probably not, though there is a tempting argument that it is.

Lifting may enlarge W′, the reserve above critical power that an attack or a short, steep climb draws on (Chapter 1). In an eight-week trial it raised young men’s W′ without changing their critical power, though not by every method of calculating it [12]. People with bigger thigh muscles also tend to have a bigger W′ on a bike [13]. Put the two together and you get a rule you may hear in a gym or from a coach: build bigger muscles and you’ll build a bigger W′.

The second finding is observation, Chapter 4’s second kind of evidence. It says that people who differ in muscle size differ in W′. It doesn’t say what happens when one rider’s muscles grow. In that study, thigh muscle size accounted for about a third of the differences in W′ between 17 men, which leaves two thirds to something else. And size travels with strength. In 11 elite cyclists, W′ tracked the force of the muscles that straighten the knee much more closely than the size of the thigh, and the volume of the quadriceps themselves was unrelated to it [14]. The trials that raised W′ raised strength as well, so they can’t say which did the work.

The cycling trials trained for force, with heavy weights and few repetitions, and the muscle that grew was a by-product. A rider who sets out to get bigger is chasing something those trials never aimed for, and will carry it up every climb. C

How much, and for how long

The programmes in the 17 studies were similar enough to describe an average. They used about four exercises a session, loads of about 84% of the one-repetition maximum, which is a weight that can be lifted about seven times, and ran for about 14 weeks. The squat was the commonest exercise, used in 12 of the studies, followed by calf exercises, leg curls and the leg press [9]. All of it is heavy lifting for the legs. The review by Rønnestad and Mujika concludes that for cycling the evidence favours heavy loads over light, explosive work, and it adds a detail about how to lift them. The weight will move slowly because it is heavy, but the rider should try to push it up as fast as possible. In one study it cites, lifting with that intent produced larger gains in strength and in the rate of force development than lifting at a deliberately moderate speed [8].

Its recommended programme is two sessions a week for 12 weeks, with two or three sets of four to ten repetitions and two to three minutes’ rest between sets. The exercises should work the same muscles through a similar movement to pedalling. It warns that at first the legs feel heavy and sore for a few days after each session, and advises cutting back the riding for the first two or three weeks. The suggested time to begin is straight after the end of the season, when riding matters least [8].

Strength gained in the winter can be kept through the season on very little. The Norwegian group had six cyclists lift twice a week for a 12-week preparation period and then once a week for the first 13 weeks of the racing season. They kept the muscle and the strength they had gained, and by the end of the 25 weeks had improved their 40-minute power more than six riders who had not lifted at all [s2]. Twelve riders is very few, but the finding fits the pattern from Chapter 2 that an adaptation is cheaper to keep than to build.

Nobody has compared replacing riding with lifting against adding lifting on top. The 2010 review suggested that the trials which replaced some riding did better than those which added to it [7]. The Norwegian trials added it and found a benefit. The question is open, and it matters to a rider with a fixed number of hours.

From the saddle. I’ve started lifting recently, mainly for upper-body strength. I’m getting older, and I want to keep my muscle. I use dumbbells, and one of my aims this year is to add leg exercises.

The case that has nothing to do with speed

Cycling is weight-supported. The skeleton does not carry the rider’s weight on a bike the way it does in running or walking, and bone responds to load.

A study in California compared 27 male masters cyclists, average age 51, who had raced for an average of 20 years, with normally active men of the same age and weight who were not athletes. The cyclists had lower bone mineral density at the spine and the hip. Four of them, 15%, had values in the range used to diagnose osteoporosis. None of the non-athletes did [s3].

A 2012 systematic review of 31 studies reached the same conclusion. Adult road cyclists have low bone density in key regions, the lumbar spine in particular, and road cycling “does not appear to confer any significant osteogenic benefit” [15]. Mountain bikers and cyclists who did other sports as well were better off. C

These comparisons cannot show that cycling caused the difference. Nor have I found a trial showing that lifting restores bone in cyclists. Loading the skeleton is standard advice for bone health, and a squat loads the spine and hips. For a rider over 40 whose only exercise is the bike, this may be a better reason to lift than anything in a time trial.

What to do with it

Lift heavy, for the legs. The trials used squats, leg presses and similar exercises at weights that could be lifted four to ten times, for about three sets. Light weights for many repetitions are not what was tested.

Twice a week for about three months builds it. Once a week keeps it. Start just after your season ends, and ride less for the first two or three weeks, because your legs will be sore.

Push the weight up as fast as you can. It will still move slowly. The intent is what the evidence supports.

Expect a small gain where it matters and none in VO2max. The benefit showed up in efforts of a few minutes to an hour, and in one trial at the end of a three-hour ride.

Train for strength, not size. Don’t expect to bulk up either: riders doing a full endurance programme gained strength with little or no gain in weight.

Learn the lifts properly. The Norwegian review advises developing technique with lighter loads before lifting heavy ones [8]. The trials do not give injury figures I can cite. If you have not lifted before, get the movement taught.

If you are over 40 and only ride, lift for your bones as well. The evidence that road cyclists have low bone density is consistent, and the bike will not fix it.

What survives
  • Heavy leg lifting probably makes trained cyclists a little faster in efforts from minutes to an hour. B
  • Road cyclists tend to have low bone density, and the bike won’t fix it. C
  • If you are over 40 and only ride, lift for your bones as well.

Chapter 15: Heat training

Draft · 3,825 words · 27 October 2026

Ice vests on the start line

The 2026 Tour de France began in Barcelona in temperatures above 30 °C and got hotter. Stage 3, from Granollers over the border to Les Angles, was raced in 36 °C while wildfires burned near Perpignan. Tadej Pogačar won it and called the day “a logistic nightmare”, by which he meant the quantity of water and ice his team had to get to its riders. The next stage, out of Carcassonne, had up to 40 °C forecast. Riders that week waited for the start in frozen vests. Ineos had its riders stand with their forearms in iced water. Alpecin handed out carbohydrate gels that had been frozen solid. Ice socks are stockings packed with ice and pushed down the back of a jersey. They are banned once the racing starts, and were everywhere before and after it [s1]. Four days later the organisers cut 30 km from stage 9, between Malemort and Ussel, after the Corrèze was put on a red heatwave alert [s2].

Cooling a rider on the day is one answer to heat. The other is to send him to the race already adapted to it. Jeroen Swart has spent six years as a sports scientist at UAE Team Emirates. In January 2025 he described part of how the team had prepared Pogačar the previous season. They had been running training sessions at 35 °C and 90% humidity. Altitude training, he explained, thickens the blood by shrinking its liquid part, and heat does the opposite: plasma volume, he is quoted as saying, “can be increased by up to 25 per cent” [1].

The practice has spread well beyond one team. A group of Danish researchers who work with professional riders wrote in 2024 that heat training had become widespread among them. Riders were using it to go faster in ordinary temperatures as well as to prepare for hot races [2]. The equipment has followed. A Swiss company sells a sensor the size of a matchbox that clips to a heart rate strap and shows an estimate of core body temperature on a bike computer. Its maker has announced partnerships with 10 professional teams [s3].

Preparing for a hot race is well supported. Two weeks of training at about 35 °C improved cyclists’ time-trial performance in the heat by 16% in one study [3]; 10 days improved it by 10% in another [4]. A

The disputed claim is that heat also makes you faster on a cool day, acting as a training stimulus much as altitude does.

Where the idea came from

The modern interest dates from a single paper. In 2010 Santiago Lorenzo and Christopher Minson at the University of Oregon had 12 trained cyclists ride for 10 days in a room at 40 °C. The riding was easy, at about half of VO2max. Eight matched controls did the same riding at 13 °C [5].

When the heat group was tested afterwards in the cool room, their VO2max had risen by 5%, from 66.8 to 70.2 mL/kg/min [5]. The work they could do in a time trial had risen by 6%, and their power at the lactate threshold by 5%. The control group had not changed. Plasma volume in the heat group was up 6.5%, and the heart’s maximum output had risen with it.

Other labs tried to repeat it, and the first attempts did not go well. The two-week study mentioned earlier tested its cyclists in the cool as well as the heat. After two weeks their VO2max had gone from 4.79 to 4.82 L/min. Their power in a 43 km outdoor time trial went from 300 W to 302 W [3]. The 10-day study used a crossover, in which the same seven men did 10 days of training at 38 °C and, separately, 10 days at 18 °C. The heat block raised their VO2max and time-trial power in a hot room by about 10% each. In a room at 18 °C, both were unchanged [4].

By 2016 the disagreement was formal. The Journal of Physiology ran one of its set-piece debates. Minson and James Cotter argued that heat acclimation does improve performance in the cool, and Lars Nybo and Carsten Lundby argued that it does not [6,7]. Even the proposers hedged. Their summary describes the benefit as unresolved and possibly “modest or absent in some settings and individuals”. They pointed out that nobody had yet tested truly elite athletes or run the heat for longer than a couple of weeks.

Length turned out to matter, because the blood adapts to heat in two stages.

How it works

Within about a week of daily heat exposure, the liquid part of the blood expands. The studies here put the increase at 6% to 7% [5,4,8], well short of Swart’s 25%, although he did say “up to”. More plasma helps the heart fill on each beat and supply the skin.

Sweating starts sooner and becomes more copious and more dilute. In one five-week study, sweat rate rose by 0.44 litres an hour [2]. Core temperature at a given workload comes down, helping the rider cope with heat.

For performance in the cool, the same change cuts both ways. Chapter 1 described VO2max as mostly a matter of oxygen delivery, which is the amount of blood the heart can pump multiplied by the oxygen each litre carries. Extra plasma helps the first and hurts the second, because the same number of red cells is now spread through more liquid. The Copenhagen group suggested that the two roughly cancel [8]. That would explain why 10 days of heat does so much in a hot room and so little in a cool one.

The second stage is slow, and it is the reason for the current fashion. If heat exposure continues for several weeks, the total amount of haemoglobin in the body starts to rise. Haemoglobin is the protein in red cells that carries oxygen, and its total mass, measured in grams, sets how much oxygen the blood can carry in all. Raising it is the whole point of altitude training.

The proposed explanation is that the kidney, which makes the hormone driving red cell production, responds to blood concentration. Dilute the blood with extra plasma for long enough and the kidney reads a shortage of red cells and orders more [2]. The evidence is indirect: Copenhagen researchers found no change in the relevant hormones during five and a half weeks of heat training, although haemoglobin rose [9].

That suggests a longer heat block could raise haemoglobin mass and perhaps performance. Since 2019, trials lasting four or five weeks have tested it.

From the saddle. It was crazy hot in the 2026 heatwave. My watts were way down when the pain cave was hitting 37 degrees. On a holiday in Greece soon afterwards I felt I was hitting some good power numbers in the Greek heat. When it cooled down, it was good to see my watts go back to normal.

What the five-week trials show

Six have been published, and their designs are similar enough to compare. Riders add about five hour-long sessions a week of easy riding in the heat, for five weeks, and are compared with a control group doing the same training in normal temperatures. The heat comes either from a chamber at 38 to 40 °C or from a heat suit worn while riding in an ordinary room.

Question
QuestionDoes five weeks of easy riding in the heat raise haemoglobin mass, and does it make elite athletes faster in the cool?
Haemoglobin mass, against controlsPerformance in the cool, against controls
23 elite male cyclists [10]
23 elite male cyclists [10]Up 42 g, from 893 to 935 g; controls up 6 gVO2max no better; threshold and 15-minute power up by small to intermediate amounts, not significant
Cyclists, heat suit or chamber [11]
Cyclists, heat suit or chamber [11]Up 2.6% with the suit and 2.4% in the chamber; controls down 0.7%Threshold and one-minute power better with the suit only; heat beat control, 4.9% against 1.7%, only with both heat groups and three measures combined
25 elite cross-country skiers [12]

20 elite male cyclists, 2024 [2]
20 elite male cyclists, 2024 [2]Up 3% after three weeks and 4% after fivePeak power up 12 W in a ramp test; VO2max change not significant

On haemoglobin every trial points the same way, and the size of the effect, 30 to 40 g or 3% to 4%, is about what an altitude camp delivers. One study made that comparison directly in seven riders who did both: 5.4% from five weeks of heat, 3.5% from three weeks at 3,000 metres [14]. B

On performance they do not agree: two say yes, one says yes after pooling and two say no. A meta-analysis of 28 heat studies of all lengths put the effect on cool-weather VO2max, against control training, at 0.30 standard deviations, conventionally called small, with a confidence interval from 0.06 to 0.54 [15]. My reading is that there is probably a real effect on performance in elite riders, that it is small, and that it is much less certain than the effect on haemoglobin. B

Carsten Lundby, who argued the “no” side of the 2016 debate, is an author on every one of these five-week trials. The evidence comes from one connected group of labs in Copenhagen and Lillehammer; nobody outside it has yet repeated the result.

The riders were nearly all elite, and the men among them had VO2max values in the mid-70s [10,13]. An elite rider has little room left to improve by ordinary training, so a 3% rise in haemoglobin is worth chasing.

And the gain does not last. In the 2024 trial, haemoglobin mass was back to its starting value two weeks after the heat sessions stopped [2]. Rønnestad’s group found that three sessions a week were enough to hold it [11]. Heat training is therefore something you keep doing or time carefully, like a taper.

One study, up close: the Copenhagen amateurs

In 2019 Nybo and Lundby’s group published the first trial long enough to test the haemoglobin idea, and it remains the only one in riders who resemble the readers of this book [8,9].

Hypothesis
HypothesisTraining in the heat would raise VO2max, peak power and performance in a 15 km time trial, all tested in the cool.
Design

Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionTraining in the heat was no better than normal training for aerobic power or time-trial performance in cool conditions. Replacing a large part of the riders’ training with heat sessions did not reduce what they gained from training either.

The heat sessions were harder than “an hour at 60%” sounds. Rectal temperature at the end of every one was above 39 °C, 39.9 °C in the first and 39.4 °C in the last. By every standard test the riders acclimated: their sweat became more dilute, their heart rate in the heat fell, and they lasted longer in a hot endurance test [8].

They were no faster in the cool for it. Both groups gained 17 W in the time trial. The difference in haemoglobin mass between the groups fell just short of statistical significance, at p = 0.061 [9]. The elite trials later found a similar gain, and here it bought nothing.

Twenty-one riders is few, and a real performance difference of a few watts could be hidden in a group that size. The controls improved by 17 W over five weeks, which suggests the whole group was coming into form after winter. A rising tide of that kind can swamp a small effect [8]. Only men took part. But the central result is hard to argue with for an amateur weighing this up. Riders much like you gave five of their eight and a half weekly hours to riding in a 40 °C chamber, and were no faster than the riders who trained normally. C for the claim that heat training improves cool-weather performance in amateurs.

Reading the research: a marker is not a performance

Haemoglobin mass measures a proposed route to better performance. Time-trial power measures whether the rider actually got faster. The heat trials show why the distinction matters.

Haemoglobin rose in all six trials, but the skiers and the Copenhagen amateurs gained no performance advantage over controls [12,8]. A headline saying “heat training increases haemoglobin mass” leaves that out.

When a study reports a marker, look for the performance measure in the same paper. If it is missing, the study has shown that a mechanism was engaged. If it is present and didn’t move, that is the finding, whatever the title says.

The table shows the same thing from the other side. In the trial where only the heat-suit group improved, heat beat control only once both heat groups and three tests were combined [11]. A choice of that kind, made after the data are in, raises the odds of finding something. A result that appears only after pooling deserves less weight than one that was there in the first comparison. What survives is the marker itself, which rose in every trial, and the gain in hot conditions, which is well established.

The sensor

The device most riders mean is called CORE, made by a Swiss company, greenTEG. It doesn’t measure core temperature, which can only be measured from inside the body. It measures the temperature of the skin on your chest and the rate at which heat is flowing out through it. It can also use heart rate, and an algorithm turns these into an estimate of the temperature deep in the body [16].

I don’t own one. I found three independent studies comparing it with a direct measurement.

One group tested it against a rectal probe during indoor cycling. It was repeatable: when 12 men did the same ride twice, the sensor’s readings on the two days differed by an average of 0.02 °C. Against the probe it did less well. At 19 °C it read 0.23 °C high on average, and only 51% of its readings were within 0.3 °C of the true value. At 31 °C it read 0.10 °C low on average, with 45% of readings within 0.3 °C. Most individual readings fell somewhere between 0.6 °C below the probe and 0.7 °C above it [16]. The authors concluded that their results did not support the maker’s claim of a valid measure.

Two other independent tests found it reading low as people got hotter, or lagging behind the real rise [s4,s5]. One was in hockey players at a heat camp, the other in a 5 km run at 30 °C. I found no independent test of the newer, smaller CORE 2.

For heat training, an error of half a degree matters a good deal. The sessions in the Copenhagen trial ended with core temperatures between 39.4 and 39.9 °C [8]. Heat illness is usually associated with core temperatures above 40 °C [17]. The useful range is about one degree wide. The sensor’s error in the published tests is about half a degree in either direction, and in two of the three studies it tended to read low when the body is hottest. A reading of 38.8 °C could mean you are not yet in the range, or that you are at the top of it.

It is also worth knowing that none of the trials in this chapter used the sensor. The Copenhagen group used rectal probes. They have obvious drawbacks for home use. Rønnestad’s group prescribed time, a suit or a room temperature, and an easy intensity. The haemoglobin results came from riders who were simply made hot for 50 minutes, five times a week [11].

A repeatable but inaccurate reading might help track your own sessions, though it cannot tell you your true temperature. The sensor is optional: the training benefits were demonstrated without it.

Cooling on the day

The ice on those start lines has more trial evidence behind it than most of this chapter. A 2015 meta-analysis pooled 28 trials of cooling, all in men exercising at above 30 °C. Cooling before the effort improved performance by an average of 5.7%, and cooling during it by 9.9%; the difference between those two was not statistically significant. During exercise, ice vests were the most effective method. Beforehand, combining several methods worked best [18]. A

The slushy has studies of its own. Ice absorbs a great deal of heat as it melts, so a drink that is partly ice takes more heat out of the body than the same drink served cold. In one study, 10 men drank either an ice slurry or cold water before running to exhaustion at 34 °C. The slurry lowered their rectal temperature by 0.66 °C before they started, against 0.25 °C for the water, and they ran for 50 minutes instead of 41 [19]. Ten cyclists drank a sports drink as a slushy through 90 minutes of riding at 32 °C. It cut their time in a time trial straight afterwards from 20:24 to 18:28 [s6].

That cycling study had a third arm, in which the riders swilled the slushy round their mouths and spat it out. They finished in 19:45, between the other two. Some of the benefit of cold is in the sensation, with nothing swallowed. The meta-analysis points the same way [18]. Across its 28 trials, the size of the drop in core temperature did not predict the size of the gain in performance. Feeling cooler lets you work harder. In the running study the men who had drunk the slurry stopped at a higher rectal temperature than they reached after cold water, 39.4 °C against 39.1 °C [19]. The ice had bought them room to go further into the heat, and they used it.

Cooling and acclimation have been compared directly. Thirteen triathletes did a 20 km time trial at 35 °C before and after an eight-day training camp in the heat, each time with and without an ice vest beforehand [s7]. Before the camp the vest was worth 10 W. The camp was worth 28 W. After the camp the vest added 4 W, an effect the authors called unclear, although the riders still felt more comfortable with it. So a rider who has adapted gets less from the ice, and a rider who hasn’t had the chance to adapt gets the most. For an amateur flying to a hot sportive from a British spring, that second case is the usual one.

What to do with it

If your target event will be hot, heat training is worth doing, and the case is as strong as any in this book. One to two weeks of regular riding in the heat before the event is what the 2015 studies used, with gains of 10% to 16% in hot conditions [3,4]. The sweating and cardiovascular adaptations were largely complete within three weeks in the 2024 trial, and they were gone two weeks after stopping [2]. So the block needs to run up close to the event. On the day itself, cool down before the start and keep the coldest, iciest drink you can carry.

If the aim is to be faster in ordinary temperatures, my advice for most readers is not to bother. The dose that raises haemoglobin is about five hours a week for five weeks. For a professional training 25 hours a week, five easy hours in a heat suit are a small part of the programme. For a rider with eight hours, they are most of it, and they are hours at low power in conditions that make quality work impossible. The one trial in riders at that level found no advantage [8]. The time is better spent on the things the earlier chapters covered.

If you want to try it anyway, perhaps because you are short of ways to add load without adding hours on the road, the trials give a template. Ride indoors at a genuinely easy intensity for 50 to 60 minutes, with no fan and enough clothing to make you sweat heavily. Do it four or five times a week for five weeks, and then two or three times a week to hold what you have gained [11]. Expect your power at a given heart rate to be well down in these sessions. Keep your hard sessions cool, as the riders in the trials did.

Be careful. The sessions in the trials were supervised, the riders were young and screened, and their core temperatures were being measured properly. Riding alone in a spare room until your core temperature passes 39 °C is a different undertaking. Drink, stop if you feel dizzy, confused or chilled, and don’t do it at all without medical advice if you have a heart condition or take medication that affects sweating or blood pressure.

The longer trials established an increase in haemoglobin more clearly than an increase in speed. For an amateur weighing five hot hours against ordinary training, the one direct comparison found no advantage.

What survives
  • Training in the heat makes you faster in the heat. A
  • It raises haemoglobin mass by 3 to 4%, about what an altitude camp gives. B
  • In the one trial in amateurs, it didn’t make them faster in normal weather. C
