Chapter 16: Drugs

Draft · 4,088 words · 27 October 2026

Ninety-six finishers

The 1998 Tour de France started in Dublin on 11 July with 189 riders. Three days earlier a car belonging to the Festina team had been stopped at the French-Belgian border carrying EPO, steroids and other drugs. The team was expelled after the sixth stage. Six more teams left the race before the end, and 96 riders reached Paris [1,2].

Fourteen years later the United States Anti-Doping Agency banned Lance Armstrong, the rider who won the next seven Tours, for life and struck out his results. Its published decision described a team-wide doping programme [3]. He admitted it the following January. No winner is listed for those seven races [s1].

I assume today’s riders are clean. Nothing here is meant to suggest otherwise about anyone, and nobody is connected with doping in this chapter unless an official body has found it or the rider has admitted it. What I do think is that professional teams look for every advantage the rules allow, and that the rules keep having to catch up with them.

What they were trying to achieve

The commission that investigated cycling’s doping history in 2015 summarised decades of it in one sentence. The aims, it wrote, had stayed the same throughout: to raise the blood’s capacity to carry oxygen, and to build muscle and speed recovery [4]. The drugs changed as new ones reached the market and as tests caught up with old ones, while those two targets stayed fixed.

The second aim covers testosterone, growth hormone and the corticosteroids, which riders told the commission were used both to dull pain and to strip weight. The first is the one that defined the era, and it maps directly onto the model in Chapter 1. Among well-trained riders, VO2max is limited mainly by how much oxygen the heart and blood can deliver to the muscles. Training raises delivery slowly, over years, and by amounts that shrink as a rider approaches their ceiling. A drug that raises it by a tenth in a month is acting on the one link in the chain that an elite athlete can no longer improve much by working harder.

One way to do it was to transfuse blood. A rider had a bag or two of their own blood taken out and stored, waited some weeks for the body to replace it, and had the red cells put back before a race. The other, from about 1990, was a drug that made the body produce the extra red cells itself.

How it works: the biology of EPO

Erythropoietin, EPO for short, is a hormone that everyone makes. Its job is to keep the number of red blood cells matched to the body’s need for oxygen.

It is made mainly in the kidneys, by cells in the outer layer called the cortex [5]. Those cells contain a sensor for oxygen. The sensor is a protein, hypoxia-inducible factor or HIF. The cell makes it continuously and, as long as oxygen is plentiful, destroys it almost as fast as it makes it. The enzymes that mark HIF for destruction need oxygen to work. When the oxygen reaching the kidney falls, because you have lost blood, or moved to altitude, or become anaemic, those enzymes slow down, HIF survives, and it switches on the gene for EPO.

EPO then travels in the blood to the bone marrow, where red cells are made. The marrow constantly produces red cell precursors, many of which die before maturing. EPO is the signal that lets them live. More EPO means more precursors survive, multiply and mature into red cells, each packed with haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen [5]. As the red cell count rises, more oxygen reaches the kidney, HIF is destroyed again, and EPO production falls back. It is a thermostat for the blood.

Altitude and heat, covered elsewhere in this book, work through the same thermostat. Altitude training lowers the oxygen in the blood, so the kidney makes more EPO for as long as you stay high. Heat training, on one theory, dilutes the blood until the kidney reads it as short of red cells. Both are slow and both stop when the stimulus stops.

People whose kidneys fail lose the ability to make EPO and become severely anaemic. In the 1980s the human gene was inserted into cultured cells to make the hormone, and in June 1989 the United States approved this recombinant EPO as a treatment for the anaemia of kidney failure [s2]. For those patients it replaced regular blood transfusions, and it remains one of the most useful drugs biotechnology has produced.

Injected into a healthy person, the same drug overrides the thermostat. The marrow receives a signal to make red cells that the body doesn’t need. In 2007 Carsten Lundby, who appears in the heat training chapter, measured what happens next in eight healthy volunteers given EPO for 15 weeks [6]. Their red cell volume rose from 2,933 mL to about 3,200 mL. Their plasma volume fell, from 3,645 mL to about 3,270 mL. Total blood volume barely changed. The body made room for the new red cells by removing liquid. Between 38% and 54% of the rise in the blood’s oxygen content came from that concentration, not from the extra cells.

That is the reverse of what heat does, which is why a team scientist in the heat training chapter describes altitude and heat as opposites. It is also why the measure everyone talked about was haematocrit, the percentage of the blood’s volume taken up by red cells. Riders told the 2015 commission that their natural levels were in the low to middle 40s [4]. EPO pushed the number up from both directions at once, by adding cells and by taking away plasma, and blood with that many cells in it is thicker and harder to pump.

How much it was worth

In the laboratory the effect is large. In a second study from the same group, eight healthy non-athletes given EPO raised their VO2max by 12.6% in four weeks, and the time they could ride at 80% of it rose by 54% [s3]. A 2025 review of 10 studies in well-trained athletes found the same direction in all of them: haemoglobin up, VO2max up, peak power usually up [7]. A for the claim that EPO raises VO2max.

Transfusion works too, and it takes very little blood. In a double-blind study, highly trained men were given back about 135 mL of their own red cells, roughly half of what one donated bag contains. Their power in a time trial improved from 213 W to 223 W, about 5%. After a sham transfusion nothing changed [s4].

What these numbers meant in a professional race is harder to establish, because nobody can run a trial in the Tour. The commission’s report says it “was told” that gains had been 10% to 15% in the years of unrestricted use, and perhaps 3% to 5% from the small doses riders moved to once blood values were being tracked [4]. Those figures are testimony from people inside the sport. They aren’t measurements, and the report doesn’t say who offered them.

Race speeds give indirect support. One analysis took the fifth-placed finisher in each Tour, Giro and Vuelta from 1990 to 2009, to avoid depending on any one champion. Average speed rose by 0.16 km/h a year until 2004 and then fell by 0.22 km/h a year [8]. Its author read the turn as compatible with anti-doping efforts taking hold. But a second analysis, of the winning times of 181 Grand Tours going back to 1947, found no sharp break in the 1990s. It concluded that the effect of EPO on results may have been overestimated [9]. Speed depends on the route, the weather, the tactics and the tarmac as well as the riders, and two careful people looking at similar data reached different conclusions.

One study, up close: EPO up Mont Ventoux

In the spring of 2016 a clinical research unit in Leiden tested EPO on amateur cyclists the way a new medicine is tested, and ended the trial with a race up Mont Ventoux [10].

The race came about 12 days after the last injection, with haemoglobin still 12% above where it started, and 40 of the 44 riders who started it finished [10]. The authors’ conclusion is easily shortened to “EPO doesn’t work”, and the trial does not show that. For the avoidance of doubt, this book is not suggesting that you find out.

Reading the research: when a trial finds nothing

A result of “no difference” can mean that there is no effect, or that the study could not have seen one. The way to tell is the confidence interval, the range of true effects the data are compatible with.

In their planning, the authors worked out the size of effect that would matter: a gain in sustained power of a little over 3%. They estimated that was worth about two minutes on a climb like Ventoux [10]. Now look at what the race could detect. The difference in time between the groups was 0.3%, with a 95% confidence interval from 8.3% faster on EPO to 9.6% slower. On a 100-minute climb that is a range of roughly eight minutes either way. A two-minute effect is well inside it. So is a five-minute one.

The paper itself gives the reasons the race was so imprecise. There was an 85 km/h wind and 5 °C at the summit that afternoon, four riders gave up from exhaustion, and each had one attempt, at the end of a long day [10].

The 45-minute laboratory test was far better controlled, and it is the stronger evidence. Its result was a difference of 5.9 W in favour of EPO, with an interval from 0.9 W the wrong way to 12.7 W the right way. As a percentage, that runs from about zero to about 4.5%. The best estimate is a gain of 2%. The commission was told that micro-dosing was worth 3% to 5%. The trial’s own laboratory time trial does not rule that out [10,4].

Who was studied matters too. These riders trained five to six hours a week, which the authors acknowledge is far below a professional’s load. For an amateur, a 2% change in sustained power is lost among everything else that varies from one rider to the next on the day. For a professional racing against riders who have all spent years removing those other differences, the same 2% is a decisive margin.

Two months of a professional’s dose raised these recreational riders’ VO2max measurably, and most who received it could not tell. The sustained-power result remained uncertain. B for the claim that EPO improves sustained performance in the laboratory; C, resting on testimony and race speeds, for its size on the road in professionals.

The risks

The risk everybody knows about is that EPO thickened riders’ blood until their hearts stopped in the night. The story usually comes with a number: 18 Dutch and Belgian cyclists dead between 1987 and 1990.

The 2015 commission repeats it, and its wording is careful. “The media speculated”, it says, that the deaths of 18 European cyclists were related to EPO [4].

In 2011 a Spanish academic, Bernat López, went looking for the evidence behind the number [11]. He collected 61 texts that mention the deaths, 36 of them academic. Only two cited anything resembling an original source, and both of those were newspaper articles. The rest cited one another, or nobody. The details changed from text to text: the number of dead ran from “half a dozen” to “around 40”, the nationalities from Dutch and Belgian to Scandinavian, and the dates across two decades. One paper put the deaths between 1997 and 2000 [11].

López then searched newspaper archives for every sudden death of a competitive cyclist he could find. Between 1987 and 1992 there were 17, nine of them Dutch and six Belgian, which is about one a year in each country. Several had retired before EPO was available, some died in the off-season, and seven were amateurs with little access to an expensive new drug. He was left with two cases that could even plausibly involve it. In one of the best-known cases, a Dutch professional who died in his sleep in 1990, the rider’s widow said the post-mortem had found nothing linking his death to the drug. Studies of sudden death in young athletes, which López also reviewed, attribute about nine in 10 to underlying heart conditions [11].

His paper has an argument to make. He calls the story anti-doping propaganda, and he concedes that his own count is not watertight and that nothing he found proves EPO played no part. But the central finding stands on its own: a claim repeated in dozens of scholarly works had no traceable evidence behind it.

That doesn’t make the drug safe. In one large trial that López cites, dialysis patients with heart disease had their haematocrit pushed up to 42% with EPO or held at 30%. Those at 42% had more heart attacks [11]. Those were sick people, and the finding can’t simply be transferred to athletes, but it shows the concern about thick blood was not invented. Riders described to the commission how they got up in the night to turn the pedals on a stationary bike and keep their blood moving [4]. Whether that fear was justified by the physiology or by the rumour is hard to know now. What the episode shows is how a plausible mechanism, repeated often enough, comes to be treated as an observed fact, and that is the thing this book keeps warning about.

In 1997 the governing body brought in a rule that any rider with a haematocrit above 50% would be stood down for 15 days. It was presented as a health check, because there was then no test for EPO itself. The commission thought it probably prevented deaths [4]. It was also told what the rule did to behaviour. A rider whose natural level was 43% now had seven points of headroom, and riders described carrying centrifuges to stay inside it. One former rider said the rule “was perceived by riders as legalising EPO up to a certain limit” [4]. Its best-known application came in June 1999. Marco Pantani, the winner of that 1998 Tour, was removed from a Giro d’Italia he was leading by more than five minutes after a reading of 52% [12]. Because the rule was a health measure, that was a two-week stand-down and not a doping sanction.

In the Leiden trial, with weekly blood checks and the dose held back whenever haematocrit reached 52%, there was no difference in adverse events between the groups and no sign of clotting. Two blood markers involved in clot formation did rise in the EPO group, and the authors point out that a study of 48 people could not have detected a rare event such as a stroke [10].

The costs that are fully documented are of a different kind. Careers ended in bans and some in court. Seven Tours have no winner. And for every rider caught there were others who didn’t dope and finished where nobody remembers, in a generation of results that can’t be read.

What the era teaches

Tests catch only a fraction of doping. A review of prevalence studies across elite sport estimated that between 14% and 39% of athletes had doped intentionally, during years in which 1% to 2% of tests came back positive [13]. The German blood-doping ring was broken in 2019 by police acting on a skier’s confession, and the cyclists who then admitted using it had not been caught by a test [14]. A clean test record, on its own, shows little.

Since January 2008 professional riders have had a biological passport, a running record of their blood values against which each new sample is compared. In its first two years the programme covered more than 850 riders and almost 20,000 samples [15]. It aims to catch the effect of doping when the drug itself has gone. In 2011 researchers gave 10 volunteers small, frequent doses of EPO for up to 12 weeks. Their haemoglobin mass rose by 10%, about the equivalent of two bags of blood, and the passport software flagged none [16]. The 2015 commission named micro-dosing as its biggest concern. It also judged that forcing riders to use less had shrunk the gain enough for a clean rider to win again [4].

The 50% rule shows how a safety limit can become a target. Riders who treated it as permission to raise their haematocrit changed the purpose of the rule.

Race performances cannot establish guilt or innocence. Climbing times depend on the wind, the pace into the foot of the climb, the tactics and the road surface. The prevalence review concluded that performance data cannot be used to estimate how much doping there is [13]. Even people inside the sport disagreed: one “respected cycling professional” told the commission 90% of the peloton still doped, another said 20%, and many said they didn’t know [4].

The commission also wrote that doping in amateur cycling was “becoming endemic”, and that masters races were “said to have middle-aged businessmen winning on EPO” [4]. It blamed cheap drugs, easy access through gyms and the internet, and the near absence of testing at that level. The Leiden trial found no measurable mountain-race gain in amateurs, although its wide uncertainty leaves a small gain possible. That is a poor basis for risking health and a ban for an age-group result.

Getting faster without it

Several legal practices could contribute to modern racing speeds, although they cannot establish how much has changed since the EPO era.

Fuelling has a clear effect on late-ride power. In the Durability trial, critical power after three hours was 236 W on water and 266 W on 120 grams of carbohydrate an hour [s5]. That is about 13%, but it compares fuelling with water, not modern practice with the 1990s. Chapter 13’s older food diaries show why we should not treat the whole gain as a recent discovery.

Haemoglobin can be raised legally. Three weeks at 3,000 metres raised it by 3.5% in elite cyclists, and five weeks of heat training by about the same or more [s6]. Those are smaller than the 10% a course of EPO micro-doses produced in the Australian study, they fade within a fortnight, and they have to be timed. They are also available to every team.

I can’t put a number on equipment from the sources I have read for this book, and I would rather say so than quote a manufacturer. Tyres roll more easily than they did, and frames and clothing are more aerodynamic. On any climb ridden at over 20 km/h, some of the rider’s power still goes into the air. Training has changed too, in the ways the rest of this book describes.

I find these plausible contributors to modern speeds. Adding up their separate effects would not show how much faster they have made the peloton, or prove anyone clean.

The edge of the rules

The line between clean and doped is drawn by a list, and the list moves.

Tramadol is an opioid painkiller. For years it was legal, and the 2015 commission was told it was “used widely” in the peloton for that reason [4]. In one trial, cyclists produced 220 W in a 20-minute time trial on tramadol against 209 W on a placebo, although a second experiment in the same paper found no difference [17]. Cycling banned it in competition from March 2019 and the World Anti-Doping Agency followed in 2024 [s7,s8]. A rider who took it in 2018 broke no rule. The same act six years later is a doping offence.

Carbon monoxide is a more recent case. Inhaling a small, measured amount is the standard way to measure haemoglobin mass, and it is how the heat training studies in the previous chapter got their numbers. Used once, it is a measuring tool. Used repeatedly, in theory, it could starve the body of a little oxygen and prompt the kidney to make more EPO, which would be altitude training from a cylinder. In February 2025 the sport’s governing body banned possession of carbon monoxide rebreathing kits outside a medical facility, giving rider health as its reason. It allowed a single supervised measurement, with a second no sooner than two weeks later, and asked the World Anti-Doping Agency to take a position on it [18]. I know of no evidence that any rider used it for anything except measurement. The rule was written because the possibility existed.

Ketone drinks are legal. In October 2025 the governing body said there was “no compelling evidence” that they help and that it did not recommend them, but it did not ban them [19].

Tramadol, carbon monoxide measurement and ketones illustrate how the rules change around practices that were permitted. Looking for legal gains is what a professional team is for; describing that search is not an accusation of doping. As the 50% rule showed, riders can also interpret a limit as permission to approach it.

For anyone riding below that level the conclusion is simpler. The gains this chapter has described as certain are the legal ones: eating enough on the bike, training consistently for years, and for those with the time, altitude or heat. The one trial of the era’s signature drug in riders like us found nothing on the road. Whatever is true of the professionals, there is nothing in that pharmacy for an amateur.

Part VPutting it together

Chapter 17: The training week

Draft · 3,142 words · 27 October 2026

Build the week in this order. Put in two hard sessions first, at least 48 hours apart and ideally 72 [1]. Add a long ride if your events are long and the week has room for it. Fill the rest with easy riding near the top of Zone 2. Leave the remaining days empty.

The hard sessions produced most of the improvement in Part III’s trials on a few hours a week [2]. Planning them first protects their spacing and leaves the easy riding to fit around them [1].

The order to build it in

The hard sessions. Two a week is the best-supported default for a rider on six to ten hours. The reasons are in Chapter 12. Two sessions build about as much as three over a few weeks, and the heart’s nervous control takes 48 hours or more to recover from a hard session [1]. One of the two should be long intervals of four to eight minutes per effort, adding up to about half an hour of hard work. In recreational cyclists on about six hours a week, 4 × 8 minutes doubled the gain from 4 × 4 [2]. The other can be 30/15s, more long intervals, or a controlled threshold session. A threshold session costs less to recover from, and builds the fraction of VO2max you can sustain more than VO2max itself (Chapter 11). A third hard session belongs only in a short block of a week or two, followed by an easier week, and only when the rest of the week can be genuinely easy. Beyond three the trials found no further gain, and the warning signs of overreaching came first (Chapter 12). B for two sessions and their spacing; C for the choice of the second

Riding them. For long intervals and 30/15s, ride at the hardest effort you can sustain to the end. Keep threshold sessions controlled below the second threshold. Judge by power and effort; heart rate can make short intervals look closer to VO2max than they are (Chapter 11). When a session becomes comfortable, add a repetition before adding power. B for the sessions; C for the advice on progression

The long ride. If your events last four or five hours, a weekly ride of three or four hours is a reasonable bet for durability. Chapter 9 explains why it is a bet and not a finding. If your events are an hour, it is optional. Where the week is too short to hold it after the hard sessions, the hard sessions win.

The easy riding. Everything else is easy, and Chapter 7’s rule sets how easy: as much work as the ride can carry without taking anything from the hard sessions. For a rider on these hours that means the top of Zone 2, a few beats under the ceiling. It is the part of the week that grows with the hours. A ride that drifts between the thresholds is not a better easy ride. It is an extra hard session, and it should be counted as one, because it costs about as much to recover from as an interval session does [s1].

The rest. No trial I found tested how many days off a rider needs each week. A rest day or a short easy ride before each hard session helps you arrive fresh. Regular riding also matters: the Norwegian analysis found larger gains at four or five sessions a week [3], and regularity is my likeliest explanation for the winter’s improvement in Chapter 7.

Three weeks

The figure shows one way to lay out a week at 4, 8 and 12 hours. Each total is the time on the bike, including warm-ups and cool-downs.

At 4 hours, the week is two hard sessions and two short easy rides: 4 × 8 minutes on Tuesday, an hour easy on Thursday, three sets of 30/15s on Saturday and 45 minutes easy on Sunday. The hard sessions are 96 and 72 hours apart. Their efforts total about 52 minutes, or 21% of the week. The short easy rides keep the riding regular. If three riding days suit your life better than four, you could combine them into one longer ride, which Chapter 7’s account of the mechanism slightly favours.

At 8 hours, the hard sessions move to Tuesday and Friday, 72 hours apart. An easy ride of an hour and a half goes on Wednesday and an hour on Thursday, and a three-hour long ride on Saturday. Sunday and Monday are rest. The hard work is the same 52 minutes, now 11% of the week.

At 12 hours, the long intervals grow to 5 × 8 minutes, the long ride to four hours, and the easy days to two hours and an hour and a half. Another easy hour and a half goes on Sunday. The hard work comes to about an hour, 8% of the week.

From 4 hours to 12, the hard dose stays within Chapter 12’s trial range of about 40 minutes to an hour a week. Most extra hours are easy. The falling percentage of hard training follows from that arrangement; it is not a target to aim at. C

The days are movable. Put the hard sessions where you are fresh and have time to ride them properly, and keep at least 48 hours between them [1]. Put the long ride where you have the hours, which for most people is the weekend. If a hard session follows the long ride, eat well on the long ride. If the long ride follows a hard session, it should be genuinely easy.

From the saddle. My training week has massively changed since I started on this book. My mates used to tease me about how much Zone 2 I was doing. I’ve introduced structured intervals and seen a massive benefit within a few weeks, and it’s still building. My Zone 2 output has notched up, and I’m feeling stronger. I now do two interval sessions a week, two Zone 2 sessions and a longer ride at the weekend. Now that I know what I’m doing, I’m confident I’m on the right track.

That is one rider over a few weeks, and it can’t separate the intervals from anything else that changed at the same time.

Building up

Most advice about adding training comes with a number. The best known is to add no more than 10% a week. It has been tested once, properly, and it made no difference [4].

One study, up close: the 10% rule

Hypothesis
HypothesisA graded programme for novice runners would reduce the number of running-related injuries compared with a standard programme.
Design
DesignRandomised trial in 532 novice runners preparing for a recreational 4-mile (6.7 km) event. Injuries were recorded in an online running log. An injury was any complaint of the lower limbs or back that stopped running for at least a week [4].
Graded programmeStandard programme
Length
Length13 weeks8 weeks

How the training roseBy no more than 10% a weekAs in a standard beginners’ plan

Authors’ conclusionA graded 13-week programme applying the 10% rule did not reduce injuries compared with a standard 8-week programme.

Five extra weeks of slower build-up bought no measurable reduction in injuries.

The runners were beginners, the outcome was injury and not fitness, and running hurts the body in a way cycling mostly doesn’t. Each footstrike loads bones and tendons, and the bike, apart from crashes, spares them. So the trial doesn’t say that a cyclist can add hours at any rate. It says that the most quoted number for safe progression has no evidence behind it where it was tested, and nothing better has replaced it. B for the trial; C for what it means on a bike

What does seem to matter, in the research that followed, is the size of sudden jumps rather than any steady rate. A widely read review in 2016 argued that athletes used to high loads get injured less often, and that “excessive and rapid increases” in training are behind many injuries [5]. The idea is plausible and fits what coaches see. The tool that came with it is another matter.

Reading the research: a ratio that correlates with itself

The review proposed a number for spotting a dangerous jump: the acute:chronic workload ratio, this week’s training load divided by the average weekly load over the last four weeks. Above a certain ratio, the risk of injury was said to rise. It became the most popular measure of its kind [6], and the review called it “a best practice predictor of training-related injuries” [5].

Look at how the conventional version is calculated. The four-week average includes this week. So the top and the bottom of the ratio share a quarter of their content. A week with a high load raises the top of the ratio fully and the bottom by a quarter as much, and the ratio rises whatever was happening to the rider. A week of 400 units after three weeks of 200 gives a ratio of 400 divided by 250, which is 1.6. The same 400 after three weeks of 400 gives exactly 1.0. The ratio is partly measuring this week twice.

That matters when the ratio is correlated with something else that depends on this week’s load, such as injury. In 2019 a group of sport scientists published a short paper with the plain title “Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations” [s2]. A ratio whose top and bottom share a term will correlate with anything that correlates with that term, even when the ratio itself adds nothing.

In 2020 a fuller critique concluded that “There is no evidence supporting the use of ACWR in training-load-management systems or for training recommendations aimed at reducing injury risk” [6]. No study had tried to estimate a causal effect properly. The ratio failed to normalise what it claimed to normalise, behaved differently depending on how it was calculated, and was not consistently related to injury. In the authors’ words, it “adds noise and creates statistical artifacts”.

When a training tool claims to predict an outcome with one number, check whether its calculation already contains something related to that outcome. Overlapping terms can manufacture a correlation.

For a cyclist, the useful part survives without the ratio. Don’t double your training in one week after a quiet month. Rebuild gradually after a break, which Chapter 19 covers. Neither needs a number to two decimal places.

Monotony

In 1998 Carl Foster followed 25 experienced athletes who logged each session as its rated effort multiplied by duration [7]. He defined weekly monotony as the average daily load divided by its standard deviation: similar days score high, varied days low. Illnesses clustered when athletes went over individual thresholds, mostly of strain: the week’s load multiplied by its monotony.

This was an observational study with self-reported illness. It does not establish a cause, but it supports varying the days rather than riding seven identical sessions between the thresholds. C

Where the rest goes

The other things Part IV weighed fit around the riding, not into it.

Strength. Chapter 14’s advice is heavy lifting for the legs twice a week for about three months, starting after the season ends, and once a week after that to keep it. In a week, that is one or two short sessions in the gym, and they compete with the hard rides for fresh legs. One arrangement, which no trial has tested, is to lift on the same day as a hard ride, after it or several hours later. The easy days then stay easy, and the legs are not heavy from squats at the start of an interval session. For the first two or three weeks of lifting, expect soreness and ride less. C

Fuel. Arrive at the hard sessions fuelled, because a hard session ridden on empty is a hard session wasted. Eat on anything longer than about 90 minutes. Chapter 13 has the amounts. The long ride is also the place to practise eating what you will eat in your events.

Heat. Chapter 15 found little for an amateur in deliberate heat training, apart from a week or two of riding in warm conditions before a hot event. A rider training indoors in summer is getting some of it anyway, and Chapter 18 covers what that does to heart rate.

Indoors. A trainer makes the hard sessions easier to ride well and the long ride harder to bear. The same effort indoors also tends to produce less power than outdoors. Chapter 18 has the numbers. None of it changes the shape of the week.

Across a season

This is an example, with different evidence behind each part.

Building the hours. The rider adds about half an hour a week until the hours reach what life allows, then holds. No trial tells a cyclist how fast to add hours, and the 10% rule’s one trial found no benefit from going slowly [4]. Going slowly costs little, though, and the jump to avoid is the sudden one.

Lighter weeks. Every fourth week in the figure is about 30% lighter, with one hard session instead of two. This is coaching convention. I searched for a trial in cyclists that compared a regular pattern of lighter weeks with steady training and found none. The nearest evidence is indirect. Unrelieved load leads to the stagnation and fatigue of overreaching [8], and fitness shows up better after volume is cut and intensity kept, which is what a taper is. Take a lighter week when the hard sessions stop going well, or when life makes one for you, and don’t worry about the rhythm. C

Blocks. Some riders concentrate their hard sessions into a block of a week or two, followed by easier weeks. The 2019 meta-analysis of block periodisation found small advantages over traditional arrangements, an effect size of 0.40 for VO2max and 0.28 for peak power [9]. The studies behind it were rated as small and generally of low quality, with an average score of 3.7 out of 10 on its quality scale. A block is a reasonable way to use a free week, and the evidence doesn’t make it necessary. C

Order. In the largest trial of cyclists, 63 riders did the same 24 interval sessions over 12 weeks in three different orders, with similar improvements [s3]. There was no advantage to starting with either the long or the short intervals. B

The taper. The best evidence in this chapter is for the last two weeks. A 2007 meta-analysis of 27 studies in competitive athletes found the largest gains from a two-week taper. It cut training volume by 41% to 60%, without reducing the intensity or the number of sessions [10]. The figure’s taper does that: the hours fall to about 6 and then about 4, and both hard sessions stay, shortened. The effects were measured as changes from before the taper to after it, without a group that kept training normally. So some of the gain is simply being rested for the event. That is the point. B

Not everyone has a target event. A rider who rides for fitness and the odd sportive can hold a steady week for months, take a lighter week when tired, and skip the taper. Kiely’s 2012 review of periodisation argued that the classic models rest on assumptions that are “no longer scientifically justifiable” [11]. Because responses to training vary so much between people, he argued, a plan should respond to how the rider is going rather than follow a fixed calendar.

When the week goes wrong

The weeks in the figure have the advantage of never having been ridden. When life cuts into yours, protect the hard sessions by dropping easy hours first.

Drop easy riding first. Missing an easy hour costs very little.

Drop to one hard session when you are new to intervals, busy or travelling, or when two leave you flat. Hickson’s volunteers kept their VO2max for 15 weeks after cutting from six training days to two at the same intensity [s4]. A later minimum-dose review reached a similar conclusion [12]. I would use one hard session alongside reduced easy riding as a fallback for a busy period. As Chapter 12 explains, that exact mix is a practical inference, rather than a tested maintenance dose. C

Don’t make up missed sessions by doubling up. The spacing matters before the number. The spacing rule exists to prevent two hard sessions on consecutive days, or a hard session on the day after the long ride. Easy days ridden too hard between hard sessions undo it in the same way.

After illness or a long break, come back on easy riding for a few days before the first hard session. Chapter 2 has my experience of how quickly it returns after a short illness, and Chapter 19 covers how much is lost in longer breaks.

What to do with it

Two hard sessions, well spaced and well ridden, are the core, and they look much the same at 4 hours and at 12. The easy riding fills the rest, and it is where extra hours go. The long ride is for long events. The season adds shape, and of all the shapes on offer only the taper has good evidence behind it. The rest is convention, which is no reason not to use it and every reason not to argue about it. B for the core of the week; C for the rest

What survives
  • Two hard sessions, well spaced and well ridden, are the core, at 4 hours a week or 12. B
  • Easy riding fills the rest, and extra hours go there. C
  • Of all the shapes a season can take, only the taper has good evidence. B

Chapter 18: Special cases

Draft · 2,747 words · 27 October 2026

Twenty-one older track athletes, with an average age of about 50, had their maximum oxygen uptake measured, and then measured again ten years later and twenty years later, when their average age was 70. Nine of them had remained at an elite level. Every group had lost fitness at each test, and the nine who had kept training hardest had lost the least [1].

For older riders, women and riders training indoors, there is less direct evidence than for the young men in most training trials.

Older riders

Pollock’s athletes were tested in three groups by what they had done over the 20 years [1]. Nine had remained elite, ten had carried on with frequent moderate-to-hard endurance training, and two had greatly reduced their training. The elite group’s VO2max fell 8% in the first decade and 15% in the second. The moderate group’s fell 13% and 14%. The two who had largely stopped lost 18% and then 34%. The authors’ summary was that older athletes’ capacities fall despite continued vigorous training, by about 8% to 15% a decade.

Their maximum heart rate fell by about 5 to 7 beats a minute per decade, and the fall was the same whether they trained or not [1]. That has a direct consequence for anyone who sets zones from a maximum. A maximum measured ten years ago is now too high by several beats, and every zone hung from it is too high with it. Chapter 6 argued for setting the top of Zone 2 from a threshold, not from a percentage of a maximum, and the argument is stronger for an older rider.

In a 2008 review of how endurance performance changes with age, Hirofumi Tanaka and Douglas Seals describe the usual pattern in masters athletes. Peak performance holds to about 35, falls modestly to between 50 and 60, and falls more steeply after that [2]. Of the three factors in Joyner and Coyle’s model, VO2max falls most and does most of the damage. The lactate threshold falls too, perhaps as a consequence. Efficiency, in trained athletes, does not change with age. The heart’s maximum output falls because both its maximum rate and its maximum stroke volume fall, and the muscle extracts less oxygen from the blood.

A large part of the decline, the authors write, appears to come from a fall in the intensity and volume of training that older athletes can do. Some of that fall is ageing itself. Some of it is that older athletes train less hard, because they have less time or less appetite for it or because they expect to recover slowly. Pollock’s elite group, who kept training hardest, lost the least. With nine people and no randomisation, though, it is impossible to say how much of that was the training and how much was the kind of person who keeps racing at seventy. B for the decline; C for how much training slows it

Recovery

Age may slow recovery, but the studies have struggled to separate it from inactivity. A 2008 review found that older participants were usually less active than younger ones, and that the exercise the studies used to cause muscle damage rarely resembled normal training [3]. A later review of masters athletes also concluded that age may slow recovery less than is often assumed, and that a sedentary life explains more of the decline in performance [4]. C A rider reading a book about training is unlikely to be leading one.

That leaves an older rider with an experiment to run on themselves. Chapter 12’s default of two hard sessions a week, at least 48 hours apart, is where to start. If the second session keeps going badly, stretch the gap to 72 hours or more, or drop to one hard session a week alongside easy riding as a practical fallback (Chapter 12). Chapter 19 covers how to judge your response. C

Lifting

Strength training matters more with age, for reasons that have little to do with speed. Pollock’s athletes lost lean mass at each test, and those who had begun lifting weights tended to keep more of it. Leg strength and bone density held up reasonably well across the group, and the ones who lifted had denser bones in their arms [1]. Chapter 14 described the consistent finding that road cyclists have low bone density in the spine, which the bike does nothing to correct. For a rider over 40 whose only exercise is cycling, heavy lifting twice a week is probably the most useful thing to add to the week, for reasons that have nothing to do with going faster. C

Is hard training safe?

For a healthy older rider, the trials are reassuring. Generation 100 assigned 1,567 Norwegians aged 70 to 77 to interval training, moderate training or the national guidelines. The interval group had the fewest deaths, although the mortality differences were not significant (Chapter 10) [s1]. In 2007 a Trondheim group gave patients with heart failure after a heart attack, average age 75.5, the same 4 × 4-minute intervals that Chapter 11 describes [s2]. Age alone is not a reason to avoid hard training, but these studies do not establish its safety for everyone. If you have a heart condition, chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness out of proportion to the effort, see a doctor before changing your training.

Women

Reading the research: who was in the study?

In 2014 a count of participants in three leading sports medicine journals found that 39% were women. A 2025 group repeated the count for 2021 to 2023 [5]. Of 1,441 studies, 268 studied only men and 103 only women. The average study’s participants were 40% women. Only 66 studies, 5.6% of those including women, took account of the menstrual cycle.

Those are general sports medicine journals, and training studies are worse. Almost every training trial in Parts II and III of this book is of men or mostly men. Chapter 11 noted that most interval trials are of men, and the few that compared the sexes directly found similar responses.

The few direct comparisons give no reason to prescribe different interval formats for women. Differences in the size of the response are less well studied. I would use the book’s advice as a starting point and judge it by your response, while recognising how much of the evidence comes from men.

What has been measured

How much training raises VO2max. The one meta-analysis I found that set out to answer this pooled eight studies of untrained people, 90 men and 85 women, who were given the same training [6]. The men’s VO2max rose more: by 191 mL/min more in absolute terms, and by 1.95 mL/kg/min more relative to body weight. There was no sign of disagreement between the studies. It is one small analysis of untrained people, and it measured VO2max alone, not threshold, efficiency or performance. In trained women, the Trondheim 4 × 4 trial found a rise in VO2max of 7.3%, much as in men. The 30/15 study in Chapter 11 found the same advantage in time near VO2max in both sexes [s3,s4]. C

Fatigue. According to a 2014 review by Sandra Hunter, women usually tire less than men in sustained, static muscle contractions at the same relative intensity. The difference depends on the task: how fast and how hard the muscle works, which muscle it is, and the conditions [7]. In 82,303 marathon runners, the women’s heart rate drifted less than the men’s relative to their pace, and the drift came later in the race [s5]. Chapter 9 called that quality durability. Whether it means women should train differently has not been tested.

The menstrual cycle. A 2020 meta-analysis of 78 studies found that performance might be trivially lower in the early follicular phase, the days around the start of a period, than at other times [8]. The pooled effect was so small that its credible interval included no effect at all. The largest contrast between any two phases was also small, and the authors rated the quality of the evidence as low. Their conclusion was that general guidelines can’t be drawn, and that women should take a personal approach, based on how they themselves respond.

That conclusion matters because a fashion has grown up around the opposite idea: that training should be scheduled around the phases of the cycle, with hard sessions in one phase and easy riding in another. The evidence doesn’t support a general rule of that kind. It does support paying attention. If hard sessions on particular days of your cycle go badly, move them, as you would for a bad night’s sleep. B that the average effect is trivial; C for anything more specific

Hormonal contraception. A meta-analysis of 42 studies found that women on the oral contraceptive pill might perform slightly worse on average than women not taking it, an effect most likely to be trivial. It also found that performance was consistent across the pill cycle [9]. Most of the studies were of moderate or low quality. The authors did not think the evidence justified general advice either way.

Eating enough. Chapter 13 described relative energy deficiency in sport, the syndrome of persistently eating less than training costs, with effects on hormones, bones and performance. It affects men as well as women [s6]. If you are losing weight on a hard training load, or your periods stop, treat it as a medical matter.

Pregnancy and menopause. Neither is covered by the research in this book, and I would not give advice on either from it. Both are matters for a doctor or a specialist in women’s sports medicine.

Indoors

Riding indoors changes the numbers more than it changes the training.

From the saddle. I was fine with the boredom. In fact I was never bored, whether I was watching Netflix or chess videos on YouTube, or listening to music. Zone 2 was my sacred decompression time, great after a busy day at work. I could think things through and solve life’s problems. I’d also enjoy the kids roaming into the pain cave to chat. They might go on the rowing machine, or we’d just catch up. Luckily, in Zone 2 it’s still easy to talk.

One study, up close: same effort, indoors and out

In 2014 a group of American researchers had cyclists ride a 40 km time trial twice, once in the laboratory and once outdoors, in random order, at the same perceived effort [10].

Aim
AimTo compare the physiological and psychological responses to cycling in the laboratory and outdoors.
Design
Design12 recreationally trained male cyclists. Two 40 km trials, one in each setting, in random order, with the same instruction to give the same perceived effort in both. Wind 2.5 metres a second outdoors and none in the laboratory; other conditions similar [10].
OutdoorsLaboratory
Average power
Average power208 W163 W
Average heart rate
Average heart rate152 bpm143 bpm
Core temperature
Core temperatureSimilarSimilar
Skin temperature
Skin temperature31.4 °C33.0 °C
Rated effort
Rated effortNo differenceNo difference
Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionOutdoor cycling lets cyclists exercise at a higher intensity at the same perceived effort, so cyclists may want to ride at a higher perceived effort indoors to get the same benefit.

At the same sense of effort, the riders produced about a fifth less power in the laboratory, and their heart rate was 9 beats lower. Their core temperature was the same in both places; their skin was warmer indoors, where nothing moved the air.

The abstract doesn’t identify the indoor bike, and a laboratory ergometer may feel different from your own bike on a smart trainer. With twelve men and one ride each, the study cannot give a universal indoor correction. It suggests that riding by feel may produce less power indoors, while matching outdoor power may feel harder. C

Heat and still air

The reason indoor riding feels hard is mostly heat. A rider outdoors makes their own wind, and the air moving over the skin carries heat away. Indoors, without a fan, it doesn’t. In a 2005 study, nine riders cycled for two hours at 33 °C with fans set to air speeds from almost nothing to 50 km/h [11]. With little or no moving air, their heat storage, body temperature and rated effort were all higher. At the speeds a rider actually rides at, the differences disappeared, and drinking more made no difference to heat storage once the air was moving. The authors’ point was that laboratory studies done in still air overstate the heat stress of riding outdoors.

Heat drives heart rate up over a long ride, the drift that Chapter 9 measured. The heart pumps less blood with each beat as the body sends more to the skin and as fluid is lost, so it beats faster to keep up [s7]. Indoors, with poor airflow, drift comes sooner and goes further. Good fans, a cool room and a drink on every long session are the remedies, and they matter more for the long easy rides than for short intervals.

Holding power, or holding heart rate

Smart trainers can hold a set power whatever the cadence, which riders call ERG mode. It makes intervals precise and recoveries genuinely easy, and Chapter 11 discussed what that does for hard sessions. For a long Zone 2 ride it means that heart rate does all the drifting. An hour in, a power that started a few beats under the ceiling may have taken heart rate over it, especially in a warm room.

Chapter 9 explained why no way of handling it is perfect late in a long ride. One is to hold power and accept the drift, setting the power 10 to 15 W under the top of the zone for long rides, the rule of thumb in Chapter 9. The other is to hold heart rate and let the power fall. That keeps the body under its threshold, but it may lower the work more than it needs to, because the threshold heart rate itself rises as you tire. I found no study of either approach indoors. Pick one, keep the room cool, and judge the ride by Chapter 19’s measures over weeks, not minutes. C

Short of time

Use Chapter 17’s four-hour week as a starting point: two hard sessions and two short easy rides. If that won’t fit, Chapter 12 suggests one hard session alongside whatever easy riding you can manage as a practical fallback. Sprints save time, but long intervals have better evidence for long efforts (Chapter 11). What matters most is what mattered in my own winter: riding regularly. C

What to do with it

For an older rider, keep the intensity, expect the numbers to fall slowly anyway, reset heart-rate zones from a recent threshold, lift for your bones, and stretch the gap between hard sessions if two leave you flat. For a woman, train as the book describes, knowing that most of the evidence comes from men and that the average effect of the cycle on performance is trivial, and track your own response if you are curious. Indoors, expect less power at the same effort, use fans, and decide whether you are holding power or heart rate on long rides. C overall: most of this chapter rests on small studies, reviews and reasoning

What survives
  • Women appear to respond to training much as men do, though far fewer have been studied. C
  • Age may slow recovery less than is often assumed. C
  • Over 40, lift twice a week for your bones. C
  • Short of time, what matters most is riding regularly. C

Chapter 19: Knowing it’s working

Draft · 2,856 words · 27 October 2026

Start with a ride you already do every week. On the same steady stretch, after the same warm-up and in similar conditions, note your power at a fixed heart rate, or your heart rate at a fixed power. Look at the average over a month. It is a practical way to follow your training without adding another test to the week.

The reason is noise. Every measure of fitness a rider can take at home moves from day to day for reasons that have nothing to do with fitness: sleep, heat, food, caffeine, a cold coming on, the calibration of a power meter. Only the last can be blamed on the manufacturer. A real change of a few per cent over a couple of months is the size that training produces in a trained rider. It is also about the size of the noise in a single reading. The practical skill is to measure something repeatable often enough that the change shows through.

Power at a fixed heart rate

A 2014 review by Martin Buchheit favoured two heart-rate measures for following training: variability recorded at rest for a few minutes, and heart rate during a fixed submaximal effort, averaged over 30 to 60 seconds [1]. A change needs to exceed measurement error before it tells you much about your fitness.

The best-tested version of the fixed effort for cyclists is the Lamberts Submaximal Cycle Test. Riders ride three short stages at fixed heart rates, and the power they produce at each is recorded, with their rated effort and how fast the heart rate falls afterwards. In 17 well-trained road cyclists who did it four times, the power in the second and third stages was highly repeatable, with a typical error of 1.3% to 4.4%. The power in the third stage tracked their performance in a 40 km time trial and a peak power test closely, with correlations of 0.91 to 0.94 [2]. A later study from the same group added heart-rate variability in the minute after the test, which was repeatable to within about 6% and also tracked performance [3].

A laboratory protocol is not the same as a stretch of road or a session on a trainer. I know of no study that has validated a rider’s own version, and it will be noisier. But the principle is the test’s own: hold the strain on the body fixed, and see what power comes out.

To do it at home:

  1. Choose a fixed heart rate a little under the top of your Zone 2, or a fixed power that sits there.
  2. Ride the same warm-up each time, and measure over the same 10 to 20 minutes of the ride: on a trainer, or on a flat road or a steady climb without junctions.
  3. Keep the conditions as similar as you can. A cool room with a fan indoors; similar weather outdoors; the same time of day; not the day after a hard session.
  4. Note the average power at the heart rate, or the average heart rate at the power, and write it down.

Heart rate moves from day to day even when nothing else has changed. Forty-four people who repeated the same submaximal running test on five consecutive days varied by about 5 beats a minute at the stage where they were most consistent, and more at easier stages [s1]. A single week’s reading carries that wobble with it.

From the saddle. My main indicator of how my training is going is the average watts I can hold while keeping my heart rate in Zone 2. My other measure is how my heart rate responds to the same interval sessions. They are close to maximal efforts for me, and when I see my maximum heart rate for a session going down, or the effort feeling easier, I ratchet the intervals up by 5 W.

Signal and noise

In this simulation, power at a fixed heart rate truly rises by 5% over twelve weeks. A typical error of 3% makes several weekly readings look like losses; even the final one is lower than the first. Reacting to each reading would lead the rider to change training that was working.

Averaging four independent readings halves their noise, from 3% to about 1.5%, making the 5% gain easier to see. That is why I suggest measuring weekly and judging monthly. C: the method is mine, built on the published error of the laboratory test

Best efforts from ordinary riding

The same logic applies to maximal efforts. A rider who races, or rides hard in groups, already produces best efforts over a range of durations without doing a test. One validation study took riders’ best 3-, 7- and 12-minute powers from their ordinary training and racing files, worked out critical power from them, and compared it with critical power measured in the laboratory [4]. The standard error was 5.2%, and the limits of agreement ran from 34 W too low to 44 W too high. A dedicated test of three all-out efforts in one session did a little better, 4.5% and −26 W to +29 W.

That makes best efforts a useful but rough measure. They track fitness when they come from rides of the same kind. They drift when the season changes what kind of rides you do: a spring of hard group rides will produce better best efforts than a winter on the trainer, whatever is happening to your fitness.

Drift on long rides

Chapter 9 described a simple test of durability: on a long ride at steady power, compare your heart rate in the last half hour with the half hour after you warmed up. The more it rises, the more you are fading. Repeated over a season, on cool days, the drift should shrink as durability improves.

The largest study of this kind is of marathon runners. In 82,303 of them, the researchers compared heart rate with pace in the last 5 km of the race against the early kilometres [5]. The third of runners whose heart rate stayed most closely coupled to their pace ran faster relative to their estimated critical speed. They finished in 217 minutes on average against 225 and 239 for the moderate and high groups. They also began to decouple later, at 33 km against 23 and 19. Adding decoupling to a model of marathon performance reduced its prediction error from 6.5% to 5.2%.

It was an observational study of runners in one kind of race. It shows that decoupling goes with performance, not that training to reduce it will make anyone faster. It does show that the measure carries information, and a rider can take it from every long ride without any extra effort. B that decoupling goes with performance; C for using it to judge training

How you feel

A 2016 systematic review collected 56 studies comparing athletes’ questionnaires about mood, stress, fatigue and soreness with objective measures such as blood markers and heart rate [6]. The two generally did not agree. The questionnaires tracked training load “with superior sensitivity and consistency”: well-being fell during heavy training and recovered when training was reduced.

Write down how you feel, how you slept and how your legs were during the hard session. Using a simple scale makes it easier to compare weeks. B

Heart-rate variability

Heart-rate variability is the variation in time between one beat and the next. At rest it is higher when the parasympathetic nervous system, which slows the heart, has more control, and it tends to fall after hard training, poor sleep or illness. Many watches and chest straps now measure it each morning, and some training plans adjust the day’s session to it: hard if the reading is normal, easy if it is low.

One study, up close: training by the morning’s heart-rate variability

In 2019 a Spanish group tested this in cyclists [7].

Aim
AimTo examine the effect on road cycling performance of prescribing training from heart-rate variability.
Design
Design17 well-trained cyclists. After a week of tests, four weeks of standardised training to establish each rider’s normal morning heart-rate variability. Then eight weeks in two groups, with tests before and after: a graded test for VO2max, peak power and the power at both ventilatory thresholds, and a 40-minute time trial [7].

After eight weeks

Authors’ conclusion
Authors’ conclusionDaily prescription from heart-rate variability could improve performance more than a traditional plan in well-trained cyclists.

The direct comparison found no significant difference between groups. As in Chapter 12, one group’s significant improvement does not establish that it beat the other. There were only 17 riders, and the authors also used magnitude-based inference to call the time-trial effect “likely beneficial”. Chapter 4 described how that method produced false positives at two to six times the rate of standard tests [s2].

The wider evidence agrees with the cautious reading. A 2021 meta-analysis of heart-rate-variability-guided training found that it improved heart-rate variability itself. Its advantages for VO2max, threshold power and endurance performance were small and not statistically significant, with effect sizes of 0.20 to 0.26 [8]. If it is better than a sensible plan, the authors concluded, it is only by a small margin.

Morning heart-rate variability is still worth having if your watch records it. A reading far below your normal, on a morning when you also feel poor, is a reason to make the day easy. Used that way it is one more input to how you feel, which is the measure with the best record. B

The watch’s VO2max

Many watches estimate VO2max from heart rate, pace or power and personal details. A 2022 meta-analysis of 14 validation studies found that devices whose estimates used exercise data were accurate on average, with a bias of almost zero. But their limits of agreement ran from about 10 mL/kg/min too low to 10 too high [9]. Devices that relied on resting data overestimated by about 2 on average, with limits from 13 too low to 17 too high.

For a rider with a measured VO2max of 50, that is an estimate anywhere from about 40 to 60. The authors’ summary was that such estimates are good enough to describe a population and not yet good enough for an individual. A change in the watch’s number from one month to the next is more likely to be a change in your recent rides than in your VO2max. A that the error for individuals is large

Reading the research: a model is not a measurement

Training software often draws a chart of fitness, fatigue and form. The idea goes back to a model that Eric Banister and his colleagues published in 1975 [s3]. Each session adds to two quantities: a fitness that builds slowly and fades slowly, and a fatigue that builds quickly and fades quickly. Performance is fitness minus fatigue. The speed at which each fades is set by a time constant, a number of days.

The chart’s curves depend on the model’s settings. In 2006 a French group fitted the model to a season of training and competition in nine elite swimmers [10]. It explained about 79% of the variation in their performances, yet the settings were highly uncertain.

The time it took fitness to fade was estimated at 38 days, but the true value could have been anywhere from 17 to 59. Fatigue’s was 19 days, from 6 to 32. The time to recover performance after training, 19 days, could have been 7 or 35. The time to peak after training stopped, 43 days, could have been 25 or 61. Some of the settings were so closely tied to each other that, in the authors’ words, it made “their interpretation worthless”. These were elite swimmers with a full season of competition results to fit the model to. A recreational rider has far fewer.

A chart using preset values assumes those settings suit you. It can show how training load has changed, including sharp jumps or falls during a break. Its estimate of your “form” on a given day depends on the assumptions, however precise the line looks. Check what the software measured and what it assumed.

When you stop

Fitness built over months fades over weeks, and how fast depends on how long it took to build.

A 2000 review of detraining by Iñigo Mujika and Sabino Padilla described two stages [11]. In the first four weeks without training, highly trained athletes quickly lose VO2max and blood volume. Their heart rate during exercise rises but does not quite make up for a smaller stroke volume. Their muscles rely more on carbohydrate, and their lactate threshold falls. In people who had trained only recently, the losses were more moderate. Over longer breaks, athletes’ VO2max kept falling but stayed above that of people who had never trained, while “recently acquired VO2max gains are completely lost” [12]. The capillaries and mitochondrial enzymes of the trained declined, and in the recently trained they went back to where they started. Chapter 2’s figure shows the same pattern in seven endurance-trained people who stopped completely for 84 days.

The same review gave the remedy, which Chapter 12 reached from the training trials. The losses “can be avoided or limited” by training less, provided the intensity is kept and the frequency is reduced only moderately. Volume can be cut a great deal [12]. For a busy spell, I would keep one hard session a week alongside whatever easy riding there is time for. As Chapter 12 explains, this is a practical inference from reduced-training studies, which did not test that exact mix. C

Coming back is quicker than building the first time, though nobody has measured how much quicker in amateur cyclists. After a short illness, my own experience, which Chapter 2 records, is that the first ride feels terrible and the legs come back within two or three rides. After a longer break, come back on easy riding for a week or two before the first hard session, and expect the first few of your weekly readings to be down. That is what they are for. B for the losses; C for the advice on returning

What to do with it

Once a week, record power at a fixed heart rate, or heart rate at a fixed power, over the same stretch of a ride in similar conditions. Judge it by the four-week average.

On every long ride, the drift between the first steady half hour and the last. Compare cool days with cool days.

Whenever they happen, the best efforts: five minutes, twenty, an hour, from rides of the same kind.

And after each hard session, a line on how it felt and how you slept.

Give the routine two or three months before judging progress. C for the routine as a whole

If they don’t move, look first at Chapter 17’s order of the week. Are the hard sessions being ridden hard enough and recovered from, and is the easy riding staying easy?

What survives
  • How you feel is the measure with the best record, so write it down. B
  • Check power at a fixed heart rate each week, and judge it by the four-week average. C
  • A watch’s VO2max and a fitness chart are estimates, not measurements.

Chapter 20: The verdict

Draft · 1,781 words · 27 October 2026

No, it isn’t just Zone 2.

For a rider on six to ten hours a week, the evidence points to two hard sessions, well spaced and ridden properly, with easy riding around them. I would put most of those easy hours near the top of Zone 2. Per hour, harder training does more; Zone 2 lets you add work without taking from the hard sessions. It has no demonstrated special advantage for fat loss or health.

What I believed, and what I found

The Introduction began with a winter of easy riding and a faster climb up Sa Calobra. It also quoted a sentence I had written for my website: that easy riding was the single most effective way to build mitochondria. The largest analysis of the question, 353 training studies, found that continuous training raised mitochondrial content by about 23% and interval training by 27%. Per hour of training, the harder kinds did far more [1]. The sentence was wrong.

Chapter 7 offered a likelier explanation for the faster climb. My hours changed little, but I went from inconsistent hard rides to four or five sessions every week. The research supports regular riding [1], and easy riding made that regularity possible for me.

The claims, graded

Zone 2 as the best way to build mitochondria. Not supported, at grade A. Per programme, steady riding builds about as much as harder riding in people who aren’t yet trained. Per hour it builds less, and in well-trained people more of it was not shown to add anything measurable [1]. Easy riding works for beginners; the evidence gives it no special advantage.

Fat burning for weight loss. Not supported, at grade B. The intensity of peak fat burning is real, and it varies from rider to rider and with what they have eaten. But the fat burned over a whole day didn’t differ between days of easy and harder exercise [s1]. A pooled analysis of 31 studies found no difference in body fat between people assigned to intervals and people assigned to steady training [2]. Weight follows the work done, not the fuel mix.

Fat burning for racing. Not supported, at grade B. Training shifts the fuel mix towards fat, and intervals do it as well as steady riding [3]. A fitter rider races faster on more carbohydrate, not less [4]. A high-fat diet raised fat burning further and left elite race walkers without the improvement their training brought the others [5]. Fat burning is a sign of fitness, not a separate thing to train.

The elite pattern. Supported, at grade C, as a description. The Olympic champions whose diaries Chapter 8 analysed spent 91% of their endurance training time below the first threshold, and about 1.3 hours a week above it [6]. What is not supported is the step from their ratio to an amateur’s week. Trials of different ways of dividing the hard work found no clear winner over 4 to 16 weeks [7,8]. The elite example is better read as evidence for a large amount of training, most of it easy, around a modest and steady dose of hard work.

Two hard sessions. Supported, at grade B. Two a week, at least 48 hours apart, builds about as much as three over a few weeks, and spacing matters as much as the count [9,10]. One hard session plus easy riding is a reasonable fallback for a busy period, an inference at grade C. The trials that worked used about 40 minutes to an hour of hard work a week, close to the champions’ own dose. That suggests to me that recovery, not ambition, sets the ceiling. That last part is my inference, at grade C.

Which sessions. Supported, at grade B. In recreational cyclists on about six hours a week, 4 × 8 minutes doubled the gain from 4 × 4 [11]. The sessions that did best let a rider pile up the most work close to the top of what they can sustain. Thirty-fifteens are a good second format. Sprints are for sprinting.

Time near VO2max as the cause of improvement. Not shown, at grade C. It is a useful yardstick for comparing sessions, but riders who reached a higher share in the study also trained more and started less fit.

Long rides and durability. Plausible, at grade C. Durability matters, it differs hugely between riders, and the comparisons point to accumulated volume. No trial in trained riders has tested whether long rides build it. Fuelling is the best-supported way to protect power late in a long ride.

Health. Zone 2 is not shown to be special, at grade C. Most of the lower risk of death in the large surveys comes with the first few hours of activity a week [12], and a rider on six to ten hours is well past it. Training lowers blood pressure and blood sugar whatever its intensity. For health, the best exercise is the one that gets done.

Lactate clearance. Not shown, at grade C. The claim that riding in Zone 2 is what trains the body to clear lactate comes from a comparison of professional athletes with less active people at one moment. That describes a very fit body without showing how it was built. The one training study I found that measured the lactate transporter directly was in 20 skiers. The transporter fell after months of mostly easy training and held steady in the group that trained near the threshold.

Copying the ratio. Not shown, at grade B. Over a few months, no consistent winner emerged from trials that gave athletes polarised, pyramidal or threshold-heavy versions of mostly easy training [7]. A rider on seven hours who rides 80% easy has about an hour and a half of hard training, close to the champions’ 1.3 hours. That is a better reason for the ratio than the ratio itself.

Years of easy volume. Unknown, at grade C. Elite records are consistent with benefits that short trials miss. No trial has run long enough to test them.

Strength and heat. Heavy leg lifting probably makes trained cyclists a little faster in efforts from a few minutes to an hour, at grade B, from small studies in a few laboratories. Deliberate heat training is not shown to make an amateur faster in normal weather: the one trial in riders like the reader found them no faster than riders who trained normally, at grade C. Both have reasons beyond speed: lifting for the bones of a rider over 40, and a week or two of warm riding before a hot event.

Building up. The rule of adding no more than 10% a week is not supported, at grade B. In its one large trial, 20.8% of runners on a slower 13-week build-up were injured against 20.3% on a standard 8-week plan [13]. Avoid sudden jumps; no trial sets a safe rate of progression for cyclists.

Zones from formulas. Not supported, at grade B. The first threshold falls anywhere from 60% to 90% of maximum heart rate in different people [14], so a zone set from a formula is a guess about where your threshold is. Chapter 6 gave better ways to find it.

What Zone 2 is for

Chapter 7’s rule is to fit as much work into an easy ride as possible without taking from the hard sessions. For a rider on these hours, I think that means riding near the top of Zone 2. It produces more work than riding lower, although no trial has compared the two at equal hours.

Zone 2 made regular riding possible for me, with a job and a family. I could do it four or five times a week without feeling worn out. That is enough reason to value it without giving it special powers over mitochondria.

I built an app, JustZone2, for my own winter training. It holds a heart rate in a zone on a smart trainer, which makes the easy part of the week easier to do and does nothing for the hard part. None of the evidence in this book depends on it, and none of the advice needs it.

What the research can’t yet tell us

Years, not weeks. Almost every training trial in this book lasted between four and sixteen weeks. Elite athletes build their engines over a decade. The most important open question for anyone who trains for a long time is whether years of easy volume build something a few months of intervals can’t. That might be a bigger and more compliant heart, more capillaries or more durability. No trial has been long enough to answer it.

Riders like the reader. Most trials are of untrained people, students or well-trained athletes. Riders with jobs, on six to ten hours a week, in their forties and fifties, are rarely studied, possibly because they have no time to be. Women are studied much less than men. Older riders are studied less than either.

The top of Zone 2 against the bottom. The book’s rule for easy riding rests on mechanism and reasoning. Nobody has assigned riders on the same hours to ride their easy hours high or low in the easy range and measured the result.

The ceiling on hard work. The dose of hard training that works seems to be similar in amateurs and champions. Whether more would work for a rider who recovered well, over months rather than weeks, hasn’t been tested.

Until those trials are run, the grades reflect the uncertainty. Ask who was studied, for how long, what was compared, and whether the claim is about a mechanism or a result.

The week, once more

Two hard sessions, at least 48 hours apart: long intervals of four to eight minutes adding up to about half an hour of hard work, and 30/15s or a controlled threshold session. Easy riding for the rest, near the top of Zone 2, a few beats under the ceiling. A long ride if your events are long. Fuel on anything over 90 minutes. Lift through the winter if you can. Ride regularly. Measure the same thing every week and judge it every month. And when the next fashion arrives, which it will, ask what it was compared with. B for the core; C for the rest
